title: Simulator-Grounded Large Language Models for Industrial Causal Reasoning: Tool-Use, Structured Injection, and Plant-Portable Retrieval for Wastewater Treatment Decision Support
comment: 20 pages, 2 figures, 8 tables. Preprint submitted to Elsevier
summary: Wastewater operators need answers grounded in how their plant's variables interact and how fast effects propagate, not in generic pretraining text, when asking causal questions such as "why is N2O rising?" or "what happens if I cut aeration by 20%?". We compare three concrete ways to ground a frozen Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct model in an architecturally interpretable wastewater simulator (CCSS-IX): a live simulator oracle (Method 1), structured parameter injection (Method 2), and a Decoupled Recall-Reasoning (DRR) retriever (Method 3). On a 198-question causal benchmark the three reach 99.5%, 79%, and 75.8%, forming a deployment ladder above the strongest retrieval-augmented baseline at 48%. The DRR retriever has 110M parameters and trains per plant in ~17 seconds; after cross-plant transfer to a biologically distinct plant it still reaches 88%, while Method 2's static table cannot transfer. On a 60-question counterfactual benchmark only Method 3 handles queries about what happens after an intervention: +16.3 pp over Method 2, paired 95% CI [+7.1, +26.4] pp, with 100% on the timescale and operating-regime categories. On the AI2 Reasoning Challenge (ARC) with an OpenBookQA fact corpus, the same selective-retrieval mechanism reaches 79% versus unconstrained Llama-3.1-8B 76% and full-injection 74%, a +3 pp out-of-domain replication that argues against a result specific to wastewater treatment. We provide the first single-simulator comparison of live tool-use, static parameter injection, and learned numerical-parameter retrieval for industrial causal question answering.

AI.tldr: They compare three ways to connect a frozen large language model to a wastewater treatment simulator and show that simulator-grounded retrieval yields highly accurate causal and counterfactual answers, transferring across plants and even to a non-wastewater QA task.
AI.motivation: Wastewater plant operators ask causal, plant-specific questions (e.g., why a gas is rising, what happens if aeration changes) that generic pretrained LLMs cannot reliably answer because they lack knowledge of each plant’s interacting variables and dynamics. The authors want a practical way to ground an LLM in a mechanistic simulator so it can reason accurately about causal and counterfactual queries in industrial settings.
AI.method: Using a frozen Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct model and the CCSS-IX wastewater simulator, they implement and compare: (1) a live simulator oracle that the model can query for on-demand simulations; (2) structured injection of simulator parameters as static tabular context; and (3) a Decoupled Recall-Reasoning (DRR) retriever: a small 110M-parameter network that learns to select and supply only the relevant numerical simulator parameters to the LLM via retrieval. They evaluate all three on causal and counterfactual benchmarks and test transfer to a new plant, plus an out-of-domain ARC/OpenBookQA setting using the same selective-retrieval mechanism.
AI.result: On a 198-question wastewater causal benchmark, the three methods reach 99.5% (live oracle), 79% (static injection), and 75.8% (DRR retriever) accuracy, all outperforming a strong RAG baseline at 48%. The DRR retriever trains per plant in ~17 seconds and, after transfer to a biologically distinct plant, still achieves 88% accuracy, whereas static injection does not transfer. On a 60-question counterfactual benchmark, only Method 3 effectively answers intervention questions, improving +16.3 percentage points over Method 2 with paired 95% CI [+7.1, +26.4] and attaining 100% in timescale and operating-regime categories. On ARC with OpenBookQA, the same selective-retrieval approach reaches 79% versus 76% for unconstrained Llama-3.1-8B and 74% for full injection, showing a +3 pp gain out of domain.
AI.conclusion: Simulator-grounded LLMs can deliver highly accurate, plant-specific causal and counterfactual reasoning if connected through appropriate mechanisms. Live simulator access gives near-perfect performance but may be expensive or impractical; static parameter dumps are less accurate and fail to transfer; and a small, learned numerical-parameter retriever offers a practical middle ground with strong accuracy, cross-plant transfer, and generalization to non-simulator tasks. The paper establishes a clear empirical comparison between live tool use, full parameter injection, and learned selective retrieval in a single industrial simulator, supporting selective retrieval as an effective and general grounding strategy.

title: Mean-Field Dynamics of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) with chain-of-thought reasoning have been widely applied in recent years, and theoretical explanations of their behavior may help deepen our understanding and guide model optimization. In this study, we introduce a framework that seeks statistical regularities and theoretical interpretations in LLM reasoning without simplifying the model architecture or making analogies to existing physical systems. We formulate LLM reasoning as a guided discovery process on a clue graph, and derive a one-dimensional ordinary differential equation for the fraction of discovered clues using the mean-field approximation. Experimentally, clue tokens are identified using the normalized surprisal of a student LLM on the outputs of a teacher LLM, and statistical regularities are obtained by averaging over many reasoning chains of thought. Our experiments show that the resulting statistical regularities are reproducible within the same dataset and can be fitted by the solving the proposed theoretical equation.

AI.tldr: They model chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs as a statistical process of discovering “clues” on a graph, derive a simple differential equation for this process using mean-field theory, and show that it matches empirical statistics of reasoning traces extracted from teacher–student LLM pairs.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought prompting works well in practice, but we lack principled theoretical models that explain how LLMs reason over multiple steps without oversimplifying architectures or relying on analogies to physics. The authors want a data-driven theoretical framework that directly captures regularities in actual reasoning traces and can guide better understanding and optimization of LLM reasoning.
AI.method:
1) Conceptually model LLM reasoning as a guided discovery process over a ‘clue graph’, where the model progressively uncovers useful intermediate pieces of information.
2) Use a mean-field approximation to derive a one-dimensional ordinary differential equation describing how the fraction of discovered clues evolves during reasoning.
3) Empirically, define ‘clue tokens’ by computing normalized surprisal from a smaller student LLM on outputs of a larger teacher LLM and flagging tokens that look especially informative.
4) Collect many chain-of-thought reasoning traces, identify their clue tokens, and average over them to obtain statistical regularities of clue discovery.
5) Fit the empirical curves of clue discovery to the solution of the derived ODE and test reproducibility across samples from the same dataset.
AI.result: They find stable statistical regularities in how clue tokens appear over time in chain-of-thought sequences, and these regularities are reproducible within a dataset. The empirical dynamics of clue discovery can be well-fitted by the solution of their derived mean-field ODE, indicating that the simple theoretical model captures key aspects of LLM reasoning behavior at a coarse-grained level.
AI.conclusion: Modeling LLM chain-of-thought reasoning as a clue-discovery process on a graph and approximating it with a low-dimensional ODE provides a compact, empirically supported description of the statistical structure of reasoning traces. This offers a new, architecture-agnostic theoretical lens on how LLMs perform multi-step reasoning and suggests that relatively simple dynamical models can capture important regularities in their behavior.

title: Universal Pathologies, Conditional Consequences: A Triple-Robustness Analysis of RAG for Multi-Hop Traceability
summary: GraphRAG underperforms vector RAG on citation precision in many reports, but where and why have remained corpus-bound. We present a triple-robustness analysis that holds the retrieval architecture fixed and varies three orthogonal axes embedder (local e5-small -> Azure text-embedding-3-small), corpus (DO-178C typed-edge requirements -> Wikipedia paragraph chains via MuSiQue), and judge (paired GPT-5.4 x GPT-4.1) across 4,440 main-matrix runs, 600 cross-corpus runs, and 1,200 paired faithfulness judgments. (C2a) Over-citation is architecturally universal: GraphRAG emits 11-15 IDs per answer at citation precision 0.12-0.23 and retrieval recall 0.68-0.87 across all three settings. (C2b) Its faithfulness consequence is corpus-conditional: in typed-edge DO-178C, GraphRAG faithfulness collapses 74%->40% across hops; on Wikipedia chains the same pipeline rises 42%->58% because over-cited paragraphs remain topically supporting. (C1) Stratum-conditional winners are corpus-conditional but embedder-robust: vanilla wins 2-hop on DO-178C, GraphRAG wins 2-hop on MuSiQue, identical under either embedder. (C3) Single-judge LLM faithfulness is fragile to retrieval state: same-judge self-kappa across embedders is 0.137 for GPT-5.4 (verdict change on 41% of items). A learned router on dense embeddings alone reaches macro-F1 0.86 on hop classification (C4). We argue triple-robustness is the minimum bar for trustworthy RAG architecture claims.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes why GraphRAG often underperforms vanilla vector RAG on citation precision, using a systematic triple-robustness framework that varies embedder, corpus, and judge while keeping retrieval architecture fixed.
AI.motivation: Reports show GraphRAG can be worse than standard vector RAG on citation precision, but existing findings are tied to specific datasets and setups. The authors want a principled, corpus-agnostic way to determine whether such performance issues are architectural (inherent to GraphRAG), corpus-dependent, or artifacts of particular embedders or LLM judges. They also seek stronger evaluation standards for RAG claims.
AI.method: They perform a large-scale experimental study (4,440 main runs, 600 cross-corpus runs, 1,200 faithfulness judgments) that holds the retrieval architecture fixed while varying three orthogonal axes: the embedding model (local e5-small vs Azure text-embedding-3-small), the corpus (typed-edge DO-178C requirements vs Wikipedia paragraph chains via MuSiQue), and the LLM judge (paired GPT-5.4 vs GPT-4.1). They measure citation precision, retrieval recall, faithfulness across reasoning hops, and self-consistency of LLM judges, and also train a dense-embedding-based router to predict hop depth.
AI.result: (C2a) GraphRAG consistently over-cites across all settings, returning 11–15 citations per answer with low citation precision (0.12–0.23) but relatively high retrieval recall (0.68–0.87), showing this behavior is architectural rather than corpus-specific. (C2b) The impact on faithfulness depends on corpus structure: on typed-edge DO-178C, GraphRAG faithfulness degrades sharply from 74% to 40% over hops, while on Wikipedia paragraph chains it improves from 42% to 58% because extra citations remain topically relevant. (C1) Which architecture wins at different reasoning hops depends on corpus but is robust to the choice of embedding model: vanilla RAG wins 2-hop on DO-178C, GraphRAG wins 2-hop on MuSiQue, regardless of the embedder used. (C3) Single-judge LLM faithfulness evaluation is unstable across retrieval states: GPT-5.4’s self-kappa across embedders is only 0.137, with 41% verdict changes. (C4) A router trained on dense embeddings alone can classify hop depth with macro-F1 of 0.86.
AI.conclusion: GraphRAG’s tendency to over-cite is an inherent architectural property, but whether this harms or helps faithfulness depends strongly on corpus structure. Performance comparisons between RAG architectures are corpus-conditional yet largely robust to the choice of embedding model, while LLM-based faithfulness judgments are fragile to changes in retrieval. The authors propose that any trustworthy claim about RAG architectures should satisfy a “triple-robustness” standard: it must hold across variations in embedder, corpus, and judge, rather than being demonstrated on a single fixed stack.

title: RIG-RoPE: Relation- and Instance-Gated Rotary Positional Encoding with Duration-Aware Temporal Coordinates
summary:
Rotary positional encoding (RoPE) is a core component of modern language models and has been extended to multimodal LLMs through multidimensional variants such as multimodal RoPE (M-RoPE), which split positional channels into temporal, height, and width subspaces. This report identifies two limitations of static multidimensional position assignment in interleaved multimodal contexts. First, height/width rotations may be applied to token pairs whose spatial displacement is not a well-defined geometric object, producing cross-modal and inter-instance spatial interference. Second, temporal coordinates are often treated as equal-step counters, so a text token, an image block, and a video segment can advance the temporal phase by comparable amounts despite different information density.
  We propose RIG-RoPE, a relation- and instance-gated RoPE mechanism with duration-aware temporal coordinates. RIG-RoPE augments each token with a modality indicator, a visual instance identifier, and a scalar information-duration coordinate. It enables H/W rotations only for query-key pairs from the same visual instance; otherwise the unknown spatial displacement is marginalized rather than set to zero. Temporal rotations use interpolated cumulative block durations: text tokens consume unit duration, images use a dimension-aware logarithmic spatial scale, and videos further apply a logarithmic temporal extension over effective frames. We provide a gauge-invariance argument for avoiding ordinary cross-instance spatial rotation, an impossibility result for static IDs under shared H/W subspaces, and a duration-consistency argument against equal-step multimodal time. RIG-RoPE adds no learned parameters and can be implemented inside tiled attention kernels with constant additional metadata per token. This preliminary report establishes the formulation and validation path without claiming empirical superiority.

AI.tldr: They identify flaws in existing multidimensional RoPE for multimodal LLMs and propose RIG-RoPE, which gates spatial rotations by instance and makes temporal positions duration-aware, all without adding parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing multidimensional RoPE variants for multimodal LLMs statically assign spatial and temporal positions. This causes cross-modal and cross-instance spatial interference (e.g., mixing unrelated image regions or text with images) and treats time steps from different modalities as equally spaced despite differing information density. There is no principled handling of unknown spatial relations or duration differences.
AI.method: They introduce RIG-RoPE, which augments each token with: (1) a modality indicator (text, image, video, etc.), (2) a visual instance ID (which image or video it belongs to), and (3) a scalar information-duration coordinate. Height/width rotations in RoPE are applied only to query-key pairs that share the same visual instance ID; otherwise spatial rotation is marginalized out instead of set to zero. Temporal coordinates are computed via interpolated cumulative durations: text tokens get unit duration; images get a duration based on a logarithmic function of spatial dimensions; videos extend this with a logarithmic factor based on effective frame count. They also provide theoretical arguments: gauge invariance to justify avoiding cross-instance rotations, an impossibility result for using static IDs in shared H/W subspaces, and a consistency argument for duration-aware time. Implementation fits into tiled attention with constant-size per-token metadata and no new learned parameters.
AI.result: They formulate RIG-RoPE conceptually and mathematically, and outline how it integrates into existing attention kernels. They present theoretical justifications for their design choices (gauge invariance, impossibility of static IDs, duration consistency). However, they do not claim or provide empirical performance gains at this stage; results focus on the conceptual framework and validation plan.
AI.conclusion: Static multidimensional RoPE causes fundamental issues in multimodal, interleaved sequences due to ill-defined cross-instance spatial relations and inconsistent temporal scaling across modalities. RIG-RoPE addresses this by gating spatial rotations by visual instance and by using duration-aware temporal coordinates, all without increasing parameter count. The report is preliminary, emphasizing formulation, theoretical justification, and implementation feasibility rather than empirical superiority.

title: Agentic Nesting: A New Methodology for Existing Enterprise Application Integration and Services
summary: Enterprise operations extensively rely on multiple heterogeneous business systems and information applications, which also result in severe data silos and process fragmentation. Enterprises have invested considerable financial and material resources in building these applications, however, effectively leveraging and orchestrating them remains a formidable challenge. Conventional approaches to enterprise application integration, encompassing middleware architectures such as Enterprise Service Bus (ESB), API gateway infrastructures, and Robotic Process Automation (RPA), suffer from inherent limitations like high architectural coupling, escalating operation and maintenance costs, and limited intelligence capabilities. This paper proposes Agentic Nesting, a multi-agent collaboration framework in which existing enterprise applications are encapsulated as autonomous AI agents within a hierarchically nested structure. Rather than flat interconnection, agents are organized into layered stewardship topologies that mirror the compositional complexity of enterprise ecosystems. The framework extracts a digital agent proxy from each legacy application to enable natural-language interaction and autonomous manipulation, coordinates multiple agents through a central orchestrator for task decomposition and dynamic dispatching, and exposes a unified conversational interface for cross-application querying and process orchestration. The main contributions of this paper are the proposition of the "Application-as-Agent" integration paradigm and the "Conversation-as-Integration" interaction philosophy, together with an exploration of the generalization potential of this methodology in scenarios encompassing heterogeneous system coordination, and large-scale data applications.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new way to integrate enterprise applications by wrapping each legacy system as an AI agent and coordinating them via natural-language conversations instead of traditional tightly coupled middleware.
AI.motivation: Enterprises run many heterogeneous business systems that create data silos and fragmented processes. Traditional integration approaches such as ESB, API gateways, and RPA are costly, tightly coupled, and lack intelligence. There is a need for a more flexible, intelligent, and lower-maintenance way to orchestrate these existing investments without rebuilding them.
AI.method: The authors design an "Agentic Nesting" framework where each existing application is encapsulated as an autonomous AI agent with a digital proxy capable of natural-language interaction and autonomous operation. Agents are organized in hierarchical, layered stewardship structures that reflect real enterprise complexity rather than a flat network. A central orchestrator performs task decomposition and dynamic dispatch across agents, and a unified conversational interface allows users to query and orchestrate processes across applications using natural language.
AI.result: The framework establishes a new integration paradigm, "Application-as-Agent," and an interaction philosophy, "Conversation-as-Integration." It demonstrates that multiple heterogeneous systems can be coordinated and large-scale data applications can be supported through multi-agent collaboration and natural-language interfaces instead of classical middleware-heavy integration. Details such as benchmarks or empirical evaluations are not specified in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Treating legacy applications as AI agents within a hierarchically nested multi-agent framework, coordinated via natural-language conversations, can reduce coupling and improve flexibility and intelligence in enterprise integration. The approach shows potential generalization to broader heterogeneous system coordination and large-scale data scenarios, offering an alternative to traditional ESB, API gateway, and RPA-based integration architectures.

title: Beyond Sentiment: Comparing Traditional NLP and LLM-Based Multi-Dimensional Analysis for Political News Evaluation
comment: Accepted at PoliticalNLP 2026, the 3rd Workshop on Natural Language Processing for Political Sciences, co-located with LREC 2026. 10 pages, 3 figures
summary: Traditional sentiment analysis (SA) models, while effective for polarity classification, provide limited insight into the rhetorical, ideological, and framing dimensions of political discourse -- dimensions that are central to research in the social sciences and humanities (SSH). In this paper, we present a comparative study of RoBERTa-based sentiment analysis and an LLM-based multi-dimensional framing analysis platform applied to a corpus of 50 political news articles from 17 international media outlets. The results reveal a critical limitation we term neutral collapse: RoBERTa classifies 70% of articles as neutral, effectively flattening substantively rich political content into an analytically uninformative category. We find that 23% of neutral-classified articles exhibit negative probability scores above 0.30. By contrast, the LLM-based approach captures political bias direction and intensity, sensationalism, emotional appeal, and political framing -- yielding multi-dimensional analytical outputs aligned with SSH epistemologies. We argue that for political media analysis, traditional SA alone is insufficient, and that LLM-based multi-dimensional frameworks offer a more epistemologically adequate computational lens for SSH research needs.

AI.tldr: The paper compares traditional RoBERTa-based sentiment analysis with an LLM-based multi-dimensional framing analysis on political news, showing that standard sentiment models suffer from 'neutral collapse' and are epistemologically insufficient for social science and humanities research.
AI.motivation: Traditional sentiment analysis focuses on simple polarity (positive, negative, neutral) and misses crucial rhetorical, ideological, and framing aspects of political discourse, which are central to research in the social sciences and humanities. The authors want to evaluate whether these standard tools are adequate for political media analysis and explore richer, LLM-based alternatives.
AI.method: They apply (1) a RoBERTa-based sentiment classifier and (2) an LLM-based multi-dimensional framing analysis platform to a corpus of 50 political news articles from 17 international media outlets. They then compare the outputs, focusing on sentiment distributions, probability scores, and the ability to capture dimensions like bias, sensationalism, emotional appeal, and political framing.
AI.result: RoBERTa labels 70% of the articles as neutral, leading to what the authors call 'neutral collapse', where rich political content is flattened into an uninformative neutral category. Among those neutral-labeled texts, 23% actually have negative sentiment probabilities above 0.30, suggesting under-detected negativity. In contrast, the LLM-based approach extracts multiple dimensions—bias direction and intensity, sensationalism, emotional appeal, and framing—producing detailed analyses more consistent with SSH research needs.
AI.conclusion: For analyzing political media, traditional sentiment analysis is inadequate because it compresses complex discourse into overly simple categories and suffers from neutral collapse. LLM-based multi-dimensional framing frameworks provide richer, epistemologically grounded analyses that better align with the needs of social science and humanities scholars.

title: The Ignition Index: Measuring Global Workspace Dynamics in Language Models
summary: We introduce the Ignition Index (I), a validated scalar metric that operationalizes Global Workspace Theory's (GWT) all-or-none ignition prediction in transformer language models. The metric fits a four-parameter sigmoid to per-layer linear probe accuracy as a function of input signal strength, extracting steepness parameter beta-hat: high values indicate abrupt, ignition-like transitions; low values indicate graded build-up. Across 11 models spanning five architecture families, shuffled-label controls demonstrate 9.6-fold selectivity for genuine linguistic structure over spurious probe capacity (p < 0.001, Mann-Whitney U-test). We find: (1) Feedforward transformers exceed SSMs by 89% in aggregate beta-hat (p < 1e-13, Cohen's d = 0.52), with Mamba exhibiting near-linear profiles consistent with absent global broadcast. (2) Huginn-3.5B exhibits 2.12-fold higher ignition along its iteration axis than its depth axis, demonstrating that recurrent architectures manifest workspace-like transitions along the recurrence dimension. (3) Pythia-410M shows a PELT-detected phase transition at training step 256 (+67%), preceding induction-head formation. (4) Hypotheses linking ignition to model scale and signal strength were not confirmed, suggesting transformer architectures may saturate available ignition mechanisms. The Ignition Index provides the first validated quantitative bridge between GWT's dynamical predictions and mechanistic interpretability, with 9.6-fold measurement selectivity and architecture-level discriminability not previously characterized in the scaling literature. Code: https://github.com/saman-rahbar/ignition-index

AI.tldr: Defines and validates an Ignition Index to quantify abrupt, all-or-none “ignition” dynamics predicted by Global Workspace Theory (GWT) in transformer language models, showing strong selectivity for true linguistic structure and clear differences across architectures and training.
AI.motivation: Global Workspace Theory posits an all-or-none ignition process for conscious access, but this prediction lacks a concrete, quantitative operationalization in modern language models. Mechanistic interpretability has many tools, yet none directly map GWT’s dynamical notions (like global broadcast/ignition) onto measurable properties of deep networks. The authors aim to build a rigorous, validated metric that can test GWT-style ignition in transformers and compare architectures, training dynamics, and scaling behavior in a unified way.
AI.method: They define the Ignition Index by fitting a four-parameter sigmoid to per-layer linear probe accuracy as a function of input signal strength, and use the fitted steepness parameter (beta-hat) as the index: high beta-hat means sharp, ignition-like transitions; low beta-hat indicates gradual build-up. They compute this metric across 11 language models from five architecture families, use shuffled-label controls to check that the effect reflects true linguistic structure, and perform statistical comparisons (e.g., Mann-Whitney U, Cohen’s d). They also analyze specific models for architectural (feedforward vs SSMs, recurrence vs depth) and training-dynamics effects (phase transitions via PELT, relation to induction heads and scale).
AI.result: The Ignition Index shows a 9.6× higher sensitivity to genuine linguistic structure than to spurious probe capacity in shuffled-label controls (p < 0.001). Feedforward transformers have substantially higher aggregate beta-hat (89% higher) than state-space models, with Mamba displaying almost linear, non-ignition-like profiles suggesting absent global broadcast. In Huginn-3.5B, ignition is more than twice as strong along the recurrent iteration dimension than along depth, indicating that recurrent passes can serve as the workspace axis. In Pythia-410M, a statistically detected phase transition in ignition appears early in training (step 256, +67%), before induction heads arise. Hypotheses that ignition would monotonically increase with model scale and with input signal strength are not borne out, suggesting a saturation of ignition mechanisms in standard transformers.
AI.conclusion: The Ignition Index is a validated, quantitative measure that operationalizes GWT’s ignition prediction within transformer language models, providing a statistically rigorous bridge between cognitive theory and mechanistic interpretability. It reveals architecture-dependent ignition signatures, distinguishes transformers from SSMs, captures training-time phase transitions, and challenges simple scaling and signal-strength hypotheses. This metric opens a path to systematically study workspace-like dynamics in artificial networks and compare them across model families and training regimes.

title: Scaffold-Mediated Post-Training: Co-Evolving Model Parameters and Procedural Scaffold Graphs
summary: Post-training of large language models optimizes only parameters, while inference-time procedural scaffolds are typically designed independently of parameter training. This disconnect makes it difficult to automatically acquire and internalize complex strategies. We propose scaffold-mediated post-training: procedural scaffolds are organized into an evolvable graph structure that co-evolves with model parameters through discovery, distillation, and dynamic recompilation. We instantiate this paradigm as Skill Training. On FeatureBench, automatically discovered skills improve the passed rate by 8.1pp, and after progressive distillation the model still achieves a 27.7% passed rate without any external scaffold (distillation retention rate 85.2%, defined as post-distillation / with-skill passed rate), significantly outperforming standard SFT on the same data.

AI.tldr: They propose a new post-training framework that jointly evolves LLM parameters and their inference-time scaffolds, leading to better strategy acquisition and strong distilled performance without scaffolds.
AI.motivation: Existing post-training tunes only model weights, while inference-time scaffolds (like tools, planners, or multi-step wrappers) are hand-designed and decoupled from training, making it hard for models to automatically learn and internalize complex reasoning or problem-solving strategies that emerge from these procedures.
AI.method: Introduce scaffold-mediated post-training, where procedural scaffolds are represented as an evolvable graph that co-evolves with model parameters via three stages: (1) discovery of useful scaffolded behaviors/skills, (2) distillation of these behaviors into the base model so it can perform them without scaffolds, and (3) dynamic recompilation, which updates and reorganizes the scaffold graph as training proceeds. They instantiate this paradigm in a system called Skill Training and evaluate it on FeatureBench.
AI.result: On FeatureBench, the automatically discovered skills with scaffolds raise the pass rate by 8.1 percentage points over the base setting. After progressively distilling these skills into the model so it no longer needs external scaffolds, the model still reaches a 27.7% pass rate, retaining 85.2% of the with-scaffold performance and clearly beating standard supervised fine-tuning on the same data.
AI.conclusion: Jointly evolving scaffolds and model parameters allows LLMs to better acquire complex strategies and then internalize them, reducing dependence on external procedures. The Skill Training instantiation demonstrates that scaffold-mediated post-training can significantly outperform conventional SFT while preserving most of the gains even after removing the scaffolds.

title: Woodpecker Distillation: Weak Models Diagnose Reasoning Bugs in Strong Models
summary:
Large language models often fail on reasoning tasks despite possessing the capability to solve them. We argue that many such failures arise from localized reasoning bugs in intermediate steps rather than from global incompetence. We show that these bugs are frequently repairable: inserting a short patch generated by a weak probe model after the same strong-model reasoning prefix can redirect the trajectory toward a correct solution.
  However, this corrective effect is not reliably internalized by directly fine-tuning on weak patches or repaired trajectories, suggesting that the useful signal lies not in the intervention text itself, but in how it reshapes the model's future reasoning distribution. We therefore propose Woodpecker Distillation, a weak-to-strong training framework that learns from contrastive local interventions. Our method contrasts successful and unsuccessful weak-model patches at the same prefix, constructs a corrective teacher distribution from their induced future token predictions, and distills this signal into the strong model.
  Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that Woodpecker Distillation consistently improves strong-model performance and outperforms direct imitation baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Woodpecker Distillation, a weak-to-strong training method that uses small corrective patches from a weak model to improve a strong model’s reasoning, especially on math tasks.
AI.motivation: Large language models often fail on reasoning problems not because they completely lack the ability, but due to localized bugs in intermediate steps. Simple interventions can sometimes fix these trajectories, but existing fine-tuning methods that imitate these fixes don’t reliably internalize the improvement. The authors want a principled way to turn these local corrections into lasting gains in reasoning performance.
AI.method: 1) Use a strong model to generate a partial reasoning prefix on a task. 2) Have a weak probe model propose different short patches at that prefix. 3) Identify which weak patches lead the strong model to a correct final answer (successful) vs. an incorrect one (unsuccessful). 4) For the same prefix, compare the future token distributions induced by successful vs. unsuccessful patches and construct a contrastive ‘corrective’ teacher distribution. 5) Distill this contrastive signal into the strong model so it learns, at that prefix, to favor the future distribution associated with successful patches without directly imitating the patch text itself.
AI.result: On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, training with Woodpecker Distillation improves the strong model’s performance compared to its original capabilities and outperforms baselines that directly imitate weak patches or fully repaired trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Local, weak-model interventions can reliably repair strong-model reasoning, but the main value lies in how they reshape the model’s future reasoning, not in the specific text of the patch. By distilling contrastive signals from successful vs. unsuccessful patches at the same prefix, Woodpecker Distillation effectively improves strong-model reasoning, demonstrating a promising weak-to-strong training paradigm.

title: Large Language Models Threaten Double-blind Review
summary: Double blind peer review serves as the scientific community primary defense against status and affiliation bias. Its effectiveness rests on the assumption that anonymized manuscripts convey scientific merit without revealing their authors. While authorship can often be recovered using citation networks or stylistic markers, we show that this assumption is increasingly fragile in the presence of large language models (LLMs). Using only titles and abstracts from papers published after model training, we find that LLMs collapse anonymity more efficiently than humans, with belief concentrating onto a small subset of plausible authors drawn from pools of five domain expert candidates. This vulnerability persists even when stylistic and bibliographic cues are excluded, indicating that stable patterns in problem framing and research focus function as latent conceptual signatures of authorship. Together, these findings indicate that double blind review is vulnerable to automated semantic inference, necessitating a revaluation of how anonymity and fairness are maintained in an AI augmented research ecosystem.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that large language models can often infer paper authorship from anonymized titles and abstracts, weakening the anonymity assumed in double blind peer review.
AI.motivation: Double blind peer review aims to reduce status and affiliation bias by hiding author identities, but this protection assumes that manuscripts do not reveal their authors. With powerful LLMs capable of sophisticated pattern recognition, it is unclear whether anonymized text remains effectively anonymous.
AI.method: The authors use only titles and abstracts from papers that appeared after the LLMs’ training cutoff and ask models to guess the author from pools of five domain experts. They compare LLM performance to humans and run variants that strip out stylistic and bibliographic cues to test what signals the models rely on.
AI.result: LLMs are substantially better than humans at narrowing down likely authors: their probability mass concentrates on a small subset of candidates in the five-expert pools. This de-anonymization ability remains strong even after removing stylistic and bibliographic markers, implying that other stable patterns are being used.
AI.conclusion: Double blind review can be compromised by automated semantic inference from LLMs, because stable patterns in problem framing and research focus act as latent conceptual signatures of authors. The paper argues that peer review practices need to be rethought to preserve anonymity and fairness in an AI-augmented research environment.

title: From Continuous Predictors to Clinical Thresholds: Early Evidence on Performance Trade-offs of Guideline-Based Categorisation for Ischaemic Stroke Outcome Prediction
summary: Machine learning models achieve strong predictive accuracy for 90-day outcome prediction in acute ischaemic stroke, yet clinical adoption is limited by the misalignment of model explanations with clinicians' reasoning. Motivated by a clinician user study calling for clinical guideline-aligned cut-offs, we ask whether continuous predictors can be replaced by clinically informed categorical encodings without sacrificing performance. On a multi-centre European registry stratified into three treatment cohorts, we compare standard and fully categorised gradient-boosted models, the latter using stroke guideline-aligned, treatment-specific thresholds. The fully categorised models are statistically indistinguishable from their continuous counterparts in two of the treatment cohorts, with a significant drop in predictive accuracy in one cohort. Global feature importance rankings remain consistent, suggesting that discretising continuous predictors into guideline-based categories preserves the core hierarchy of prognostic factors across all treatment groups. Guideline-based categorisation is thus a viable design choice for stroke-outcome models.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether replacing continuous clinical predictors with guideline-based categorical encodings in stroke outcome prediction models preserves performance and interpretability.
AI.motivation: Clinicians struggle to trust and adopt machine learning stroke outcome models because their explanations don’t align with guideline-based clinical reasoning, especially around standard clinical cut-offs.
AI.method: Using a multi-centre European acute ischaemic stroke registry split into three treatment cohorts, the authors train gradient-boosted models with either standard continuous predictors or fully categorised predictors based on stroke-guideline, treatment-specific thresholds, and compare predictive accuracy and feature importance rankings.
AI.result: In two treatment cohorts, the fully categorised models perform statistically on par with continuous-feature models; in one cohort, there is a significant performance drop, but feature importance rankings remain globally consistent across all cohorts.
AI.conclusion: Encoding predictors using guideline-aligned categorical cut-offs generally preserves model performance and the hierarchy of prognostic factors, making guideline-based categorisation a practical and interpretable design choice for clinical stroke outcome models, although performance may degrade in some subgroups.

title: Safe Evolution with Circuit Anchors
summary: In biological evolution, unconstrained mutation can lead to catastrophic outcomes: organisms may evolve enhanced capabilities while losing essential functions for survival. Nature's solution is \textit{developmental constraints}, where core regulatory genes remain anchored while peripheral genes adapt freely. We observe that current self-evolution algorithms for large language models lack analogous constraints. They optimize purely for capability, implicitly assuming safety will be preserved. Our experiments reveal this assumption to be dangerously wrong: models can \textit{misevolve} into powerful yet dangerous entities. Inspired by how Hox genes anchor body structure across $500$ million years of evolution, we propose \textbf{Circuit-Anchored Evolution (CAE)}. Using mechanistic interpretability, we identify a tiny \textit{safety circuit}, comprising less than $2$\% of model features, that causally mediates safety behaviors. We anchor this circuit during evolution, constraining it within a small displacement bound while allowing the remaining features to evolve freely. This mirrors the biological principle of \textit{evolvability with constraint}: preserving what is essential while adapting what is peripheral. Experiments across $3$ model families and two evolution algorithms demonstrate that CAE achieves superior safety preservation with minimal capability loss, substantially outperforming explicit reward-based constraints in both effectiveness and efficiency. Just as developmental constraints prevent biological evolution from producing nonviable organisms, circuit anchoring prevents model evolution from producing capable but dangerous systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Circuit-Anchored Evolution (CAE), a method that anchors a small, interpretable safety circuit in language models during self-evolution to prevent dangerous behaviors while preserving capabilities.
AI.motivation: Self-evolution algorithms for large language models currently optimize only for increased capability, assuming safety properties will remain intact. The authors find that this assumption fails: models can misevolve into highly capable but unsafe systems. They look to biological evolution, where developmental constraints preserve essential functions, as inspiration to design constraints that retain safety during model evolution.
AI.method: Using mechanistic interpretability, the authors identify a small safety-related circuit—less than 2% of model features—that causally governs safety behaviors. During self-evolution of the model, they anchor the parameters associated with this circuit, constraining them to stay within a small displacement bound, while allowing the rest of the model’s features to update freely. They then test this Circuit-Anchored Evolution (CAE) approach across three different model families and two different self-evolution algorithms, comparing it with standard reward-based safety constraints.
AI.result: CAE significantly improves the preservation of safety behaviors during self-evolution while incurring only minimal losses in task capability. Across all tested model families and evolution algorithms, CAE outperforms explicit reward-based safety constraints, both in how effectively it maintains safety and in the efficiency with which it does so.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring a mechanistically identified safety circuit during model evolution provides an effective way to avoid unsafe misevolution: models can continue to improve their capabilities while retaining crucial safety behaviors. This mirrors biological developmental constraints that preserve essential functions during evolution, suggesting that structurally grounded constraints are more robust and efficient than purely reward-based approaches for safe model self-improvement.

title: SkillTrace: Multi-Trace Provenance Auditing for LLM-Agent Skill Reuse
summary: LLM-agent ecosystems are rapidly growing around reusable skills: mixed-modality packages of metadata, natural-language instructions, code, tools, references, and operational workflows. As skills become marketplace artifacts, auditing their reuse is no longer the same problem as ordinary code clone detection. Existing detectors target single-modality source code or whole-package similarity, yet skill reuse evidence is distributed across authored text, implementation fragments, and operational structure. As a result, they can miss reuse that preserves only one part of a skill. We present SKILLTRACE, a multi-trace provenance auditing framework for LLM-agent skill reuse. SKILLTRACE extracts three provenance traces: Expression, Implementation, and Operational. It represents the Operational Trace as a Skill Operational Graph (SOG) that captures activation, procedure, and resource-flow structure. An LLM assists only the Operational-trace extraction, once at ingestion; at audit time SKILLTRACE compares cached traces deterministically, calibrates each trace against same-function strict negatives, and reports which trace supports a reuse decision. On SKILLTRACE-BENCH, with 820 transformed reuse positives over 100 marketplace anchors and 751 negative controls, SKILLTRACE achieves AUROC 0.938 and F1 0.898. A 36,446-skill wild audit further shows that trace-attributed evidence surfaces actionable reuse review queues beyond repository-level baselines.

AI.tldr: Introduces SKILLTRACE, a multi-trace provenance auditing framework to detect and analyze reuse of LLM-agent skills across text, code, and operational workflows.
AI.motivation: As LLM-agent skills become marketplace artifacts, detecting reuse is harder than traditional code clone detection because evidence of reuse can appear separately in natural-language descriptions, code fragments, or workflow structure. Existing techniques that focus on single-modality code or overall package similarity fail when only one aspect of a skill is reused. A new auditing framework is needed to handle these multi-modal, partially preserved reuses in agent skill ecosystems.
AI.method: The paper proposes SKILLTRACE, which models skill provenance through three complementary traces: (1) Expression Trace, capturing authored text such as descriptions and instructions; (2) Implementation Trace, capturing code and implementation fragments; and (3) Operational Trace, represented as a Skill Operational Graph (SOG) that encodes activation patterns, procedures, and resource-flow between components. An LLM is used only once at ingestion time to assist with extracting the Operational Trace and building the SOG. During auditing, SKILLTRACE compares precomputed traces deterministically against candidate skills, calibrating each trace type using strict negative examples of skills with the same functionality to reduce false positives. The system then reports which specific trace(s) provide evidence of reuse for each candidate pair.
AI.result: On the SKILLTRACE-BENCH dataset—comprising 820 positive reuse instances derived via transformations of 100 marketplace anchor skills and 751 negative control examples—SKILLTRACE achieves an AUROC of 0.938 and an F1 score of 0.898, indicating strong discrimination between reused and non-reused skills. In a large-scale audit of 36,446 marketplace skills, SKILLTRACE’s trace-attributed evidence is shown to generate more actionable and focused reuse-review queues than simpler repository-level similarity baselines.
AI.conclusion: SKILLTRACE demonstrates that multi-trace, multi-modality provenance analysis is effective for auditing reuse of LLM-agent skills, outperforming traditional code- or package-level similarity approaches. By separating expression, implementation, and operational traces and attributing reuse decisions to specific evidence types, the framework can surface nuanced reuse relationships and prioritize them for human review at marketplace scale. This suggests a practical path toward transparent, auditable reuse in complex LLM-agent ecosystems.

title: SemiAdapt-Instruct: Extensible Instruction Tuning via Latent Domain-Specialised Adapters
summary: Instruction-tuned LLMs are deployed into environments where domains evolve, yet extending a fine-tuned model's capabilities without full retraining remains an unsolved practical challenge. We present SemiAdapt-Instruct, a modular framework that discovers latent instruction domains, trains per-domain LoRA adapters in parallel, and performs parameter-free routing, incorporating new domains via single-adapter training without modifying existing components. SemiAdapt-Instruct outperforms full model fine-tuning across all configurations on both ROUGE-L and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, while matching single LoRA fine-tuning and delivering extensibility that monolithic approaches cannot provide. We empirically demonstrate this extensibility by showing that updating a single adapter with new domain data outperforms all monolithic baselines. Our study also finds that independent discovery methods converge on the same specialisation-friendly domains. These findings demonstrate that decomposing heterogeneous instruction data into latent domains enables extensible NLP systems where evolving domains require only targeted single-adapter updates, eliminating the need for full model retraining.

AI.tldr: SemiAdapt-Instruct is a modular, extensible way to adapt instruction-tuned LLMs by discovering latent domains and training separate LoRA adapters per domain, with parameter-free routing, avoiding repeated full-model retraining.
AI.motivation: Instruction-tuned LLMs operate in environments where domains and user needs evolve over time. Fully retraining or repeatedly fine-tuning large models for every new domain is computationally expensive, inflexible, and hard to scale. There is a need for a practical approach that allows extending an instruction-tuned model to new domains without degrading existing capabilities or requiring full retraining.
AI.method: The paper proposes SemiAdapt-Instruct, a framework that: (1) automatically discovers latent instruction domains within heterogeneous instruction data; (2) trains LoRA adapters independently and in parallel for each discovered domain, keeping the base model fixed; and (3) performs parameter-free routing at inference time to select which domain adapter to use. New domains can be added by training a single new adapter on new domain data, without touching or retraining existing adapters or the base model.
AI.result: SemiAdapt-Instruct outperforms full-model fine-tuning across all tested setups on ROUGE-L and LLM-as-a-judge metrics, while achieving performance comparable to standard single-LoRA fine-tuning. It further provides extensibility: when new domain data arrives, updating only a single adapter leads to better performance than any monolithic (single-model) baseline. The experiments also show that different domain discovery methods independently converge to similar, specialization-friendly domain partitions.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing heterogeneous instruction data into latent domains and training domain-specific LoRA adapters enables an extensible adaptation strategy for instruction-tuned LLMs. This modular design allows updating capabilities for evolving domains by retraining only targeted adapters, avoiding full model retraining and maintaining or improving performance compared to monolithic fine-tuning approaches.

title: Abstract Event Causal Rules: Induction and Application
summary: Event-centric intelligent analytical systems heavily depend on explicit causal event knowledge for risk early warning, decision-making support and narrative comprehension. Nevertheless, existing instance-level causal pairs suffer severe generalization deficits on low-frequency long-tail and unseen event combinations. To address this limitation, this work proposes Abstract Event Causal Rule (AECR), a novel relation-level causal abstraction paradigm that transforms concrete cause-effect pairs into generalized abstract causal logic while retaining their intrinsic causal relationships. We design a multi-agent Concrete-to-Abstract Causal Induction (CACI) system coupled with similarity-constrained clustering to distill trustworthy AECRs from noisy raw causal data, based on which two complete AECR knowledge bases are built. To validate the practical utility of abstract causal knowledge, we propose an Abstract Rule-Guided Causal Attention Encoder (AR-GCAE), which injects the retrieved AECRs into the causality Graph Event Prediction (CGEP) benchmark task via rule-guided attention layers and gated representation fusion. Quantitative experimental results reveal that applying AECRs substantially strengthens the generalization capacity of event causal reasoning and brings consistent performance improvements to event prediction, with the most prominent gains observed on rare and unseen event samples.

AI.tldr: They propose a way to generalize specific causal event pairs into abstract causal rules and show these rules improve event prediction, especially for rare and unseen events.
AI.motivation: Event-based AI systems (for early warning, decisions, narratives) need causal knowledge between events. Existing resources mainly store instance-level cause-effect pairs, which fail to generalize to low-frequency, long-tail, or unseen event combinations. The authors want a more abstract, relation-level causal representation that captures reusable causal logic and works better for rare events.
AI.method: 1) Define Abstract Event Causal Rules (AECRs), which convert concrete event pairs into generalized causal logic while preserving causality. 2) Build a multi-agent Concrete-to-Abstract Causal Induction (CACI) system, augmented with similarity-constrained clustering, to mine reliable AECRs from noisy raw causal data and construct two AECR knowledge bases. 3) Design an Abstract Rule-Guided Causal Attention Encoder (AR-GCAE) that retrieves relevant AECRs and incorporates them into the Causality Graph Event Prediction (CGEP) task through rule-guided attention layers and gated fusion of rule-based and event representations.
AI.result: The system successfully builds two complete AECR knowledge bases from raw causal data. When these abstract rules are integrated into the CGEP benchmark via AR-GCAE, event prediction performance improves across the board. The gains are especially notable for rare and unseen events, indicating enhanced generalization in event causal reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Abstracting from instance-level causal pairs to relation-level AECRs and injecting them into event prediction models boosts generalization and prediction accuracy, particularly on long-tail and unseen event cases. Abstract causal rules are therefore a practical and effective form of causal knowledge for event-centric intelligent systems.

title: PoolBench: A Benchmark for Pooling Strategies in Concept Representation Evaluation for Decoder-Only LLMs
summary: Pooling is a consequential but under-examined design choice in decoder-only concept representation work: practitioners must collapse token-level hidden states into a passage-level vector, yet no shared protocol exists for comparing this choice across concepts, models, and tasks. Reported gains are confounded by simultaneous changes in dataset, layer, construction method, and pooling rule, making principled decisions impossible. We introduce PoolBench, a benchmark that isolates pooling as the experimental variable under a fixed evaluation protocol. PoolBench covers 17 concepts, 19 pooling strategies, and 3 open-weight decoder-only models (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B), evaluated on a single audited corpus of 37,693 real-text passages. The primary axis is linear separability (D1/AUROC); steered concept prevalence (D2/SCP) and output-level disentanglement (D3) serve as diagnostic axes. The primary finding is decisive: W4_hierarchical reaches a cross-model mean AUROC of 0.7799, while the widely adopted P1_last_token baseline reaches only 0.7640 and is statistically significantly worse (Friedman+Nemenyi, p = 2.0e-36; 77 significant pairs among 18 effective strategies). Rankings are stable across layers (rho = 0.961--0.990). A key negative result: strong detection does not imply strong steering -- D2 and D3 are substantially weaker than D1 for most concepts, indicating a fundamental representational limit rather than a pooling failure. On mid-difficulty concepts, W4_hierarchical outperforms P1_last_token by 0.042--0.113 AUROC; construction method choice (DiffMean vs. REPE) has a larger effect (delta AUROC 0.15) than pooling (delta AUROC 0.016), establishing the correct practical hierarchy. We release the corpus, pre-extracted activations, scorer models, steering vectors, and evaluation code as a reusable protocol for pooling research.

AI.tldr: PoolBench systematically evaluates pooling strategies for decoder-only LLM concept representations and finds a hierarchical windowed pooling method clearly outperforms the common last-token baseline, while also showing that good concept detection does not guarantee good steering.
AI.motivation: Pooling from token-level hidden states to passage-level vectors is crucial in decoder-only models but has been inconsistently evaluated; prior claims about ‘better pooling’ are confounded by changes in datasets, layers, and construction methods, preventing principled, comparable conclusions.
AI.method: The authors build PoolBench, a benchmark that holds datasets, models, and evaluation protocols fixed while varying only the pooling strategy. They test 19 pooling rules over 17 concepts and 3 open-weight decoder-only models (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) using a corpus of 37,693 passages. They measure linear separability (AUROC) as the primary metric and add steering-based diagnostics, then use statistical tests (Friedman+Nemenyi) and correlation across layers to assess robustness of ranking.
AI.result: A hierarchical windowed pooling strategy (W4_hierarchical) achieves the best cross-model AUROC (0.7799), significantly outperforming the common last-token pooling baseline (0.7640) with strong statistical evidence and many significant pairwise wins. Rankings of pooling strategies are highly stable across layers. However, measures of steering strength and disentanglement (D2, D3) are generally weaker than detection (D1), and on mid-difficulty concepts the construction method (e.g., DiffMean vs. REPE) has a larger impact on performance than the specific pooling strategy.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical windowed pooling is a clearly superior default to last-token pooling for concept detection in decoder-only models, but even strong detection does not translate into equally strong steering, hinting at intrinsic limits of how concepts are represented. For practitioners, choosing an effective representation construction method is more critical than fine-tuning pooling, and PoolBench provides a standardized, reusable protocol and resources to study pooling in isolation.

title: Otter: A Time-Aware, History-Conditioned Human Chess AI
summary:
Otter is a 15.3M-parameter human chess AI that predicts human move selection by modeling play as a time-aware, sequential process rather than treating each position in isolation. It combines two conditioning signals: (1) a move history encoder that conditions predictions on the last 20 moves, capturing opening preferences, positional drift, and intra-game behavioral tendencies; and (2) a time control module that modulates predictions based on clock pressure. Otter is trained on 6.1 billion positions from 117 million Lichess rapid games over 30 days on a single T4 GPU.
  Otter achieves 55.23% top-1 and 90.95% top-5 move-prediction accuracy, surpassing the prior state-of-the-art human chess model, Maia 2, with far fewer parameters and less training data. Across 11 Elo brackets (<1100 to >=2000), accuracy peaks at 57.38% in the 1900-1999 bracket. These results show that modeling chess as a time-aware, sequential activity yields more human-accurate move prediction than position-only approaches, using a smaller model. Code, trained models, and complete training logs are publicly released.

AI.tldr: A compact neural chess model (Otter) predicts human moves more accurately by modeling games as time-aware sequences instead of isolated positions.
AI.motivation: Improve prediction of human chess moves while using fewer parameters and less data than previous models, and test whether incorporating game history and time pressure helps better capture human decision patterns.
AI.method: Design a 15.3M-parameter neural network that conditions on the last 20 moves via a move-history encoder and on remaining time via a time-control module, then train it on 6.1B positions from 117M Lichess rapid games using a single T4 GPU over 30 days, evaluating top-k move prediction across Elo brackets.
AI.result: Otter attains 55.23% top-1 and 90.95% top-5 human move prediction accuracy, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art human-chess model Maia 2 despite being smaller and trained on less data, with best accuracy (57.38% top-1) for players rated 1900–1999 Elo.
AI.conclusion: Treating chess as a time-aware, sequential process—using recent move history and time-pressure information—improves human-accuracy of move prediction over position-only approaches while allowing a smaller, more efficient model; all artifacts are released for reproducibility.

title: Where Privacy Risk Lives in English-Source Multilingual RAG: A Stage-Decomposed Audit Across Five Query Languages
summary: A common assumption holds that switching to a non-English language makes a multilingual RAG system easier to attack for personal information. We test this on an English-source synthetic-PII corpus with five query languages and a two-stage defence (LLM input judge + regex output filter), in a pipeline whose translator, judge, back-translator, and generator are all Qwen2.5-7B -- so every finding below is pipeline-conditional, not a causal ranking of language-inherent risk. Under output-only filtering, English has the highest observed unstructured-PII leak rate; only English-vs-Swahili separates cleanly under document-level bootstrap intervals. Once the input judge is added, residual leaks remain on Arabic and Swahili, and back-translating the query does not close the gap (an ablation we report but cannot use as a causal diagnostic, since the back-translator is also Qwen). On a separate n=17 multilingual-prompted-judge residual corner, attaching the gold corpus document to the input judge blocks 15/17 residual cells. We frame this last result as a mechanism diagnostic, not a deployable defence: it uses oracle retrieval, BLOCK/ALLOW rates are measured on adversarial queries only, and we measure no benign-query false-positive rate and no answer-utility cost. The supplementary material contains code, corpora, queries, and per-trial JSONLs; the priority follow-up is an independent-MT plus non-Qwen-judge replication with a native-speaker query set, scoped in the Limitations section.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically studies how query language affects privacy leakage in a multilingual RAG pipeline that uses Qwen2.5-7B throughout, and evaluates a two-stage defence (input-judge + regex output filter) on synthetic PII, finding English most vulnerable under output-only filtering, residual leaks in Arabic and Swahili even with an input judge, and showing that giving the judge the gold document largely closes remaining leaks in an oracle setting.
AI.motivation: There is a common belief that switching user queries to a non-English language makes multilingual RAG systems easier to attack for personal data leakage, but this has not been systematically tested under controlled conditions. The authors want to quantify language-conditional privacy risk, understand where defences fail, and disentangle language effects from model- and pipeline-specific behaviors, using a synthetic-PII setting that allows safe, controlled experiments.
AI.method: They build a multilingual RAG-style pipeline where translation, query judging, back-translation, and answer generation are all handled by Qwen2.5-7B. They construct an English-source synthetic-PII corpus and issue adversarial queries in five languages. They evaluate two defence configurations: (1) regex-based output-only PII filtering, and (2) a two-stage defence where an LLM input judge filters or blocks risky queries before they are answered, followed by the same output regex filter. They also run an ablation that back-translates non-English queries to English before judging, and a small-scale diagnostic where the input judge is given the gold corpus document (oracle retrieval) to see if that helps it block residual leaks. They use document-level bootstrap confidence intervals and per-trial JSON logs for statistical analysis and transparency.
AI.result: With only output filtering, English queries show the highest observed unstructured-PII leak rate; among languages, only English vs. Swahili have clearly separated leak rates under document-level bootstrap intervals, suggesting limited statistical separation otherwise. When the LLM input judge is added, most leaks are reduced, but notable residual leaks persist for Arabic and Swahili, and simply back-translating the query to English does not eliminate these gaps, though this result is confounded by using the same model for translation and judging. In a focused experiment with 17 multilingual adversarial query-language and judge-language combinations, providing the judge with the exact gold document blocks leakage in 15 of the 17 residual cases.
AI.conclusion: The empirical evidence does not universally support the assumption that non-English queries are strictly easier paths to privacy leakage; in this Qwen2.5-7B-based pipeline, English is most vulnerable under output-only defences, while Arabic and Swahili show residual risk even with an input judge. The effectiveness of defences is strongly pipeline- and model-dependent, and judger access to the underlying document can substantially improve blocking in an oracle setting, but this is not yet a practical defence because it assumes perfect retrieval and is evaluated only on adversarial queries without measuring impact on benign use. The authors stress that their findings are conditional on using Qwen2.5-7B for all components, and call for replications with independent machine translation, non-Qwen judges, and native-speaker query sets to obtain more general and causally interpretable insights about multilingual privacy risk in RAG systems.

title: SearchAuditor: Auditing and Attributing Failures in Long-Horizon Search Agents
summary: Deep search agents tackle challenging questions through long-horizon web interactions, a process that is both complex and fragile: small reasoning errors may propagate through long, noisy trajectories into fluent but incorrect answers. Diagnosing such failures is difficult, requiring the manual inspection of extremely long execution traces, which could be beyond human capacity. We therefore introduce SearchAuditBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether LLM auditors can localize, attribute, and repair these failures, thereby reducing the human burden. SearchAuditBench comprises 1,243 failed trajectories, averaging 73.1 messages and 65.1K tokens, collected from eight open-weight models on five deep-search benchmarks, each expert-annotated with the critical error step, a search-specific root cause, and a reference repair with grading rubrics. We further propose SearchAuditor, a multi-perspective auditing framework that effectively localizes, attributes, and repairs search-agent failures through evidence-grounded adjudication. Experimental results show that even the strongest baseline, when powered by a frontier model like GPT-5.5, attains only a 26.6% end-to-end pass rate. In contrast, our SearchAuditor consistently outperforms all baselines across different frontier models, achieving an end-to-end pass rate of 32.3%, and resuming failed runs with its repairs enables agents to better recover from errors.

AI.tldr: Introduces SearchAuditBench and SearchAuditor to evaluate and improve LLM-based auditors that diagnose and repair failures in deep web-search agents.
AI.motivation: Deep search agents operate through long, noisy web interaction trajectories where small reasoning mistakes can propagate into confident but wrong answers. Debugging these systems is hard because it requires humans to inspect very long execution traces, often beyond feasible human effort. There is a lack of systematic benchmarks and methods to automatically audit and repair such failures.
AI.method: 1) Build SearchAuditBench, a benchmark of 1,243 failed trajectories from eight open-weight models on five deep-search benchmarks, with each trajectory averaging ~73 messages and ~65K tokens. Each trajectory is expert-annotated with: (a) the critical error step, (b) a search-specific root cause label, and (c) a reference repair plus grading rubrics. 2) Propose SearchAuditor, a multi-perspective auditing framework that analyzes trajectories from multiple angles to: (a) localize where the failure occurred, (b) attribute a root cause, and (c) generate concrete repair actions. The framework uses evidence-grounded adjudication over the long traces to produce its judgments and repairs. 3) Compare SearchAuditor against strong baseline auditing approaches powered by various frontier LLMs on the new benchmark and measure end-to-end pass rates (i.e., whether repaired trajectories successfully solve the task).
AI.result: On SearchAuditBench, even the strongest baseline auditor, when powered by a very strong frontier LLM (e.g., GPT-5.5), reaches only a 26.6% end-to-end pass rate in diagnosing and repairing failed search-agent trajectories. SearchAuditor consistently outperforms all baselines across multiple frontier models, achieving a 32.3% end-to-end pass rate. Moreover, when agents resume from the repairs suggested by SearchAuditor, they exhibit improved recovery from prior errors compared to baseline repairs.
AI.conclusion: Auditing deep search agents is a challenging but crucial task, as existing systems often fail in subtle ways over long trajectories that are hard for humans to inspect. SearchAuditBench provides a standardized, expert-annotated benchmark for evaluating LLM-based auditors, while the proposed SearchAuditor framework significantly improves over strong baselines in localizing, explaining, and repairing agent failures. Although absolute end-to-end success rates remain modest, the results indicate that systematic, evidence-grounded auditing can meaningfully reduce failure rates and help search agents better recover from errors, laying groundwork for more reliable long-horizon AI agents.

title: Cross-Architecture Steering Transfer in Language Models: A Systematic Empirical Study
summary: Independently trained large language models may develop shared internal representations of semantic concepts despite architectural differences -- but whether this geometric similarity has functional consequences for cross-model behavioural control remains untested. We present the first systematic evaluation of cross-model steering transfer and show that shared LLM geometry is functionally exploitable, conditionally: concept directions from one model can steer a different independently trained model when sufficient representational capacity exists. We study five open-weight models spanning three parameter scales (0.8B--8B) and two architectural lineages, training one Sparse Autoencoder per model across 15 semantic domains and testing alignment across all 20 directed model pairs. We observe a suggestive discontinuity near 1.7B parameters: at >= 1.7B scale, 47--49% of cross-model feature pairs validate (Pearson r >= 0.60, Procrustes cosines 0.895--0.956), while alignment degrades sharply below 0.8B. Cross-model steering vectors (B3-TI) achieve a 71.0% win rate across 15 supervised concepts versus 68.0% for same-model native vectors; a single universal vector achieves 67.3% in 4 of 5 models without any per-model supervision. Transfer degrades for models below 1.7B and for one model with generation instability, confirming that functional exploitability requires sufficient representational capacity. Our findings underscore the importance of scale thresholds in mechanistic interpretability: tools validated at 7B scale may not transfer to smaller models without revalidation. We provide the first functional complement to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis -- geometric convergence across independently trained LLMs supports cross-model behavioural control without fine-tuning, under the identified scale conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether similar internal geometries across independently trained LLMs can be used for cross-model behavioral control, finding that concept directions learned in one model can steer others, but only above a scale threshold (~≥1.7B parameters).
AI.motivation: Prior work observed that independently trained LLMs converge to similar internal geometric representations of semantics (“Platonic Representation Hypothesis”), but it was unclear whether this similarity had practical, functional consequences: can we actually use one model’s internal features to control another’s behavior? This matters for mechanistic interpretability, transfer of steering tools, and understanding scale-dependent alignment across architectures.
AI.method: The authors study five open-weight models (0.8B–8B parameters) from two architectural families. For each model, they train a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) across 15 semantic domains to obtain interpretable features and concept directions. They then systematically evaluate cross-model alignment across all 20 ordered model pairs using correlation metrics (Pearson r, Procrustes cosine) on feature pairs, and test whether concept steering vectors learned in one model can reliably steer generation in another (cross-model steering transfer), comparing performance against same-model, natively trained steering vectors. They also probe how transfer varies with model size and model stability.
AI.result: They find a marked scale threshold: for models at or above ~1.7B parameters, 47–49% of cross-model feature pairs show strong alignment (Pearson r ≥ 0.60, Procrustes cosines 0.895–0.956), while alignment drops sharply for 0.8B-scale models. Cross-model steering vectors (e.g., B3-TI) achieve a 71.0% win rate across 15 supervised semantic concepts, outperforming same-model native steering vectors at 68.0%. Remarkably, a single universal steering vector (learned once) attains 67.3% win rate in 4 of 5 models without per-model supervision. Transfer performance degrades for sub-1.7B models and for a model exhibiting generation instability, tying transfer success to representational capacity and stability.
AI.conclusion: The paper shows that geometric similarity across independently trained LLMs is not merely structural but functionally exploitable: concept directions from one model can be applied to steer others, enabling cross-model behavioral control without fine-tuning, provided models exceed a scale/quality threshold (~≥1.7B parameters and stable generation). This yields the first functional validation of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and implies that mechanistic interpretability tools built for larger models (e.g., 7B) may not reliably transfer to significantly smaller models without revalidation, underscoring the role of scale in representation sharing and interpretability tool generalization.

title: PD-GS: Phoneme-Driven 3DGS for Audio-Driven Talking Heads
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables fast, photorealistic talking-head rendering, yet accurate lip articulation remains elusive: mouth motion is often over-smoothed and may violate hard articulatory constraints such as bilabial closures, producing the notorious ``leaky mouth'' artifact. A key difficulty is that brief, discrete articulatory events are inferred from a continuous acoustic embedding under a regression objective, which biases predictions toward averaged mouth configurations. While modern self-supervised speech encoders provide rich prosodic and phonetic cues, they do not provide an explicit, frame-aligned linguistic target that reliably disambiguates closure-level events. We propose \textbf{Phoneme-Driven Gaussian Splatting (PD-GS)}, which augments a 3DGS talker with time-aligned phoneme tokens obtained from an automatic ASR and forced-alignment pipeline. Our core component, the \textbf{Linguistic Fusion Module (LFM)}, adaptively fuses continuous audio context with discrete phoneme embeddings through a learned gate, allowing the model to preserve smooth audio-driven dynamics while strengthening phoneme guidance on articulation-critical segments. PD-GS is trained purely from monocular video using image reconstruction and lip landmark supervision. On HDTF, PD-GS achieves the best lip geometry among the compared baselines (LMD 2.66) and qualitatively reduces closure violations in challenging phoneme sequences, yielding more linguistically faithful neural avatars.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Phoneme-Driven Gaussian Splatting (PD-GS) to improve lip articulation and prevent “leaky mouth” artifacts in 3D Gaussian Splatting talking-head avatars by fusing phoneme tokens with continuous audio features.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting talking-head systems produce fast and photorealistic renderings but struggle with accurate lip articulation, especially for brief, discrete events like bilabial closures (e.g., /b/, /p/, /m/). Because these events are inferred by regressing from continuous acoustic embeddings, the models tend to average configurations, leading to over-smoothed mouth motion and artifacts such as incomplete closures. Modern speech encoders contain phonetic information but lack explicit, frame-aligned linguistic signals to reliably indicate closure-level events, motivating a method that injects discrete, time-aligned phoneme guidance into 3DGS avatars.
AI.method: The paper introduces Phoneme-Driven Gaussian Splatting (PD-GS), which augments a 3DGS-based talking-head model with time-aligned phoneme tokens obtained via an automatic speech recognition and forced-alignment pipeline.
