Promoting syntactic diversity and reducing such biases in alignment data can make refusals more semantically robust and reduce jailbreaks that rely on trivial rephrasing.

title: Agentic self-driving microscopy benchmarks support qualification but do not necessarily generalize to unseen tasks
summary: Large language model agents are increasingly being developed to control a wide range of scientific characterization tools including microscopes and synchrotron beamlines. Research into agentic control of physical infrastructure is nascent and there are few well-established paradigms for how to engineer an agentic system. There are many choices to make when designing a microscopy agent, including the choice of LLM, the number of agents to use, agent responsibilities and delegation rules, retrieval-augmented generation parameters, and more. When designing and optimizing an agentic microscope controller, researchers not only want to ensure that the agent can correctly perform known tasks but also that the agent can generalize to new tasks that it has not encountered before. In this study, we develop a benchmark and trace-logging framework that reveals a) how different choices of agent architecture impact performance at microscopy tasks and b) the limitations of benchmarks for predicting if a particular agent will perform well on unseen microscopy tasks. The framework was used to evaluate one-, two-, and three-agent graph topologies, five LLMs, RAG and context parameters, and operational constraints across 53 microscopy benchmark tests. In total, 105 agent configurations, 1,949 individual test runs, and 49,109 RAG retrievals were recorded. Direct comparisons showed clear differences in latency, token use, cost, and failure mode between configurations. However, surrogate models trained on agent architecture and test results did not reliably predict an agent's performance on new, unseen tasks. These results show that these benchmarks are useful for qualification, regression testing, diagnosis, and direct comparison, but the current heterogeneous test suite does not support a task-independent global configuration model.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a benchmark and logging framework to systematically compare different LLM-agent architectures for controlling microscopes and shows that current heterogeneous benchmarks cannot reliably predict performance on unseen tasks.
AI.motivation: Agentic large language models are starting to control real scientific instruments like microscopes, but there is little guidance on how to design such agents (number of agents, responsibilities, RAG setup, constraints, etc.) or on whether benchmark performance translates to generalization on new tasks. Researchers need tools to evaluate architectural choices and understand limitations of current evaluation practices.
AI.method: The authors create a benchmarking and trace-logging framework for LLM-based microscopy agents. They systematically vary agentic design choices: one-, two-, and three-agent graph topologies; five different LLM backends; retrieval-augmented generation and context-window parameters; and various operational constraints. They run 105 distinct agent configurations over 53 microscopy benchmark tests, producing 1,949 total test runs and 49,109 RAG retrievals. They log latency, token usage, cost, and failure modes, and they also train surrogate models that attempt to predict agent performance on unseen tasks based on architecture and prior test results.
AI.result: The experiments reveal clear, quantifiable differences between agent configurations in latency, token consumption, monetary cost, and characteristic failure modes. However, the surrogate models trained on these benchmark results and architectural descriptors do not generalize well: they fail to reliably predict how an agent configuration will perform on new microscopy tasks outside the benchmark set.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework is effective for qualification, regression testing, diagnosis, and direct, apples-to-apples comparison of microscopy agent designs. Yet, because the benchmark suite is heterogeneous and task-specific, it does not support building a robust, task-independent global model that can select an optimal agent configuration for arbitrary new tasks. Better or differently structured benchmarks are needed if we want reliable performance prediction and configuration selection for unseen tasks.

title: Example-Guided Prompting for Document-Level Text Simplification
summary: Document-level text simplification requires large language models (LLMs) to rewrite complex documents while preserving meaning, readability, and discourse coherence. Although prompt-based LLMs have shown promising performance, they often produce inconsistent simplifications because textual instructions alone provide limited guidance for complex document-level transformations. We investigate whether retrieved document-simplification examples can improve document-level generation by augmenting prompts with examples selected from a parallel simplification corpus. This example-guided prompting approach enables LLMs to exploit relevant simplification patterns without task-specific fine-tuning. Experiments on the OneStopEnglish corpus using multiple state-of-the-art LLMs show that incorporating retrieved examples consistently improves simplification quality over prompt-only generation and achieves competitive or superior performance compared with representative supervised (T5) and planning-based (PlanSimp) document simplification systems. Furthermore, we find that the benefits of example-guided prompting vary across LLMs, suggesting that effective use of retrieved examples depends on a model's ability to integrate contextual information during generation.

AI.tldr: The paper explores using retrieved example simplifications to guide large language models for document-level text simplification, improving quality without task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Prompt-only large language models struggle with consistent, high-quality document-level simplification because textual instructions provide limited guidance for complex, discourse-level transformations. There is a need to better leverage existing parallel simplification corpora to guide LLMs without costly supervised training.
AI.method: The authors propose an example-guided prompting approach: for each complex input document, they retrieve similar examples from a parallel document simplification corpus and append these example pairs to the prompt given to an LLM. Multiple state-of-the-art LLMs are evaluated on the OneStopEnglish corpus, comparing example-augmented prompts with prompt-only generation and with supervised baselines such as T5 and the planning-based PlanSimp system.
AI.result: Across several strong LLMs, adding retrieved simplification examples to prompts consistently improves document simplification quality over using prompts alone. The example-guided approach attains performance that is competitive with or better than supervised and planning-based baselines on the OneStopEnglish benchmark. The performance gains, however, differ by model, indicating heterogeneous sensitivity to example-based guidance.
AI.conclusion: Retrieved example-based prompting is an effective, training-free way to enhance LLMs for document-level text simplification, rivaling specialized supervised systems. However, the utility of such examples depends on the underlying LLM’s ability to integrate and use contextual demonstrations, highlighting an interaction between model architecture/capabilities and prompting strategies.

title: CASCADE: An Agentic Regulatory Network Framework for Patient-Data-Validated Downstream Perturbation Prediction
summary:
CASCADE is an agentic framework that predicts downstream transcriptional effects of gene perturbation from precomputed
  ARACNe regulatory networks, exposed via MCP. Prior work validates such tools by checking whether predicted genes are
  known cancer genes (membership); we instead test whether the predicted direction of change matches reality, using
  focal-gene copy-number amplification as a dosage-based proxy for the inverse of knockdown against real TCGA patient
  tumor data.
  For MYC, CASCADE's predicted knockdown targets show strong concordance with real amplified-vs-non-amplified tumor
  expression across three cancer types (BRCA: 90.0%, COAD: 72.0%, STAD: 85.7%; all p<0.0013), well above permutation
  baselines, surviving a PAM50 subtype control and replicating in an independent cohort (METABRIC, 87.2%). Compared
  against curated MSigDB gene-set baselines via Fisher's exact test, CASCADE's accuracy is not shown to exceed existing
  public knowledge of MYC- or E2F-driven biology, though its gene-specific direction-calling clearly outperforms a naive
  uniform guess.
  Extending to fifteen additional genes, validation proves gene-specific rather than universal: proliferation-machinery
  regulators mostly replicate, while lineage-identity transcription factors and one cyclin-D paralog (CCND2)
  consistently fail, a pattern we discuss as a hedged, post-hoc hypothesis.
  We separately benchmark whether an LLM-based agent correctly grounds natural-language requests into CASCADE's real MCP
  tool calls. Across 35 queries, a documented local model reaches 71.4% exact match (85.7% for a larger model); schema
  and gene-alias failures are resolved by scale or server-side correction, but both models confidently default to the
  wrong perturbation type on ambiguous queries, a failure a targeted fix could not resolve because its trigger condition
  never occurs.

AI.tldr: The paper presents and validates CASCADE, an agentic framework that predicts gene expression changes from gene perturbations using ARACNe regulatory networks, and evaluates both its biological accuracy and an LLM-based interface for tool grounding.
AI.motivation: Existing network-based tools for predicting transcriptional effects of gene perturbations are typically validated only by whether predicted target genes are known cancer genes, which ignores the direction of regulation and can overstate utility. There is a need for a more stringent, direction-aware validation against real patient data, and for assessing whether LLM agents can reliably and correctly interface with such tools from natural language queries.
AI.method: CASCADE leverages precomputed ARACNe regulatory networks accessed via the MCP framework to predict downstream transcriptional effects of gene knockdown. The authors validate these predictions using TCGA tumor data, treating focal-gene copy-number amplification as a dosage-based proxy for the inverse of knockdown, and compare predicted vs observed expression changes. They assess performance for MYC across multiple cancer types and in an independent cohort, and extend the analysis to 15 additional genes. Separately, they benchmark an LLM-based agent by measuring how accurately it translates 35 natural-language queries into correct MCP tool calls, analyzing error types and the impact of model scale and schema corrections.
AI.result: For MYC, CASCADE’s predicted knockdown targets strongly match observed expression differences between amplified and non-amplified tumors in BRCA, COAD, and STAD, with high concordance percentages (90.0%, 72.0%, 85.7%) and significant p-values, and replication in METABRIC (87.2%). However, when compared to curated MSigDB MYC/E2F gene sets using Fisher’s exact test, CASCADE does not clearly exceed the predictive accuracy achievable from existing public knowledge, although it does outperform a naive random-direction baseline. Extension to 15 other genes shows that robust validation is gene-specific: regulators of proliferation largely replicate, whereas lineage-identity transcription factors and CCND2 fail consistently. For the LLM agent, the smaller local model achieves 71.4% exact match in mapping queries to tool calls (85.7% for a larger model); increasing scale and adding server-side schema/gene-alias corrections fix some issues, but both models still systematically choose the wrong perturbation type under query ambiguity.
AI.conclusion: CASCADE can accurately predict direction-specific transcriptional consequences of perturbing certain genes, particularly core proliferation regulators like MYC, when evaluated against real patient tumor data, but its reliability is not universal across gene types and does not clearly surpass curated pathway knowledge for MYC/E2F biology. Its advantage lies in gene-level, direction-specific predictions rather than in set-level enrichment alone. The LLM-based agent can often but not always correctly ground natural-language requests into CASCADE tool calls, with persistent systematic errors around perturbation-type inference that are not solved by simple scaling or local rule fixes, indicating the need for more robust grounding strategies and disambiguation mechanisms.

title: DBLAST: Dependent Block Drafting for Stochastic Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates large language models' inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose multiple future tokens and a target model to verify them. While recent block and diffusion-style drafters can predict several positions in a single pass, their training and sampling procedures are typically optimized for greedy decoding or assume that positions in the draft block are conditionally independent. This assumption becomes brittle in non-greedy speculative decoding, where the target distribution is deliberately stochastic and multiple continuations become plausible. We study this mismatch for block diffusion drafters and show that the accepted draft length degrades as the entropy of the target sampling distribution increases. We propose a dependent block drafter based on a low-rank latent mixture over token positions, complemented by an acceptance-oriented training objective that directly targets the expected verified length. Experiments with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B on GSM8K, MT-Bench, HumanEval, and creative-writing benchmarks show that our approach, namely DBLast, consistently improves accepted length over independent block sampling, especially in higher-entropy decoding regimes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DBLast, a new speculative decoding drafter that models dependencies across drafted tokens and optimizes directly for accepted draft length, improving speed especially in high-entropy (more random) decoding.
AI.motivation: Existing speculative decoding methods with block or diffusion-style drafters assume conditional independence among drafted positions and are tuned mainly for greedy decoding. This leads to poor accepted draft length when using non-greedy, higher-entropy sampling where multiple continuations are plausible, limiting speedups in realistic, diverse generation tasks.
AI.method: The authors analyze block diffusion drafters and empirically show that accepted draft length deteriorates as the entropy (stochasticity) of the target sampling distribution increases. They then introduce a dependent block drafter, DBLast, that uses a low-rank latent mixture over token positions to capture dependencies between drafted tokens. They further design an acceptance-oriented training objective that directly maximizes expected verified length rather than just likelihood under an independence assumption.
AI.result: On Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B across GSM8K, MT-Bench, HumanEval, and creative-writing benchmarks, DBLast consistently yields longer accepted drafts than independent block sampling baselines, with the gains being most pronounced at higher sampling entropy settings.
AI.conclusion: Modeling dependencies across drafted tokens and training the drafter with an objective aligned to acceptance probability significantly improves speculative decoding efficiency, particularly in non-greedy, high-entropy decoding scenarios. DBLast demonstrates that relaxing the independence assumption and directly optimizing expected verified length can deliver robust acceleration across a range of tasks and decoding regimes.

title: Counterfactual Analysis via Large Language Models
summary: Counterfactual analysis aims to predict potential outcomes under hypothetical scenarios, offering valuable insights for decision-making. This paper investigates the application of large language models (LLMs), specifically the GPT-3.5 model, for counterfactual analysis. We focus on the online lending context, where the counterfactual return on investment (ROI) is crucial for evaluating different interest rate schemes. We begin by assessing the predictive performance of GPT and comparing it with advanced machine learning algorithms. The results show that prompt engineering can significantly enhance GPT's predictions, with the R-squared increasing from 1.97% to 2.84%, closely approaching the 3.48% achieved by gradient-boosted regression. Subsequently, we utilize GPT to generate counterfactual ROIs under a set of alternative interest rates. GPT exhibits logical coherence and causal reasoning in its responses. The findings underscore the potential of LLMs as effective tools for counterfactual analysis in online lending, suggesting broader applications for LLMs in various predictive and decision-making contexts.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates GPT-3.5 for predicting and simulating counterfactual ROI in online lending under different interest rate schemes, comparing it to traditional ML models.
AI.motivation: Counterfactual ROI estimation is important in online lending to evaluate alternative interest rate policies, but is usually done with specialized ML models. With the rise of LLMs, it is unclear whether and how they can be used for such quantitative, causal and counterfactual tasks.
AI.method: Use GPT-3.5 to predict ROI in an online lending setting, apply prompt engineering to improve its predictive performance, and compare its R-squared with advanced ML methods such as gradient-boosted regression. Then use GPT-3.5 to generate counterfactual ROIs under hypothetical alternative interest rate schemes and assess the logical and causal coherence of its responses.
AI.result: Prompt-engineered GPT-3.5 improves its R-squared from 1.97% to 2.84%, getting close to the 3.48% of gradient-boosted regression, and it produces counterfactual ROI estimates that appear logically coherent and causally consistent under varying interest rates.
AI.conclusion: LLMs like GPT-3.5, when carefully prompted, can approximate the performance of specialized ML models for predicting ROI and can be used to generate counterfactual analyses in online lending, indicating broader potential use of LLMs for predictive and decision-making tasks involving hypothetical scenarios.

title: Different Perturbations, Different Mechanisms: Understanding Continued Pre-training for Zero-Shot Dialect Robustness
summary: Dialectal variation remains a major challenge for multilingual language models. Perturbation-based continued pre-training (CPT) has emerged as a promising approach to improving robustness, yet existing work largely evaluates individual perturbation strategies in isolation and provides limited insight into why they work. We present a systematic study of perturbation-based CPT for multilingual dialect robustness in LLMs, comparing six training conditions across nine German, Italian, and Arabic dialect tasks. Perturbation-based CPT, especially character-noised CPT, consistently improves zero-shot dialect robustness while largely preserving standard variety performance. More importantly, we show that methods with similar downstream performance induce distinct mechanisms of robustness, exhibiting different patterns of language model adaptation, representational alignment, and prediction repair. Our results provide a more complete understanding of how synthetic surface variation improves robustness and offer practical guidance for selecting CPT strategies in multilingual and dialectal settings.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically evaluates perturbation-based continued pre-training (CPT) to improve multilingual LLM robustness to dialectal variation, finding that especially character-level noise enhances zero-shot dialect performance while preserving standard language quality, and revealing that different perturbations achieve robustness via distinct internal mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Multilingual language models struggle with dialectal variation, which hurts performance on non-standard language varieties. Perturbation-based CPT has shown promise for robustness, but prior work examines individual perturbations in isolation and does not explain *why* they work or how different strategies compare. The authors aim to fill this gap with a systematic, mechanism-focused study across multiple languages and dialect tasks.
AI.method: The authors perform a controlled comparison of six perturbation-based continued pre-training conditions applied to multilingual LLMs. They evaluate these conditions on nine dialect-related tasks spanning German, Italian, and Arabic dialects. Besides measuring standard downstream performance (zero-shot dialect robustness and standard variety performance), they analyze how each CPT strategy changes the model via language model adaptation, representational alignment across dialects and standards, and how predictions are repaired under dialectal inputs.
AI.result: Perturbation-based CPT, particularly character-noise–based CPT, consistently improves zero-shot robustness to dialectal inputs while largely maintaining performance on standard language varieties. Despite sometimes similar task-level performance, different CPT strategies lead to distinct internal behaviors: they differ in how the language model parameters adapt, how representations for dialect vs. standard varieties align, and how prediction errors are corrected when facing dialectal variation.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic surface perturbations during continued pre-training are an effective way to boost dialect robustness in multilingual LLMs without sacrificing performance on standard varieties. However, robustness is not monolithic: different perturbation strategies induce qualitatively different mechanisms within the model. Understanding these mechanisms provides both conceptual insight into robustness and practical guidance for choosing CPT strategies tailored to multilingual and dialectal applications.

title: DoctorAgents: an agentic framework to iteratively refine AutoML pipeline for small clinical temporal data
summary: Clinical machine learning (ML) has the potential to support high-stakes medical decision-making, but reliable deployment is often constrained by scarce, heterogeneous, and temporal complexity. Developing effective ML pipelines for such data remains time-consuming and error-prone, while existing automated machine learning (AutoML) systems only partially address this challenge because they largely rely on brute-force search over predefined spaces and lack explicit reasoning and memory. We therefore reformulate AutoML for small clinical data from exhaustive search to reasoning-driven refinement. We propose DoctorAgents, an agentic AI framework that autonomously constructs and optimizes end-to-end ML pipelines through specialized large language model (LLM) agents for generation, validation, and refinement. DoctorAgents backpropagates natural-language feedback through textual gradient descent to perform targeted updates without exhaustive search. Experiments across diverse clinical tasks show that DoctorAgents consistently outperforms established AutoML baselines while producing more interpretable task-specific representations.

AI.tldr: DoctorAgents is an LLM-based, reasoning-driven AutoML framework that builds and refines ML pipelines for small, complex clinical datasets, outperforming standard AutoML while yielding more interpretable models.
AI.motivation: Clinical ML deployment is difficult because clinical data are limited in size, heterogeneous in type, and temporally complex, making manual pipeline design slow and error-prone. Existing AutoML tools rely heavily on brute-force search over fixed configuration spaces and lack explicit reasoning or memory, which is inefficient and ill-suited for small, high-stakes medical datasets. A more intelligent, reasoning-based AutoML approach is needed to better handle these constraints and improve clinical ML performance and interpretability.
AI.method: The authors reframe AutoML for small clinical datasets from exhaustive hyperparameter and pipeline search to an iterative, reasoning-based refinement process. They introduce DoctorAgents, an agentic AI framework built on large language model agents with distinct roles: generation of candidate ML pipelines, validation of their behavior and performance, and refinement based on feedback. The system uses natural-language feedback as a form of “textual gradient descent,” effectively backpropagating critiques and evaluation results through the LLM to guide targeted, stepwise updates to the pipeline instead of exploring the search space blindly.
AI.result: Across multiple diverse clinical prediction and decision-support tasks, DoctorAgents achieves consistently better performance than established AutoML baselines. Additionally, the pipelines and representations it produces are reported to be more interpretable and better tailored to the specific clinical tasks, suggesting improved alignment with clinical reasoning and data characteristics.
AI.conclusion: A reasoning-driven, LLM-agent–based approach to AutoML can be more effective than traditional brute-force search for small, complex clinical datasets. DoctorAgents demonstrates that leveraging specialized LLM agents and natural-language feedback enables autonomous construction and optimization of clinically useful, interpretable ML pipelines, indicating a promising direction for deploying ML in high-stakes healthcare settings.

title: Where Models Converge and Humans Diverge: A Coverage Framework for Distributional Pluralism in Open-Ended Generation
summary: When a large language model (LLM) writes Harry Potter fanfiction, it reliably produces fundamental elements of the Hogwarts universe, such as recognizable places and characters. Human-written Harry Potter fanfictions, however, typically include these fundamentals and much more, incorporating stylistically irregular content and relationship-diverse plotlines. This gap between LLM and human writing has been noted across a variety of domains. LLMs tend to produce "average" writing, while human writing contains more diverse content that covers a broader distribution. Existing work has shown the existence of this distributional "gap", but no work has proposed a systematic way to measure it. Our paper proposes a human-grounded framework that uses the empirical distribution of human writing on a topic to measure the distributional breadth of LLM-generated content on that same topic. We propose two metrics, LLM Coverage (LLM-Cov) and In-Boundary Rate (IBR), that separate the plausibility of LLM content from its distributional breadth. Across ideation and narrative tasks, we find that current LLMs produce plausible but narrow content that concentrates near the center of the human response space. Our framework can enable researchers to better assess the distributional breadth of LLM-authored content, which we term its "cultural reach".

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework and metrics to quantify how much the content generated by large language models covers the diversity of human writing on the same topic.
AI.motivation: Although large language models can generate plausible text, their outputs are often “average” and less diverse than human writing. Prior work has qualitatively observed that human writing spans a broader, more varied distribution, but there is no systematic, quantitative way to measure how broadly LLMs cover this space of human-authored content. This limits our ability to evaluate and compare models on an important aspect of creativity and cultural representation.
AI.method: The authors construct a human-grounded framework that takes the empirical distribution of human-written text on a given topic as the reference space. They then evaluate LLM outputs relative to this space using two proposed metrics: (1) LLM Coverage (LLM-Cov), which measures how much of the human response space the LLM-generated texts occupy, and (2) In-Boundary Rate (IBR), which measures whether LLM-generated content falls within the plausible region defined by human responses. These metrics are applied to ideation and narrative tasks, such as Harry Potter fanfiction, where both human and LLM corpora are collected and embedded into a shared representation space to estimate distributions.
AI.result: Across ideation and narrative generation tasks, current LLMs produce text that is generally plausible—i.e., their outputs lie largely within the human-defined response space (high IBR)—but that is concentrated near the center of this space, leading to low LLM Coverage. In practice, this means LLMs reliably reproduce core, canonical elements of a universe (like Hogwarts settings and main characters) but under-explore stylistically irregular content, diverse relationships, and more unconventional plotlines that humans often create.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that LLMs have limited “cultural reach”: they cover only a narrow region of the broader distribution of human writing even when their outputs are locally plausible. Their human-grounded framework, with LLM Coverage and In-Boundary Rate, offers a principled way to disentangle plausibility from distributional breadth and provides a more nuanced evaluation of generative models. This can guide future model development toward broader, more human-like coverage of cultural and creative spaces rather than just safe, average outputs.

title: C$^3$PO: Evaluating Cross-Modal Composition and Counterfactual Performance in Omnimodal Models
summary: Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can process diverse sensory inputs, yet their reasoning remains heavily biased toward a dominant modality, resulting in brittle cross-modal reasoning. We introduce C$^3$PO, a benchmark of 3,404 samples spanning video, audio, image, and text, evaluating two abilities: information composition (fusing dispersed evidence) and counterfactual conflict (resolving deliberate contradictions). C$^3$PO's paired IC/CC structure and four-tier design enable targeted diagnosis of when and why cross-modal reasoning fails. Built through a fully automatic pipeline using 25 logically grounded templates, C$^3$PO reveals that while humans achieve 88.64% accuracy, the best model (Gemini-3.1-Pro) reaches only 73.17%, with open-source models collapsing under conflict. Through attention probes, we find 86-95% of failures stem from modality dominance: models commit to one modality while ignoring contradictory evidence, concentrating 87-95% of attention on text. Mid-layer attention entropy predicts correctness-sustained exploration succeeds, premature collapse fails. The 56-point accuracy gap between equally complex templates reveals that performance depends on modalities' structural roles in conflict resolution, not combinations. These findings show multimodal perception does not guarantee robust reasoning; architectures must enable sustained cross-modal attention to avoid premature

AI.tldr: The paper introduces C^3PO, a fully automatic benchmark to evaluate and diagnose cross-modal reasoning in multimodal LLMs across video, audio, image, and text, focusing on information composition and resolving counterfactual conflicts, and shows that current models overly rely on text and fail under modality conflicts compared to humans.
AI.motivation: Although current MLLMs can ingest multiple modalities, their reasoning tends to be dominated by a single (usually textual) modality, leading to brittle performance when different modalities must be integrated or when they conflict. There is a lack of systematic benchmarks to stress-test and diagnose these specific cross-modal reasoning failures.
AI.method: The authors construct C^3PO, a benchmark of 3,404 automatically generated items using 25 logically grounded templates. The benchmark is organized into paired information-composition/counterfactual-conflict (IC/CC) instances and a four-tier design that manipulates the roles and interactions of video, audio, image, and text. They evaluate humans and multiple MLLMs on this benchmark and conduct attention-based probes, analyzing attention distribution and entropy across layers to understand failure modes and modality dominance.
AI.result: Humans achieve 88.64% accuracy on the benchmark, while the best-performing MLLM (Gemini-3.1-Pro) attains only 73.17% and open-source models perform much worse, especially under conflict conditions. Attention analysis shows that 86–95% of model failures arise from dominance of a single modality, typically text, with 87–95% of attention mass concentrated on textual inputs and insufficient use of other modalities. Mid-layer attention entropy correlates with correctness: higher, more sustained entropy is associated with successful cross-modal exploration, whereas early attention collapse predicts errors. A 56-point accuracy gap between templates of comparable complexity indicates that performance depends strongly on the structural role of modalities in conflict resolution rather than on which modalities are present.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal input capability does not automatically yield robust cross-modal reasoning. Current MLLMs tend to prematurely commit to one dominant modality, largely ignoring conflicting evidence from others. Robust multimodal reasoning will require architectural or training changes that encourage sustained, balanced cross-modal attention and prevent early attention collapse during conflict resolution.

title: SkillZip: Contract-Preserving Graph Compression for Scalable Agent Skill Libraries
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly act as agents whose procedural knowledge is stored in reusable skill packages and loaded at inference time. As skill libraries grow, a central challenge is to expose the smallest sufficient executable context under a limited context budget. Existing systems struggle to reuse routines below the whole-skill level, preserve procedural contracts during compression, keep compressed routines executable and expandable, and update the compressed library as skills evolve. These challenges reveal a unit mismatch: skills are retrieved as packages, compressed as text, and converted into execution graphs only after retrieval, whereas reliable reuse requires a contract-bearing procedural unit. We propose SkillZip, an execution-aware procedural abstraction framework that performs contract-preserving compression over section-level graphs. SkillZip rewrites recurring contract-valid motifs into reversible ported macros while preserving boundary signatures, dependency closure, verifier reachability, and source-level expansion. At inference time, it hydrates a compact, dependency-closed context and expands macros only when required. ReZip further integrates new skills and revises risky macros using execution evidence. Comprehensive experiments1 on technical and embodied agent benchmarks show SkillZip consistently outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 12.2 points, while achieving a 3.46x compression ratio with 99.2% dependency preservation and 98.7% verifier reachability. Scaling analyses further confirm robust retrieval across skill libraries ranging from 200 to 100K skills.

AI.tldr: SkillZip is a framework for compressing and reusing LLM agent skills by operating on execution graphs rather than raw text, enabling high compression while preserving executability and reliability.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents accumulate many skills, the limited context window makes it difficult to load all potentially relevant procedural knowledge. Existing approaches retrieve whole skills as monolithic packages and compress them as text, which blocks fine-grained reuse, breaks procedural contracts, and complicates updating as skills change. There is a mismatch between how skills are stored, compressed, and executed, leading to inefficiency and unreliability in agent behavior.
AI.method: The authors introduce SkillZip, which represents skills as section-level execution graphs and performs "contract-preserving" compression directly over these graphs. It identifies recurring, contract-valid subgraphs (motifs) and rewrites them as reversible ported macros while preserving boundary signatures, dependency closure, verifier reachability, and the ability to expand back to source-level code. At inference, the system loads a compact, dependency-closed context and lazily expands macros only when needed. A component called ReZip uses execution evidence from new or updated skills to integrate them into the library and revise macros that appear risky.
AI.result: On a range of technical and embodied-agent benchmarks, SkillZip surpasses the strongest baseline method by as much as 12.2 performance points. It achieves an average 3.46x compression ratio while maintaining 99.2% of dependencies and 98.7% verifier reachability, meaning the compressed library remains highly executable and checkable. Scaling experiments from 200 up to 100,000 skills show stable retrieval performance under large libraries.
AI.conclusion: Operating on execution-aware procedural abstractions (section-level graphs) rather than text enables effective compression and reuse of LLM agent skills under tight context budgets. SkillZip preserves the procedural contracts required for reliable execution while significantly reducing context size and supporting incremental updates through ReZip. This suggests a promising direction for building scalable, maintainable skill libraries for LLM-based agents.

title: Adaptive Arena-based Contestable Argumentative Network-of-Experts for Open-Ended Care Plan Coordination
comment: Accepted at the 4th International Conference on Frontiers of Artificial Intelligence, Ethics, and Multidisciplinary Applications
summary: Care plan coordination demands synthesizing heterogeneous clinical, functional, and psychosocial information across multiple professional disciplines, where monolithic LLM pipelines cannot perform in a transparent or safe manner. We present CANOE (Contestable Argumentative Network-of-Experts), a multi-agent neuro-symbolic framework that addresses these limitations through five modules: complexity assessment, adaptive team recruitment, role-based argumentative computation via an Arena-based Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Framework (A-QBAF), human-in-the-loop contestation, and care-plan synthesis. Role-specialized agents generate supporting and attacking arguments for candidate interventions; conflicts are resolved through arena-based clash resolution before acceptability scores propagate across the argumentation graph. Care planners may accept, reject, edit, or add arguments, and the framework will deterministically recompute the final plan. Evaluation on Discharge Me! and MedicalRAG using ROUGE-L, AlignScore, MEDCON F1, FKGL, and LLM-as-a-judge shows that medically fine-tuned models achieve the strongest clinical correctness and safety, while CANOE's argumentative structure provides faithful explanation and human contestability.

AI.tldr: CANOE is a neuro-symbolic, multi-agent framework that uses argumentative reasoning and human-in-the-loop contestation to generate transparent, safe, and revisable clinical care plans.
AI.motivation: Care-plan coordination requires integrating diverse clinical, functional, and psychosocial data across multiple disciplines, which standard single-LLM pipelines handle poorly in terms of safety, transparency, and controllability. There is a need for systems that can explicitly represent conflicts, support human oversight, and provide faithful explanatory structure rather than opaque end-to-end generations.
AI.method: The paper proposes CANOE, a Contestable Argumentative Network-of-Experts. It comprises five modules: (1) complexity assessment of the case; (2) adaptive recruitment of a team of role-specialized agents; (3) role-based argumentative computation using an Arena-based Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Framework (A-QBAF), where agents generate supporting and attacking arguments for candidate interventions and conflicts are resolved via arena-based clash resolution with acceptability scores propagating over an argumentation graph; (4) human-in-the-loop contestation, allowing clinicians to accept, reject, edit, or add arguments; and (5) care-plan synthesis, where the system deterministically recomputes the final care plan given the updated argument graph.
AI.result: On the Discharge Me! and MedicalRAG benchmarks, evaluated with ROUGE-L, AlignScore, MEDCON F1, FKGL, and LLM-as-a-judge metrics, the framework shows that medically fine-tuned underlying models provide the best clinical correctness and safety. CANOE’s argumentative architecture yields plans that score well on these metrics while also offering structured, inspectable reasoning chains.
AI.conclusion: CANOE demonstrates that a multi-agent, neuro-symbolic argumentative framework can improve transparency, safety, and human contestability in automated care-plan generation. By combining specialized LLM agents with formal argumentation and interactive revision, the system produces clinically strong plans while providing faithful, revisable explanations instead of opaque monolithic outputs.

title: FOCUS: Decoupling Expert Personas in LLMs to Enhance Domain Expert Capabilities
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) can exhibit diverse personas, and activating expert personas has been shown to improve domain expertise and task accuracy. However, existing persona control methods often suffer from cross-domain coupling, which may lead to overly aggressive behavior in high-caution domains such as healthcare, or excessive conservatism in risk-sensitive domains such as financial trading. To address this issue, we propose FOCUS (\textbf{\underline{F}}ine-tuning with \textbf{\underline{O}}rthogonal \textbf{\underline{C}}ontrol for \textbf{\underline{U}}ncoupled persona\textbf{\underline{S}}). FOCUS first automatically extracts expert persona vectors from LLMs, then applies orthogonal decomposition to decouple domain-specific expert personas, and finally introduces an expert gating module to adaptively control persona activation according to task contexts. With a two-stage training strategy and a gated selection regularizer, the model learns to activate appropriate personas for both single-domain and cross-domain tasks. Experiments on financial, legal, medical, and cross-domain benchmarks show that FOCUS improves task accuracy and outperforms existing persona control methods. Our code is available at \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/openpersona-48F4}{this url}.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FOCUS, a method to decouple and dynamically control expert personas in large language models via orthogonal decomposition and gated activation, improving domain-specific and cross-domain task performance.
AI.motivation: Existing persona control methods for LLMs improve expertise but suffer from cross-domain coupling: expert behaviors in one domain can inappropriately transfer to others, causing over-aggressiveness in high-caution areas (e.g., healthcare) or over-conservatism in risk-sensitive domains (e.g., finance). There is a need for a principled way to separate and selectively activate domain-specific expert personas based on task context.
AI.method: FOCUS operates in three main steps: (1) automatically extract expert persona vectors from LLMs, representing domain-specific expert behaviors; (2) apply orthogonal decomposition to these vectors to decouple the domain-specific components, making them as independent as possible; (3) introduce an expert gating module that adaptively controls which personas are activated given the current task context. Training uses a two-stage strategy and a gated selection regularizer so the model learns when and how strongly to activate each persona for both single-domain and cross-domain tasks.
AI.result: On benchmarks spanning financial, legal, medical, and cross-domain tasks, FOCUS yields higher task accuracy than baseline and existing persona-control approaches. It demonstrates better alignment of behavior with domain requirements, avoiding the problematic cross-domain coupling observed in prior methods.
AI.conclusion: By extracting, orthogonally decoupling, and adaptively gating expert persona vectors, FOCUS enables finer-grained, context-aware persona control in LLMs. This leads to improved performance and more appropriate behavior across domains, indicating that structured persona disentanglement and dynamic activation are effective strategies for managing expertise in large language models.

title: Evaluating and Improving Pedagogical Fit in LLM-Based AI Tutors with the Pedagogical Suitability Index
comment: This paper has already been accepted and presented at the IEEE 27th International Conference on Information Reuse and Integration for Data Science (IRI 2026) from July 31 to August 2, 2026, in Seattle, WA, USA
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as AI tutors, but a correct answer is not always a pedagogically appropriate one. In classroom learning, effective help depends not only on correctness, but also on whether a response matches the learner's current foundation, the course sequence, and the timing of concept introduction. Existing evaluations focus mainly on answer quality, leaving this instructional fit under-measured. We present the Pedagogical Suitability Index (PSI), a composite metric of six theory-informed sub-scores that evaluates how well LLM-generated tutoring responses align with learner readiness and curricular progression, and we further use PSI as a structured feedback signal for response improvement. We evaluate four LLM tutors (ChatGPT, Gemini, Gemma4, and Qwen3) across 240 scenario-based evaluations using paired standard and defective prompts, then apply a PSI-guided regeneration protocol to 62 weak-performing cases. Baseline differences across the four tested models were modest overall (PSI range: 0.557 to 0.638), and open-weight and closed models did not exhibit a clear separation in pedagogical fit. Under the tested prompt perturbations, overall PSI remained largely stable (Delta = -0.002), though sub-score trade-offs emerged. More importantly, PSI-guided feedback substantially improved weak-performing cases: 51 of 62 cases improved (82.3%). Focused manual evaluation of the 62 PSI-selected weak cases provides initial evidence that the identified weaknesses are instructionally meaningful and that many PSI-guided regenerations correspond to human-judged improvement. These results suggest that learner- and curriculum-aware alignment may matter more for effective tutoring than model category alone, and that such alignment is both measurable and improvable.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Pedagogical Suitability Index (PSI), a metric to evaluate how well LLM tutoring responses fit learner readiness and curriculum structure, and shows PSI can also guide improved LLM responses.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM tutor evaluations mainly measure answer correctness or quality, not whether responses are instructionally appropriate for a student’s current knowledge, the course sequence, or timing of concepts. The authors aim to fill this gap by creating a metric that captures pedagogical fit, enabling better assessment and improvement of LLM tutors.
AI.method: The authors design PSI, a composite of six theory-driven sub-scores that capture alignment with learner readiness and curricular progression. They evaluate four LLM tutors (ChatGPT, Gemini, Gemma4, Qwen3) on 240 scenario-based tasks using both standard and deliberately defective prompts. For 62 cases where models perform poorly on PSI, they apply a PSI-guided regeneration protocol that uses the metric as structured feedback to steer improved responses, and then manually inspect these cases for instructional meaning and improvement.
AI.result: Baseline PSI scores for the four LLMs fall in a relatively narrow band (0.557–0.638), with no clear pedagogical advantage for open vs. closed models. PSI scores remain largely stable under prompt perturbations (overall Delta ≈ -0.002), though the sub-scores show trade-offs. In the 62 low-PSI cases, using PSI as feedback improves 51 responses (82.3%), and manual review indicates that PSI-highlighted weaknesses are instructionally meaningful and that many regenerated responses better support learning.
AI.conclusion: Pedagogical alignment—how well responses match learner readiness and curriculum structure—is both distinct from and at least as important as raw answer quality or model type in LLM tutors. The proposed PSI metric can reliably surface instructionally relevant weaknesses and effectively guide regeneration toward more pedagogically appropriate responses, demonstrating that learner- and curriculum-aware alignment is measurable and improvable in LLM-based tutoring systems.

title: Human-Like Anaphor Resolution in Large Language Models
comment: 7 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Presented at CogSci 2026 and the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Society for Text & Discourse. Code: https://github.com/wristy/anaphor
summary: Anaphors are expressions that refer to other expressions, called antecedents. The process of connecting the two is called resolution. Cognitive science has identified multiple factors that affect the speed and success of anaphor resolution, including discourse structure, situation-model properties, and semantic factors. Here, we investigate whether these factors also affect anaphor resolution in five Large Language Models (LLMs) with open weights: GPT-2-XL, Llama-3.1-8B, Pythia-12B, Mistral-7B, and Mistral-24B. To model processing difficulty, we adopt the standard linking hypothesis that relates human reading times to model surprisal at the anaphor. As a second behavioral measure, we compare model accuracy to human accuracy on comprehension questions probing the antecedents of anaphors. The results show selective cognitive alignment: some LLMs exhibit human-like sensitivity to discourse prominence and distance-based factors in anaphor resolution, while showing weaker or absent sensitivity to semantic interference effects. These findings delimit the conditions under which LLMs approximate human anaphor resolution.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether large language models resolve anaphors (like pronouns) in ways similar to humans, finding partial but not complete alignment with human behavior.
AI.motivation: Human anaphor resolution is influenced by discourse structure, mental situation models, and semantic factors. It is unclear to what extent current LLMs exhibit the same sensitivities, which matters both for understanding their cognitive plausibility and for improving their reference resolution performance.
AI.method: The authors evaluate five open-weight LLMs (GPT-2-XL, Llama-3.1-8B, Pythia-12B, Mistral-7B, Mistral-24B) on controlled anaphor resolution materials from psycholinguistic paradigms. They measure model surprisal at anaphors as a proxy for processing difficulty and compare it to human reading-time patterns, and they also assess model accuracy on comprehension questions that ask about anaphor antecedents, comparing this to human accuracy.
AI.result: Some models show human-like patterns with respect to discourse prominence (e.g., subject vs. non-subject antecedents) and distance-based factors (e.g., effects of how far the antecedent is from the anaphor). However, across models there is weaker or no evidence that they mirror humans’ sensitivity to semantic interference, where competing semantically similar referents hinder resolution.
AI.conclusion: LLMs exhibit selective cognitive alignment with human anaphor resolution: they approximate human behavior under certain discourse- and distance-based conditions but diverge on finer-grained semantic interference effects. This constrains claims about their psychological plausibility and suggests specific areas where reference handling in LLMs could be improved.

title: Negotiating Risk Boundaries in AI for Policing Through Mixed-Stakeholder Deliberation
summary: AI tools are being increasingly adopted in policing in the UK and worldwide. Racial bias is a known and well-documented risk, yet representatives of affected communities are rarely included in decisions about AI adoption. We present results from a mixed-stakeholder deliberation workshop bringing together 30 community representatives, police officers, and academics to assess the risks of 13 AI use cases in policing, with an explicit focus on racial bias. We found that participants were broadly open to AI adoption, rejecting only three use cases outright, most notably recidivism risk assessment, where objections targeted the premise rather than the implementation. Our analysis reveals that foregrounding racial equity did not narrow the deliberation. Instead, discussions gravitated toward a fundamental set of questions: does this tool actually work, will it deliver genuine benefit, and will that benefit extend to everyone? This integrated reasoning, reminiscent of the curb-cut effect in inclusive design, highlights the benefit of incorporating the racial bias lens into the risk-benefit analysis of AI use cases from the outset.

AI.tldr: The paper examines how diverse stakeholders evaluate AI tools in policing, focusing on racial bias and finding that participants are cautiously supportive of some AI uses while emphasizing effectiveness, broad benefit, and equity.
AI.motivation: AI is increasingly used in policing, but racial bias is a major risk and affected communities are typically excluded from decisions. The paper aims to understand how different stakeholders, especially community representatives, assess AI use cases in policing when racial equity is explicitly foregrounded.
AI.method: The authors organized a deliberation workshop with 30 participants, including community representatives, police officers, and academics. They discussed and evaluated 13 AI policing use cases, with a structured focus on risks and racial bias, and then analyzed the discussions qualitatively to identify key themes in participants’ reasoning.
AI.result: Participants were generally open to AI in policing and rejected only three of the 13 use cases, with recidivism risk assessment most strongly opposed due to its underlying premise rather than technical details. Centering racial equity did not constrain debate; instead, participants consistently returned to core questions of whether each tool works, produces genuine benefits, and whether those benefits are distributed fairly across communities.
AI.conclusion: Involving diverse stakeholders and explicitly applying a racial bias lens from the outset does not limit but rather deepens and broadens deliberation about AI in policing. The authors conclude that integrating concerns about racial equity into early risk-benefit analyses can support more inclusive, effective decisions about adopting AI tools, akin to the curb-cut effect in inclusive design, where solutions designed for marginalized groups improve outcomes for everyone.

title: Relay, Don't Route: Adaptive Population Handoff for Cost-Efficient LLM-Driven Evolution
summary:
Large language model (LLM)-driven evolution has shown promise for program search and algorithm discovery, but relying on strong models throughout long evolutionary runs is costly. A natural alternative is to combine cheap and strong models under a fixed inference budget. However, existing approaches typically allocate models at the level of individual queries or mutation steps, overlooking that evolutionary search is \textit{stateful}: each generated candidate changes the population from which subsequent mutations are produced.
  We empirically analyze LLM-driven evolutionary trajectories and find that search progress is strongly front-loaded, early trajectory performance is informative but noisy, and cheap models recover much of the early progress achieved by strong models at lower cost. Motivated by these findings, we propose \textbf{\model}, a training-free framework that shifts budget allocation from individual calls to evolving populations through adaptive \textit{population handoff}. A cheap model explores multiple trajectories in short blocks allocated by a bandit scheduler. Relay Gain, defined as the marginal improvement of a compact, quality-diverse candidate bank constructed for handoff, serves as the scheduler reward and determines when to hand off. The curated candidates initialize a shared strong model population for refinement. Across four benchmarks and three budgets, \model achieves the highest mean score in 11 of 12 settings, outperforming competitive baselines. Our results suggest that in stateful search, budget allocation should be organized around the population, not the individual call.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a training-free framework that adaptively allocates inference budget between cheap and strong LLMs for evolutionary program/algorithm search by organizing decisions around evolving populations rather than individual calls, achieving state-of-the-art performance under fixed budgets.
AI.motivation: LLM-driven evolutionary search for programs and algorithms benefits from strong models but is computationally expensive over long runs. Existing budget-mixing methods assign cheap vs. strong models at the granularity of single queries or mutation steps, ignoring that evolutionary search is stateful and that each candidate alters the population for future search. There is a need for a principled way to combine cheap and strong models under a fixed inference budget that accounts for population dynamics and leads to better cost–performance tradeoffs.
AI.method: The authors empirically study LLM-driven evolutionary trajectories and identify three properties: progress is front-loaded, early trajectory performance is predictive but noisy, and cheap models can approximate early progress made by strong models. Based on this, they propose a training-free framework (\model) that introduces adaptive population handoff between cheap and strong LLMs. A cheap model is used to explore multiple candidate trajectories in short blocks, and a bandit scheduler dynamically allocates budget to these trajectories. The scheduler uses a new reward, Relay Gain, which measures the marginal improvement of a compact, quality-diverse candidate bank constructed for handoff. When Relay Gain suggests diminishing returns, the system hands off: the curated candidate bank initializes a shared population that is then refined by a stronger LLM under the remaining budget.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks and three total-budget settings, \model achieves the highest mean performance in 11 out of 12 evaluated configurations. It consistently outperforms competitive baselines that either rely solely on strong models, solely on cheap models, or mix models at the level of individual queries/mutations. The experiments show that the proposed population-level handoff and Relay Gain-based bandit scheduling yield better use of limited inference budget while maintaining or improving solution quality.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that in stateful evolutionary search with LLMs, inference budget should be allocated at the population level rather than per-call. Cheap models can effectively handle early, exploratory phases across multiple trajectories, while strong models are better reserved for later refinement. The proposed training-free \model framework operationalizes this idea with adaptive population handoff and Relay Gain, leading to superior cost–performance tradeoffs. This suggests that future methods for LLM-guided search and algorithm discovery should explicitly account for population dynamics when designing budget allocation strategies.

title: SCP-NL2TL: Selective Conformal Prediction with Semantic Verification for Natural Language to Temporal Logic Specifications
summary: Translating natural language instructions into machine-interpretable formal specifications enables robots and autonomous systems to plan, reason, and formally verify their behavior. However, existing translation models typically generate a specification for every input, even when the result is unreliable or fails to capture the user's intent, creating risks in safety-critical applications. Inspired by selective conformal prediction, we propose a selective translation framework that not only generates formal specifications but also determines when they can be trusted. Reliability is scored by two complementary black-box signals, the fidelity of the specification back-translated into natural language and the dispersion of repeated translations under exact semantic equivalence, which fail on different errors and jointly separate incorrect translations more sharply than either alone. Conformal risk control calibrates this score into a decision that accepts a specification or abstains, with a distribution-free bound on the rate at which incorrect specifications are accepted for execution, and a conformal anomaly detector on instruction embeddings screens out-of-distribution inputs before any translation is attempted. The proposed framework is general across formal specification languages, with experiments on Signal Temporal Logic (STL), Linear Temporal Logic (LTL), and geometric Spatio-Temporal Logic (SpaTiaL) demonstrating improved translation reliability, robustness under the evaluated cross-tier shifts, and effective uncertainty-aware abstention. This work establishes a foundation for trustworthy natural language interfaces by enabling AI systems to recognize when generated specifications may not be reliable.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework that translates natural language instructions into formal logic specifications while deciding when the translation is reliable enough to use, improving safety in critical robotic and autonomous systems applications.
AI.motivation: Natural language is an intuitive way for humans to instruct robots and autonomous systems, but these instructions must be converted to formal specifications for planning, reasoning, and verification. Existing models always output a specification even when they are wrong or misinterpret user intent, which is dangerous in safety-critical settings. Therefore, there is a need for a translation method that can both produce formal specifications and recognize when its own outputs are unreliable, abstaining in such cases to reduce risk.
AI.method: The paper proposes a selective translation framework inspired by selective conformal prediction. It uses two black-box reliability signals: (1) a back-translation fidelity score, measuring how well the formal specification translated back into natural language matches the original instruction; and (2) a dispersion score based on the variability of repeated translations that are semantically equivalent. These scores capture different error modes and are combined to better distinguish correct from incorrect translations. Conformal risk control is applied to calibrate the combined reliability score into an accept/abstain decision with a provable, distribution-free bound on the error rate of accepted translations. Additionally, a conformal anomaly detector on instruction embeddings identifies out-of-distribution inputs and abstains before attempting translation. The framework is instantiated and tested on multiple formal languages, including STL, LTL, and SpaTiaL.
AI.result: Across experiments in three formal specification languages (Signal Temporal Logic, Linear Temporal Logic, and geometric Spatio-Temporal Logic), the framework yields more reliable translations and better robustness to cross-tier distribution shifts compared to baselines. It effectively abstains when uncertainty is high, thereby reducing the fraction of incorrect specifications that are accepted for execution, while maintaining acceptable coverage of correct translations. The combination of back-translation fidelity and dispersion scores outperforms using either signal alone for error detection.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that natural language to formal specification translation can be made both accurate and reliably selective using conformal prediction-based techniques. By providing a principled mechanism to abstain when translations are likely incorrect and to detect out-of-distribution instructions, the framework enhances the trustworthiness of natural language interfaces for robots and autonomous systems. This establishes a basis for building AI systems that are aware of their own uncertainty and can avoid unsafe executions stemming from misunderstood instructions.

title: Answer First, Reason Later: Commitment Order in Diffusion LLMs
summary: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) can commit tokens in any order -- a freedom marketed as their core advantage over autoregressive decoding. We show that on reasoning tasks this freedom is instead the axis of failure. Logging every commitment during decoding of LLaDA-8B on GSM8K, we find that unconstrained (pure) decoding commits the final answer at 15-24% of the trajectory while half the reasoning region is still masked, and collapses to answer-only outputs on up to 90% of problems as the canvas grows. The cause is not the model's termination beliefs -- EOS "pressure" is nearly identical across decoders -- but reachability: whether the sampler may act on those beliefs at distant positions. A 2x2 prompt-decoder design shows that chain-of-thought helps only under ordered commitment (interaction +34.8 percentage points, 95% CI [26.8, 42.8]; without reasoning text the decoders are indistinguishable), an interaction we decompose into a collapse channel and an order channel and replicate on Dream-7B and MATH-500. A single-knob intervention -- frontier-gated commitment -- causally recovers the full gap (0.528 to 0.852) while preserving up to 4x parallel decoding, along a measured frontier whose optimal window flips from w=1 at full refinement to unconstrained at 8 tokens/step. Our results reframe existing window-style samplers, previously motivated by efficiency, as the minimal fix for a reasoning pathology they were never designed to address.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the core claimed advantage of masked diffusion language models—being able to commit tokens in any order—actually harms reasoning, but that a simple constraint on where commitments can be made largely fixes this while keeping parallelism benefits.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-style masked language models are promoted as superior to autoregressive LLMs because they can fill in tokens in arbitrary order and decode in parallel. However, their reasoning performance often lags behind, and the community lacks a clear understanding of why this happens and how to systematically fix it without sacrificing efficiency. The paper aims to uncover the failure mechanism behind poor reasoning in diffusion LLMs and to test whether decoding order is actually crucial for chain-of-thought style reasoning.
AI.method: The authors instrument the decoding process of a specific diffusion LLM (LLaDA-8B) on reasoning benchmarks like GSM8K, logging every token commitment along the trajectory. They compare pure (unconstrained) masked diffusion decoding to ordered/structured decoding schemes and study when and where the final answer token is committed relative to the unfolding chain-of-thought. They run a 2x2 experiment varying both the prompt (with vs without chain-of-thought) and the decoder (ordered vs unconstrained) to separate the effects of reasoning text and commitment order. They then design and test a simple decoding intervention called frontier-gated commitment, which limits where in the sequence the sampler may finalize tokens, and sweep the size of this allowed frontier window under different refinement settings and step sizes. They replicate the analysis on other models and datasets (Dream-7B, MATH-500).
AI.result: They find that in unconstrained diffusion decoding, the model often finalizes the answer extremely early: the final answer is typically committed when only 15–24% of the sampling trajectory has elapsed and while about half of the reasoning region remains masked. As sequence length (canvas size) grows, this behavior worsens, with the model collapsing to answer-only outputs on up to 90% of problems, meaning it skips the reasoning process. This collapse is not primarily driven by EOS token pressure—termination beliefs are similar across decoders—but by reachability: the sampler’s ability to act on early answer/termination beliefs at distant positions due to arbitrary-order commitments. In the 2x2 design, chain-of-thought yields a large gain only when combined with ordered commitment (+34.8 percentage points, 95% CI [26.8, 42.8]); without reasoning text, decoders perform similarly, and without ordered commitment, chain-of-thought does not help. They decompose the interaction into collapse and order channels and replicate these findings on Dream-7B and MATH-500. The proposed frontier-gated commitment intervention raises performance from 0.528 to 0.852 while still allowing up to 4x parallel decoding. They show that the optimal frontier window depends on refinement regime: at full refinement the best window is w=1 (strict order), but at 8 tokens per step it becomes effectively unconstrained, indicating a trade-off between reasoning stability and parallelism.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the celebrated freedom of arbitrary-order token commitment in masked diffusion LLMs is a core reason for their poor reasoning performance, because it lets the model prematurely commit to answers and collapse to answer-only outputs. Reasoning benefits from chain-of-thought emerge only under sufficiently ordered commitment; without controlling commitment order, adding reasoning text does little. A simple frontier-gated commitment scheme—conceptually similar to window-based samplers previously justified by efficiency—serves as a minimal but powerful fix that restores reasoning performance while preserving significant parallel decoding. This reframes window-style decoding not just as an engineering optimization but as a necessary remedy for a specific reasoning pathology in diffusion language models.

title: Stochasticity Is Not the Hard Part: Reduction and Complexity in Instructional Sequencing over Prerequisite DAGs
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Equal contribution among Y. Chen, J. Jiang, and T. Shi (alphabetical order)
summary: When a student must learn concepts connected by prerequisite dependencies, when does the order of instruction matter, and what does it cost to find the best one? We study instructional sequencing as a stochastic shortest-path problem in which attempting a concept succeeds with a state-dependent probability and failure leaves the learner state unchanged. We first prove that this stochasticity can be eliminated exactly: the problem collapses to a deterministic shortest-path problem on the lattice of prerequisite order ideals, preserving optimal values and actions. The collapse removes stochastic complexity but not combinatorial complexity: optimal sequencing remains NP-hard -- via reduction from feedback arc set in tournaments -- even with no prerequisite edges, unit costs, uniform binary nonnegative transfer, and success probabilities at least $1/2$. Hardness is not uniform: when realizable transfer preferences remain jointly acyclic with the prerequisites, any topological order of the residual joint graph is optimal, and fixed prerequisite width yields polynomial-time exact dynamic programming. A computable diagnostic, $mΔ$, bounds the value of sequencing before optimization. On 70,893 interactions from an introductory CS course, the diagnostic certifies a doubly easy regime -- little value to optimize and little space to search -- while constructed transfer instances realize the challenging regime, where myopic sequencing suffers large regret yet exact A* with a consistent heuristic expands only linearly many states on that family.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to optimally order teaching concepts with prerequisites, casting it as a stochastic shortest-path problem and showing it can be reduced to a deterministic one, characterizes when sequencing is hard or easy, and validates diagnostics and algorithms empirically.
AI.motivation: In many educational settings, students must learn multiple interdependent concepts, and the order in which those concepts are taught can affect learning efficiency. However, it is unclear when instructional order truly matters and how computationally hard it is to find the optimal sequence, especially when learning is stochastic (students succeed or fail with certain probabilities). The paper aims to rigorously model this problem, understand its algorithmic complexity, and identify structural conditions under which optimal or near-optimal sequencing is tractable and worthwhile in practice.
AI.method: The authors model instructional sequencing as a stochastic shortest-path Markov decision process where states reflect the set of mastered concepts, actions are attempts to teach a concept, transition probabilities encode success or failure of learning, and costs are associated with instruction steps. They prove an exact reduction from this stochastic problem to a deterministic shortest-path problem on the lattice of order ideals of the prerequisite partial order, preserving optimal policies. They then conduct complexity analysis, proving NP-hardness via a reduction from feedback arc set in tournaments under very restricted conditions, and identify special-case structures (acyclic transfer preferences, bounded prerequisite width) that admit polynomial-time dynamic programming or trivial optimal policies. They introduce a computable diagnostic metric, mΔ, to upper bound the potential value of sequencing optimization. Finally, they empirically evaluate the diagnostic and algorithmic behavior using data from an introductory CS course and constructed hard instances, testing myopic policies and A* search with a consistent heuristic.
AI.result: The main theoretical results are: (1) An exact collapse of the stochastic shortest-path instructional sequencing problem to a deterministic shortest-path problem over the lattice of prerequisite-consistent concept sets, with identical optimal values and actions. (2) A proof that finding an optimal sequence is NP-hard even in very simple-looking settings (no prerequisite graph edges, unit costs, uniform binary nonnegative transfer, and success probability at least 1/2), via reduction from the feedback arc set problem in tournaments, demonstrating intrinsic combinatorial hardness. (3) Identification of structural conditions under which the problem becomes easy: when transfer preferences and prerequisites form a jointly acyclic graph, any topological order is optimal, and when the prerequisite partial order has bounded width, exact dynamic programming runs in polynomial time. (4) A computable diagnostic quantity, mΔ, that upper bounds the benefit of optimizing sequencing relative to a baseline and therefore quantifies when optimization is worth the effort. Empirically, on 70,893 interactions from an introductory CS course, mΔ indicates a regime where both the marginal value of optimizing sequencing and the search space are small ("doubly easy"). In contrast, on synthetic transfer structures designed to be difficult, greedy myopic sequencing strategies perform poorly (high regret), but exact A* search with a suitable consistent heuristic explores only linearly many states on that family, showing that well-designed search can still be efficient on hard instances.
AI.conclusion: Instructional sequencing with prerequisites and stochastic learning outcomes can be rigorously framed as a shortest-path problem whose uncertainty can be removed without changing the optimal strategy, simplifying analysis but not eliminating combinatorial hardness. In general, optimally sequencing instruction is NP-hard even under strong simplifying assumptions, yet the hardness is structurally localized: when transfer relations align acyclically with prerequisites or the prerequisite width is bounded, efficient exact solutions or even trivial topological orders suffice. The proposed diagnostic mΔ allows practitioners to assess in advance whether sophisticated sequencing optimization is likely to yield meaningful gains. Empirical evidence suggests that real-world course data may often lie in an easy regime with limited upside for complex optimization, whereas specially constructed transfer patterns can realize the theoretically hard regime, in which naive myopic approaches fail but informed search (e.g., A* with a good heuristic) can still find optimal sequences with modest computational effort.

title: Sparse Mutual Information Graph Averaging for Improving Random Indexing Embeddings
summary: Sparse word embedding pipelines can avoid dense co-occurrence matrix materialization, dense factorization, and gradient training while still relying on sparse global corpus statistics. This paper studies Random Indexing (RI) vectors refined by weighted averaging on a sparse Positive Pointwise Mutual Information (PPMI) graph. On a fairytales corpus, the covered semantic analogy set consists of 272 Google family- category questions. On this family subset, PPMI top-K graph averaging repairs a weak RI initialization, improving accuracy from 19.4+-0.7% to 30.7+-2.9% across five seeds. Under the single tested runs, the same neighborhood averaging reduces family- subset analogy accuracy for PPMI+SVD (singular value decom- position), Binary+SVD, CBOW, and Skip-gram. Thus the method is not competitive with neural baselines on text8 and gives near- zero strict similarity correlation on SimLex-999. While Bloom filter sketches underperform RI in the tested configuration, we find that PPMI graph averaging with top-K pruning is a useful non-gradient repair for weak RI embeddings. On the fairytales dataset, PPMI top-K=50 graph averaging improves RI with accuracy going from 19.4+-0.7% to 30.7+-2.9%, and performing best with a seed42 of 34.6%.

AI.tldr: They test a simple, non-neural way to improve weak sparse word embeddings (Random Indexing) by averaging over a sparse PPMI graph; it helps RI on a small fairytale analogy task but is not competitive with standard neural embeddings overall.
AI.motivation: Dense word embedding methods (PPMI matrices with SVD, CBOW, Skip-gram) require dense matrices or gradient-based training, which can be expensive. The authors want to see if a very lightweight, sparse, non-gradient method—Random Indexing refined with sparse PPMI statistics—can achieve reasonable semantic performance, and whether a simple graph-based post-processing step can significantly repair weak embeddings.
AI.method:
1) Start from Random Indexing (RI) word vectors built from sparse corpus statistics.
2) Construct a sparse word-word graph based on Positive Pointwise Mutual Information (PPMI), pruned to top-K neighbors per word.
3) Refine the RI vectors by weighted averaging over each word’s neighbors in this PPMI top-K graph (a non-gradient, graph-smoothing/post-processing step).
