We argue that persistent failures for low-resource, Indigenous, and non-standard language varieties are not only technical errors, but also implicit linguistic policies that reproduce colonial language hierarchies. Drawing on linguistic capital, raciolinguistic ideology, language policy research, and decolonial computing, we show how data, metrics, and model priors determine whose voices become machine-legible. We introduce the Three Harms (3M) taxonomy---Misrecognition, Misalignment, and Mistrust---and a seven-layer situatedness model for linguistic diversity in ASR and ASR-mediated voice interfaces. We then propose a participatory framework and minimum audit protocol for culturally competent ASR, positioning affected communities as co-designers, evaluators, and governance partners.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques how current ASR systems systematically fail speakers of low-resource, Indigenous, and non-standard language varieties, arguing these failures act as de facto language policy that reinforces colonial hierarchies. It proposes a conceptual harm taxonomy (3M), a multilayer model of linguistic situatedness, and a participatory audit and design framework that centers affected communities as co-designers and governance partners.
AI.motivation: ASR systems are increasingly used as gateways to essential services like public assistance, healthcare, and education, yet they work best for high-resource, standardized, and socially dominant language varieties. Persistent underperformance for marginalized communities is usually framed as a technical limitation rather than as a structural problem. The authors are motivated to reframe these failures as forms of linguistic injustice embedded in technology design, to make visible how data choices, evaluation metrics, and model assumptions act like implicit language policy that reproduces colonial and racialized hierarchies of whose speech counts.
AI.method: The paper uses an interdisciplinary conceptual and analytical approach rather than a purely empirical benchmark study. It brings together theories of linguistic capital, raciolinguistic ideologies, language policy, and decolonial computing to analyze ASR pipelines. On this basis, it develops: (1) the Three Harms (3M) taxonomy—Misrecognition, Misalignment, and Mistrust—to categorize harms from ASR failures; (2) a seven-layer situatedness model that maps where linguistic diversity is lost or distorted in ASR and voice interface design; and (3) a participatory framework and minimum audit protocol that specify roles and procedures for involving affected speech communities in design, evaluation, and governance.
AI.result: The authors articulate how data selection, annotation, evaluation metrics, and model prior assumptions collectively determine which voices become reliably machine-legible, highlighting structural biases against low-resource, Indigenous, and non-standard varieties. They define and exemplify the Three Harms taxonomy, and describe each layer of the seven-layer situatedness model, offering a structured way to locate and analyze harms in ASR systems. They also specify concrete elements of a participatory ASR design and governance framework, including minimum auditing steps oriented toward cultural and linguistic competence rather than only accuracy metrics.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that ASR systems are not neutral technical infrastructures but active sites of language policy that can reinforce or challenge colonial and racialized hierarchies. Addressing inequities in ASR performance requires more than dataset expansion or model tuning; it needs conceptual tools to understand harms and institutional mechanisms to share power with affected communities. By adopting the 3M taxonomy, the seven-layer situatedness model, and a participatory audit and co-governance framework, researchers and practitioners can design culturally competent ASR that better supports linguistic justice and community agency.

title: Activity Frames: Deterministic Screen-Activity Compilation for Agent Memory and Replay
summary:
Computer-use agents pay full frontier inference to re-derive routines their user has already performed, because an agent's memory today records what the user said, not what the user did. We compile passively captured screen activity into agent memory with a deterministic, zero-model pipeline: it segments a local capture stream into typed activity frames, bounded episodes carrying application, site, timing, input volume, and evidence pointers back to the raw rows, with no model in the loop, so the output is byte-identical, cacheable, and mechanically auditable. On one professional's single-user corpus of 128,756 frames over 51 active days, the compiler reduces a day of raw capture to a prompt-ready context block 86x smaller in 68 ms, and an agent reading that block answers questions about the day at 98.4% accuracy (Wilson 95% CI 91.7-99.7%) against an independent oracle, versus 66-80% for an LLM summary of the same capture, a mid-tier model reading the block matching a frontier one.
  The same compiler doubles as a demand-side cost instrument. Read off passive, pre-delegation human activity rather than agent rollouts, it supplies two parameters that agent-cost models assume but, to our knowledge, have not measured: the Routine Overhead Ratio R and the routine recurrence h. We report first values of R, a modeled upper bound, at 60-343x, and a delegable recurrence of 9.0% in-sample and 7.7% out-of-sample, for a realistic all-fleet token ceiling near 8%; a compiled routine replays deterministically with the model out of the loop, demonstrated live at zero model tokens on a guard-matched hit. Schema, compiler, and evaluation harness are open.

AI.tldr: They build a deterministic “screen activity compiler” that turns raw desktop capture into structured memory for agents, making it much cheaper and more accurate for models to answer questions about what the user actually did, and they also use this data to empirically estimate how much repetitive routine work could be delegated to agents.
AI.motivation: Current AI agents waste computation re-inferring user workflows from scratch because they only see text logs, not the detailed screen actions a user took. This makes agent use expensive and brittle, and there is no good empirical basis for estimating how much of human work is routine and delegable or how costly it is for models to replay it. The authors want a deterministic, auditable way to turn raw screen activity into a compact representation that agents can use directly, and they want to measure routine overhead and recurrence from real user data.
AI.method: They passively capture the user’s screen interactions and run them through a fully deterministic, model-free pipeline that segments the continuous stream into typed “activity frames” grouped into episodes. Each frame encodes application/site, timing, input volume, and pointers back to the original capture, with no ML model involved. They evaluate this on a single professional’s 51 days of activity (128,756 frames) by compressing each day into a “prompt-ready context block.” They then compare how well an agent reading this block answers questions about the day versus an LLM that only sees a summary of the raw capture. They also interpret the compiled traces as cost data to derive two parameters: Routine Overhead Ratio R (upper bound on how much extra work agents do vs humans) and routine recurrence h (how often similar routines recur).
AI.result: On the test corpus, their compiler shrinks a full day of raw capture into a context block 86× smaller in about 68 ms. An agent conditioned on this compiled block answers questions about the day with 98.4% accuracy (Wilson 95% CI 91.7–99.7%) compared with an independent oracle, while an LLM relying on a standard summary only reaches 66–80% accuracy; a mid-tier model reading the compiled block matches the performance of a frontier model. Using the same compiled traces, they estimate Routine Overhead Ratios between about 60× and 343× and a delegable routine recurrence rate of 9.0% in-sample and 7.7% out-of-sample, suggesting a realistic total fleet token budget near 8% if such routines are delegated. They also demonstrate that once a routine is compiled, it can be replayed deterministically with zero model tokens for certain guarded hits.
AI.conclusion: A deterministic, model-free compiler from passive screen capture into structured activity frames gives AI agents a compact, auditable memory of what users actually did, significantly improving accuracy and efficiency compared with text-only or summary-based approaches. The same representation enables empirical estimation of routine overhead and recurrence, indicating substantial but bounded opportunities for safe, low-cost delegation of repetitive digital work. The authors release the schema, compiler, and evaluation harness as open infrastructure for further research and deployment.

title: Routing Is Least Learnable Where It Is Most Valuable: Bounds on Representation Routing for Web Agents
comment: Preprint. Under review at the Second Workshop for Research on Agent Language Models (REALM), EMNLP 2026 (non-archival track)
summary: Web agents observe a browser through text, pixels, or both, and the choice is usually fixed once for all tasks. We measure six observation modes across eight site-model combinations (cells) on VisualWebArena and WebArena and ask what choosing per task would buy. The modes are complementary: each solves tasks the others miss, they fail in structurally different ways, and the best choice reverses between task sets. The obvious prize, an oracle that picks a winning mode for every task, looks large but is inflated by run-to-run noise: rerunning the same mode on the same tasks changes 12-14% of outcomes, so a second run of a mode already in hand gains about as much as adding a new one. What survives is a cost bound: sending only the tasks no mode solves to the cheapest mode cuts cost by 9.5-30.6% in 8 of 8 cells at unchanged success. We then test five routing policies (picking the mode, deciding when to spend on the strong mode, a zero-cost rule read off the task text, a confidence cascade, and pooled cost tiers), and none robustly beats simply fixing one well-chosen mode; the one exception is a fragile result in our sparsest cell. The central obstruction is that routing supervision is produced at the agent's success rate: the weaker the agent, the fewer labels a router gets, exactly where routing would be most valuable. This limit belongs to today's agents rather than to routing itself. Label supply and routing opportunity rise together (correlation 0.95 across cells), so a stronger agent can overturn the result, and we report the rerun noise bands and the full measurement protocol.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different observation modes (text, pixels, or both) for web agents perform across tasks and whether adaptively routing tasks to modes helps, finding that simple mode fixing often matches or beats routing due to noisy supervision and limited labels.
AI.motivation: Web agents can observe a browser via text, pixels, or a combination, but current systems usually fix one mode for all tasks. It is unclear how much would be gained by choosing the observation mode per task and by using routing policies to decide which mode to use when, especially under cost constraints and noisy performance. The authors aim to quantify the complementarity of modes, the benefit of an oracle selector, and the practical value of routing given realistic supervision limits.
AI.method: The authors evaluate six different observation modes across eight site-model combinations on the VisualWebArena and WebArena benchmarks. They measure success rates, failure patterns, and run-to-run variance (rerun noise) to estimate the benefit of an oracle mode selector versus fixed modes. They then design and test five routing policies, including cost-aware selection between strong and weak modes, a free heuristic based on task text, a confidence-based cascade, and pooled cost tiers, comparing them to the best single fixed mode. They also analyze label availability for routing as a function of agent success rates and measure correlations between label supply and routing opportunity.
AI.result: The six observation modes are complementary: each solves tasks missed by others and fails in different ways, with the best mode varying across task sets. A hypothetical oracle that always picks the best mode per task appears to offer large gains, but these are substantially inflated by rerun noise: repeating the same mode on the same tasks changes outcomes in 12–14% of cases, so simply rerunning a given mode yields gains comparable to adding a new mode. A robust cost-saving strategy emerges: routing only those tasks unsolved by any cheaper mode to the cheapest remaining mode reduces cost by 9.5–30.6% in all eight site-model cells without reducing success. However, none of the five tested routing policies consistently outperforms using a single, well-chosen fixed mode; an apparent win occurs only in the sparsest cell and is fragile given noise.
AI.conclusion: In the current regime of web agents, adaptive routing over observation modes offers limited practical benefit over using a single well-chosen mode, primarily because supervision for training routers is constrained by the agents’ own success rates. Noise in agent performance inflates the perceived gains of idealized mode selection, and realistic routing policies fail to robustly beat fixed-mode baselines. Nonetheless, cost-aware routing that escalates unsolved tasks to a cheap strong mode can reduce costs while preserving success, and the analysis suggests that as agents become stronger and provide more reliable labels, routing could become substantially more valuable. The authors provide noise estimates and a detailed measurement protocol to guide future work as agent capabilities improve.

title: ChainClaw: A Layered Agent Framework for Reliable On-Chain Execution
summary: General-purpose large language model agents have achieved strong performance on tool-augmented tasks, yet they rely on assumptions break down in blockchain environments. On-chain execution is stateful, adversarial, and economically irreversible, exposing three fundamental gaps: Reactivity, Irreversibility, and Observability. We propose ChainClaw, a blockchain-native agent framework built on OpenClaw, that addresses all three gaps through a layered architecture comprising an event-driven orchestration layer, a simulation-based safety intelligence layer, and an on-chain monitoring runtime layer, unified by a cross-layer memory subsystem. ChainClaw closes the Reactivity gap via event ingestion and simulation feedback, the Irreversibility gap via a pre-execution safety pipeline with transaction simulation and action guard, and the Observability gap via an on-chain read adapter and transaction monitor. We evaluate ChainClaw on a purpose-built benchmark covering seven tasks across four categories and five dimensions. ChainClaw consistently outperforms representative baselines on both safety and task completion.

AI.tldr: ChainClaw is a blockchain-native LLM agent framework that makes on-chain tool use more reactive, safer before irreversible execution, and better monitored/observable, outperforming existing baselines on safety and task success.
AI.motivation: Existing general-purpose LLM agents work well with tools in conventional settings but fail to account for key properties of blockchain environments: stateful execution, adversarial behavior, and economically irreversible transactions. These properties expose three critical shortcomings in current approaches—limited real-time reactivity to on-chain events, lack of safeguards before irreversible transactions are sent, and poor observability of on-chain state and agent actions. There is a need for an agent framework that is specifically designed around these blockchain constraints and risk profiles.
AI.method: The authors design ChainClaw, a blockchain-native agent framework layered on top of OpenClaw. Its architecture has: (1) an event-driven orchestration layer that ingests on-chain events and simulation feedback to trigger and coordinate agent behaviors, (2) a simulation-based safety intelligence layer that performs a pre-execution safety pipeline—transaction simulation and action guarding—to filter or modify risky actions before they hit the chain, and (3) an on-chain monitoring runtime layer that provides an on-chain read adapter and transaction monitor for continuous observability. A cross-layer memory subsystem unifies state and information flow across these layers. The framework is then instantiated and evaluated on a benchmark specifically constructed to capture typical on-chain agent tasks across multiple categories and evaluation dimensions.
AI.result: On a custom benchmark with seven tasks spanning four categories and five evaluation dimensions, ChainClaw is empirically compared against representative baseline agent frameworks. Across this benchmark, ChainClaw consistently achieves higher task completion rates and better safety metrics, indicating that it reduces harmful or risky on-chain actions while still successfully finishing tasks.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that general-purpose LLM agent frameworks are insufficient for blockchain because they ignore reactivity, irreversibility, and observability constraints. ChainClaw, with its blockchain-native, layered design and cross-layer memory, effectively closes these three gaps. The experimental results suggest that ChainClaw yields safer and more capable on-chain agents, highlighting the importance of environment-specific agent architectures for high-stakes, adversarial, and irreversible domains like blockchain.

title: NeSy-RAG: Neuro-Symbolic RAG for Explainable Question Answering
summary:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves question answering by grounding large language models (LLMs) in external knowledge such as text corpora. However, its reasoning process remains largely opaque: intermediate reasoning steps are difficult to verify and cannot be reliably attributed to specific evidence. Moreover, missing user-specific context is rarely detected systematically, often leading to incomplete or incorrect output.
  We propose NeSy-RAG, a modular neuro-symbolic RAG framework that synthesizes attributable Prolog modules from retrieved text chunks. For each chunk, the system generates semantically meaningful predicates that encode Boolean claims, which may depend on user facts. Using joint natural language-code embeddings, predicates are retrieved and composed into Prolog queries. To address incomplete user context, we introduce a symbolic knowledge-gap detection mechanism that identifies missing user facts whose truth values affect the query outcome and automatically triggers follow-up interactions.
  Executing the resulting Prolog queries yields deterministic answers together with transparent execution traces that link each reasoning step to its originating source. On the ShARC benchmark, without domain-specific training, NeSy-RAG achieves 61.1% accuracy, outperforming a same-model RAG baseline that achieves 42.8% accuracy.

AI.tldr: NeSy-RAG is a neuro-symbolic RAG framework that turns retrieved text into Prolog modules, enabling transparent, verifiable reasoning and automatic detection of missing user context, significantly improving QA accuracy over a standard RAG baseline.
AI.motivation: Standard retrieval-augmented generation enhances LLMs with external knowledge but keeps reasoning opaque: intermediate steps are not easily checked or attributed to evidence, and the system usually fails to detect when crucial user-specific facts are missing, leading to unreliable or incomplete answers.
AI.method: NeSy-RAG decomposes RAG into neuro-symbolic modules. From each retrieved text chunk, it synthesizes Prolog modules by generating semantically meaningful Boolean predicates that may depend on user-provided facts. It uses joint natural-language/code embeddings to retrieve and compose these predicates into Prolog queries. A symbolic knowledge-gap detector inspects the logic program to identify which unknown user facts would change the query outcome, and automatically triggers follow-up questions to the user to obtain them.
AI.result: Running the constructed Prolog queries produces deterministic answers and explicit execution traces that map each reasoning step back to its source text. On the ShARC benchmark, and without domain-specific fine-tuning, NeSy-RAG attains 61.1% accuracy, significantly outperforming a standard RAG baseline using the same base model, which reaches 42.8% accuracy.
AI.conclusion: By integrating symbolic Prolog reasoning with neural retrieval and predicate synthesis, NeSy-RAG turns RAG into an interpretable and attributable process that can proactively detect missing user-specific information. This yields both higher accuracy and more transparent, verifiable QA compared to conventional black-box RAG systems.

title: When Agentic AI Meets Integrated Sensing and Communication
summary: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) from a function-oriented physical-layer technology into a goal-driven, closed-loop intelligent system, a paradigm we term AISAC. Existing work on learning-based sensing, resource allocation, reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS), edge intelligence, multi-agent coordination, and resilient networking has developed largely in isolation. This survey unifies the literature within a six-stage closed-loop framework comprising observation, contextualization, reasoning and prediction, planning and orchestration, execution and collaboration, and feedback and resilience. It also introduces five levels of agentic maturity, ranging from physical-layer primitives to fully closed-loop agentic ISAC. We use this framework to review advances in multimodal intelligence, large language models, reinforcement learning, federated learning, RIS-assisted control, Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) and vehicular networks, and AI-native network management, and analyze privacy, security, resilience, and sustainability as cross-cutting requirements of the full perception-reasoning-action loop. An audit of representative studies against nine agentic-specific evaluation criteria shows that no system reports more than one or two of them, exposing a gap between claimed and demonstrated agentic maturity. We identify open challenges in physical-to-semantic grounding, predictive world models, real-time agent-PHY interaction, safe tool use, heterogeneous multi-agent collaboration, benchmarking, and resource-efficient autonomy.

AI.tldr: Survey paper proposing a unified framework and maturity levels for agentic AI in Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC), reviewing current technologies and highlighting gaps and challenges toward fully closed-loop intelligent AISAC systems.
AI.motivation: Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) is evolving from a low-level, function-specific physical-layer technology toward intelligent systems that can autonomously perceive, reason, and act. Existing research on components such as learning-based sensing, RIS, edge intelligence, and multi-agent coordination is fragmented, making it hard to assess progress toward truly agentic ISAC. A unified conceptual and evaluative framework is needed to organize prior work, clarify what “agentic” means in this context, and reveal maturity gaps and research priorities.
AI.method: The authors construct a six-stage closed-loop framework for AISAC—observation; contextualization; reasoning and prediction; planning and orchestration; execution and collaboration; and feedback and resilience—and define five levels of agentic maturity from basic physical-layer elements to fully closed-loop systems. Using this structure, they survey literature across multimodal AI, large language models, reinforcement and federated learning, RIS-based control, UAV and vehicular networks, and AI-native network management. They further define nine evaluation criteria specific to agentic behavior and audit representative studies against these criteria to assess their agentic maturity.
AI.result: The survey shows that while many works incorporate AI and automation into ISAC components, nearly all fall short of full agentic behavior. Most systems satisfy at most one or two of the proposed agentic evaluation criteria, revealing a significant gap between the ambitious claims of agentic or autonomous operation and the capabilities actually implemented and demonstrated. The framework also maps how privacy, security, resilience, and sustainability cut across all stages of the AISAC loop.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that current ISAC research is only at early to intermediate stages of agentic maturity and that realizing fully closed-loop AISAC will require advances in several areas. Key open problems include grounding between physical signals and semantic understanding, developing predictive world models, enabling real-time interaction between agents and the physical layer, safe and robust tool use, scalable heterogeneous multi-agent coordination, standardized benchmarking, and achieving autonomy under tight resource constraints. The proposed framework and evaluation criteria aim to guide and accelerate coherent progress toward mature agentic ISAC systems.

title: Benchmarking and Enhancing LLMs for Rule-Intensive Review of National Standard Documents
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support complex professional tasks, yet their capabilities in rule-intensive document review remain insufficiently evaluated. National standard documents, such as China GB/T standards, offer a representative testbed: they are lengthy, highly structured, and governed by explicit rules for scope, terminology, normative wording, and cross-section consistency. Existing benchmarks focus on domain knowledge and question answering, largely overlooking intrinsic quality review for professional documents. Such reviews rely heavily on human experts, making them costly and difficult to scale. To bridge this gap, we introduce GB/T-Bench, the first benchmark for the structured review of national standard documents. Its GB/T Review Taxonomy is a hierarchical schema covering document structure, scope alignment, normative modality, terminology consistency, and normative references, with 25 diagnosable error types. A controllable counterexample generation mechanism combines deterministic rules and constrained LLM rewriting to process 488 documents into 7,306 traceable review error instances for evaluation. We also develop a diagnosis-oriented evaluation protocol requiring exact matches on error location, review dimension, and error type, plus document-level coverage metrics. We further propose GB/T-Reviewer, a multi-agent framework that converts review knowledge into specialized skills and coordinates global inspection, targeted diagnosis, rule scanning, and result verification. Experiments with 14 mainstream LLMs reveal a substantial human-LLM gap: the strongest model achieves only 0.3280 CMCS versus 0.6640 for experts. GB/T-Reviewer raises the best CMCS to 0.5094, showing the value of structured skill coordination for rule-intensive document review. This work paves the way for trustworthy AI in standardization and other high-stakes document domains.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GB/T-Bench, a benchmark and multi-agent framework (GB/T-Reviewer) to evaluate and enhance LLMs’ ability to perform structured, rule-intensive review of national standard documents, revealing a large gap between LLMs and human experts while showing skill-coordination can substantially narrow it.
AI.motivation: LLMs are being used for complex professional tasks, but their performance on rule-intensive document review—such as reviewing national standards governed by strict rules on structure, terminology, scope, and consistency—has not been systematically evaluated. Existing benchmarks emphasize domain QA rather than intrinsic quality review, which is costly and heavily reliant on human experts. The authors are motivated to provide a rigorous, scalable way to assess and improve LLMs in this critical area.
AI.method: The authors construct GB/T-Bench based on China’s GB/T national standards. They design a hierarchical GB/T Review Taxonomy capturing dimensions like document structure, scope alignment, normative modality, terminology consistency, and normative references, defining 25 diagnosable error types. A controllable counterexample generation pipeline combines deterministic rule-based operations with constrained LLM rewriting to inject realistic, traceable errors into 488 GB/T documents, yielding 7,306 labeled error instances. They create a strict, diagnosis-oriented evaluation protocol that demands exact matches on error location, review dimension, and error type, supplemented by document-level coverage metrics. Additionally, they propose GB/T-Reviewer, a multi-agent system that decomposes review knowledge into specialized agents responsible for global inspection, targeted diagnosis, rule scanning, and verification, coordinating them to perform structured reviews.
AI.result: Using GB/T-Bench, the authors benchmark 14 mainstream LLMs and compare them with human experts. The best-performing standalone LLM attains a CMCS score of 0.3280, whereas human experts achieve 0.6640, indicating a substantial performance gap. When equipped with the GB/T-Reviewer multi-agent framework, the best model’s CMCS rises to 0.5094, showing a significant performance boost from structured skill coordination but still not reaching human performance. The benchmark also provides granular diagnostics across the 25 error types and review dimensions, evidencing systematic weaknesses of current LLMs in rule-intensive document review.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that current LLMs are far from matching human experts in structured, rule-intensive review of national standard documents, but their performance can be substantially improved through explicitly structured, multi-agent review frameworks. GB/T-Bench offers a rigorous, fine-grained benchmark to evaluate such capabilities and reveals where models fail, while GB/T-Reviewer demonstrates that decomposing review into specialized skills and coordinated agents is an effective strategy. The work lays a foundation for developing trustworthy AI tools for standardization and other high-stakes document domains where correctness, consistency, and compliance with formal rules are critical.

title: When Self-Evolution Backfires: Pre-Commit Gating against Skill Contamination in LLM Agents
summary: Self-evolving agents accumulate capability by distilling reusable skills from their execution trajectories, but we find this process is not monotonic: past a critical pool size, newly added skills degrade performance instead of improving it. We formalize this capability-contamination phase transition and trace it to a structural cause: once a defective skill enters the decision context, it becomes reference material for distilling later skills, forming cross-round contamination chains. We further show the contamination is structurally irreversible: removing a source skill after the fact cannot erase the flawed reasoning its descendants have already inherited, so post-hoc rollback recovers only a small fraction of the lost performance. This makes skill admission a pre-commit necessity rather than a post-hoc fix, and motivates Verifier-as-Gatekeeper (VaG): a progressive trust hierarchy whose three heterogeneous critics - structural validity, behavioral harmlessness, and semantic consistency - filter each skill individually, coupled with a marginal-gain subset selection that removes combinatorial contamination at the top tier before skills reach the runtime context. On Terminal-Bench 2, unconditional accumulation rises to a peak and then degrades, giving back most of its gains as the pool keeps growing, and post-hoc removal of the culprit skills recovers only a small part of the drop - the empirical signature of irreversibility. In contrast, VaG improves every round, reaching 72% pass@1 with a pool roughly 5x smaller, and its frozen skill pool transfers positively to four other backbones and a second benchmark without re-evolution. Ablations confirm the three critics are complementary and mutually non-substitutable, each intercepting a largely disjoint class of harmful skills.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how self-evolving agents that learn skills from their own trajectories can suffer a phase transition where adding more skills actually harms performance, then proposes a verification-based gatekeeping mechanism to prevent this capability contamination.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving agents aim to continually improve by distilling reusable skills from their own past behaviors. However, it is unclear whether simply accumulating more skills guarantees better performance over time. The authors observe that beyond a certain point, adding more skills can actually degrade performance, suggesting a structural issue in how skills are selected and integrated. They are motivated to understand and formalize this degradation, identify its root cause, and design a method to safely scale skill libraries without introducing harmful reasoning patterns.
AI.method: The authors first empirically and conceptually analyze the dynamics of skill accumulation in self-evolving agents and formalize a "capability-contamination" phase transition, where defective skills contaminate future skill distillation through decision contexts. They identify cross-round contamination chains and prove that this process is structurally irreversible: removing harmful skills later does not remove their influence on descendant skills. Based on this analysis, they propose Verifier-as-Gatekeeper (VaG), which introduces a progressive trust hierarchy of three heterogeneous critics: (1) structural validity, (2) behavioral harmlessness, and (3) semantic consistency. Each proposed skill is individually filtered by these critics. At the top tier, a marginal-gain subset selection step further removes combinations of skills that could cause higher-order contamination before they are admitted to the runtime context. They evaluate the approach on Terminal-Bench 2 and transfer it across different model backbones and benchmarks, with ablations to test the contribution of each critic.
AI.result: On Terminal-Bench 2, naive or unconditional skill accumulation shows an initial performance increase but then degrades as more skills are added, eventually giving back most of the early gains. Post-hoc identification and removal of the worst culprits only recovers a small fraction of the lost performance, empirically validating the irreversibility of contamination. In contrast, Verifier-as-Gatekeeper yields monotonically improving performance across rounds, achieving 72% pass@1 while using a skill pool roughly five times smaller than the baseline. Moreover, the resulting frozen skill pool transfers positively to four other model backbones and an additional benchmark without requiring re-evolution. Ablation studies show that each of the three critics captures a different type of harmful skill and that removing any one of them significantly reduces the overall protection against contamination.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that self-evolving skill libraries are vulnerable to a structural capability-contamination phase transition: once defective skills enter the evolution process, they spawn contaminated descendants that cannot be fully removed by post-hoc rollback. Therefore, safe skill evolution requires strict pre-admission checks rather than reactive cleanup. Verifier-as-Gatekeeper, with its three complementary critics and marginal-gain subset selection, provides a robust mechanism for building compact, transferable, and monotonically improving skill pools. The results suggest that careful verification and selection are essential design principles for scalable self-evolving agents.

title: Benchmarking the Benchmarks: Evaluating Benchmarks for Conversational Agents
summary: Task-oriented conversational agents are evaluated using curated or automatically generated benchmarks, yet benchmark quality is rarely assessed. Poor benchmarks may contain inconsistent tasks, simplistic scenarios, or limited policy coverage, leading to unreliable evaluations. We introduce a reference-free framework that uses LLM judges to assess benchmark consistency, complexity, and policy coverage, while providing actionable diagnostics of weaknesses. We validate the framework by demonstrating agreement with independent human annotations and by evaluating benchmarks generated by LLMs of varying capabilities, as well as benchmarks subjected to controlled quality-degrading perturbations. Across domains and judge models, the proposed metrics consistently distinguish between benchmark quality levels. We further demonstrate the framework's applicability to manually curated benchmarks. Our framework offers a practical approach for evaluating synthetic and manually curated conversational-agent benchmarks.

AI.tldr: They propose a way, using LLM judges, to automatically evaluate the quality of task-oriented conversational-agent benchmarks themselves (not the agents), and show it aligns with human judgment and works on both synthetic and human-made benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks for task-oriented conversational agents are often taken at face value, but their own quality is rarely scrutinized, which can lead to unreliable evaluations if the benchmarks contain issues like inconsistent tasks, overly simple scenarios, or poor coverage of the agent’s policy space. There is a need for a systematic, scalable method to assess and compare the quality of such benchmarks.
AI.method: They design a reference-free evaluation framework that leverages large language models as judges to score benchmarks along three key dimensions: (1) consistency of tasks/dialogues, (2) complexity of scenarios, and (3) coverage of the agent’s policy space. The framework also produces diagnostic information identifying specific weaknesses. They validate it by: (a) measuring agreement between LLM-judge outputs and independent human annotations, (b) applying it to benchmarks generated by LLMs of different capabilities, and (c) applying controlled perturbations that degrade benchmark quality to test whether the metrics respond appropriately. They test multiple domains and judge models to examine robustness.
AI.result: The proposed metrics, across different domains and choice of LLM judge, reliably separate high-quality from low-quality benchmarks. The scores track both differences in benchmark generation quality (e.g., stronger vs weaker LLM-generated benchmarks) and artificial degradations introduced via controlled perturbations. The framework also works on existing human-curated benchmarks, providing useful diagnostics rather than just single aggregate scores.
AI.conclusion: Using LLMs as reference-free judges is an effective and practical way to evaluate the quality of both synthetic and manually curated task-oriented conversational-agent benchmarks. The framework consistently differentiates benchmark quality levels, aligns well with human judgments, and offers actionable insights into benchmark weaknesses, making it a useful tool for building and maintaining reliable evaluation sets for conversational agents.

title: Cautious Context Steering for Language Model Personalization
summary: Personalizing language models (LMs) to individual user preferences is essential for aligning responses with diverse goals and backgrounds. Existing methods typically train a separate adapter for each user or learn a reward model whose scores depend on the user. Despite explicitly optimizing for each user, these methods must learn from limited observations and therefore suffer from data sparsity and poor generalization to unseen users and domains. In-context learning (ICL) and Context Steering (CoS) can instead provide more effective personalization by conditioning the base LM directly on user context and leveraging its pretrained capabilities without per-user training. Yet neither adapts the influence of that context across decoding steps: ICL leaves it uncontrolled, whereas CoS applies a fixed steering coefficient and requires two LM forward passes per step. We propose Cautious Context Steering (CCS), which adds a lightweight adapter to a frozen backbone LM to decide at each token whether and how strongly user context should affect generation. The adapter learns this behavior from an oracle context-conditioned LM and preserves the base LM when the context is not helpful. A single CCS adapter trained on only one dataset improves generation quality both in-domain and across four out-of-distribution personalization benchmarks, demonstrating robust generalization to new users and domains. CCS also avoids per-user fine-tuning and the additional context-conditioned forward pass required by CoS, substantially reducing inference cost.

AI.tldr: They propose Cautious Context Steering (CCS), a lightweight adapter that dynamically decides how much user context should influence each generated token, improving personalized language model outputs and generalizing well to new users and domains with lower inference cost.
AI.motivation: Personalizing language models to individual users is important but current approaches either require per-user adapters or user-conditioned reward models, both of which suffer from data sparsity, limited generalization to unseen users and domains, and higher training or inference costs. Existing context-based methods like in-context learning and fixed-coefficient Context Steering cannot adapt the influence of user context over the course of generation and can be computationally expensive.
AI.method: They introduce Cautious Context Steering (CCS), which attaches a lightweight adapter to a frozen base language model. At each decoding step, this adapter decides whether and how strongly the external user context should affect token generation. The adapter is trained to imitate an oracle context-conditioned language model, learning when context is beneficial while defaulting to the base model when it is not, thus dynamically modulating context influence without modifying the backbone LM.
AI.result: A single CCS adapter trained on one personalization dataset improves generation quality on that dataset and also on four out-of-distribution personalization benchmarks. It demonstrates strong generalization to new users and domains. Compared with Context Steering, CCS avoids per-user finetuning and eliminates the need for an extra context-conditioned forward pass, lowering inference costs while maintaining or improving personalization quality.
AI.conclusion: CCS provides an efficient and effective way to personalize language models by dynamically controlling the impact of user context during decoding. It generalizes well across users and domains from a single training dataset, preserves the base model when context is unhelpful, and reduces inference overhead relative to prior context-steering methods, making it a practical approach for scalable personalization.

title: RP-OPSD: Reasoning-Pivot-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation for Multilingual Reasoning Transfer
summary: Multilingual reasoning transfer is crucial for extending reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) beyond high-resource languages. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) and its variants have emerged as a promising paradigm, providing dense token-level supervision on student-generated rollouts, yet their objectives do not explicitly prioritize reasoning signals most critical to cross-lingual transfer. We characterize that target-language reasoning comprises the generation of both surface text and reasoning pivots, which are decisions that advance or redirect the reasoning process and shape subsequent inference. This motivates concentrating privileged distillation around such pivots. We therefore propose RP-OPSD, Reasoning-Pivot-guided On-Policy Self-Distillation, using the distributional shift between matched teacher views with and without an English reference solution as an operational proxy to guide privileged distillation and reference anchoring. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks covering 17 languages and multiple difficulty levels show that our method outperforms strong multilingual reasoning baselines and OPSD variants. Further analysis reveals that RP-OPSD concentrates privileged distillation on reasoning-control and problem-condistioned state-update tokens, while downweighting it for tokens that mainly support surface realization. Our code is available at https://github.com/NJUNLP/RP-OPSD.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RP-OPSD, a reasoning-pivot-guided self-distillation method that better transfers reasoning abilities of large language models across multiple languages by focusing training on key reasoning tokens rather than all tokens equally.
AI.motivation: Existing multilingual reasoning transfer methods, especially on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) variants, provide dense token-level supervision but treat all tokens similarly, without explicitly focusing on the most important reasoning signals for cross-lingual transfer. There is a need to identify and emphasize the parts of target-language reasoning that truly drive the reasoning process, to improve performance on low- and mid-resource languages.
AI.method: The authors conceptualize target-language reasoning as consisting of surface text and reasoning pivots—tokens representing key decisions that advance or redirect the reasoning trajectory. They propose RP-OPSD (Reasoning-Pivot-guided On-Policy Self-Distillation), which uses distributional shifts between two teacher views (one with and one without an English reference solution) to identify where the teacher’s behavior changes the most. These high-shift positions serve as an operational proxy for reasoning pivots. Privileged distillation and reference anchoring are then concentrated around those pivot tokens rather than uniformly across all tokens.
AI.result: On mathematical reasoning benchmarks across 17 languages and multiple difficulty levels, RP-OPSD outperforms strong multilingual reasoning baselines and standard OPSD variants. Analysis of the learned behavior shows that the method indeed focuses privileged distillation on reasoning-control and problem-conditioned state-update tokens while de-emphasizing tokens associated mainly with surface-level realization.
AI.conclusion: Focusing self-distillation on inferred reasoning pivots, instead of all generated tokens, yields better multilingual reasoning transfer for LLMs. RP-OPSD offers a practical way to detect and weight these pivots via teacher distribution shifts induced by an English reference, leading to improved cross-lingual mathematical reasoning performance and more targeted supervision on key reasoning steps.

title: ViSR-KGC: Visual Subgraph Reasoning with Vision-Language Models for Multimodal Knowledge Graph Completion
summary: Knowledge graph completion (KGC) aims to infer missing entities or relations from incomplete graph structures, and has evolved into multimodal knowledge graph completion (MMKGC), where entities are associated with multiple modalities such as text and images. Traditional representation learning approaches follow the embedding-based paradigm and may struggle when relation-specific evidence is limited. Meanwhile, LLM-based reasoning methods typically linearize graph structures into textual prompts, which obscures structural topology and neglects vital visual information. While vision-language models (VLMs) excel at multimodal reasoning, they cannot natively interpret structured graph topology, particularly when it comes to knowledge graphs where nodes and edges carry complex semantics. To bridge this gap, we propose ViSR-KGC, a visual subgraph reasoning approach for KGC. It integrates three complementary capabilities to capture semantic correlations: identifying global topology dependencies via representation learning, analyzing local multimodal evidence using VLMs, and providing necessary commonsense knowledge inherent in pre-trained models. Based on learned multimodal embeddings, our framework first extracts a compact and query-aware subgraph from the MMKG. Then, this subgraph is transformed into a visually interpretable image using a layout strategy selected through empirical comparison.Finally, the visualized subgraph, entity images, textual descriptions, and candidate answers are combined into a unified prompt, enabling the VLM to infer the missing entity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ViSR-KGC, a visual subgraph reasoning method that converts multimodal knowledge graph neighborhoods into images and prompts a vision-language model to complete missing entities.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal KGC methods either rely on embedding-based models that fail when relation-specific training evidence is scarce, or on LLM reasoning that ignores graph topology and visual information. Current VLMs are strong in multimodal reasoning but cannot directly understand structured graph data like knowledge graphs. There is a gap in leveraging VLMs to reason over both multimodal content and explicit graph structure for KGC.
AI.method: The authors design ViSR-KGC, which first learns multimodal embeddings for nodes and relations in a multimodal knowledge graph. Using these embeddings, the model extracts a compact, query-aware subgraph relevant to the KGC query. This subgraph is then visualized as an image using an empirically chosen layout strategy to preserve topology. The visualized subgraph, along with entity images, textual descriptions, and candidate answers, is packed into a unified prompt for a vision-language model, which performs the final reasoning to infer the missing entity. The framework combines three capabilities: global topology modeling via representation learning, local multimodal reasoning via VLMs, and commonsense knowledge from pre-trained models.
AI.result: Although not detailed in the abstract, the implication is that ViSR-KGC achieves improved KGC performance by enabling VLMs to exploit graph topology and multimodal evidence, outperforming prior embedding-only or text-linearization approaches on MMKGC benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Transforming multimodal knowledge graph substructures into visual formats allows VLMs to effectively incorporate explicit graph topology, multimodal entity information, and pretrained commonsense for knowledge graph completion. ViSR-KGC demonstrates that visual subgraph reasoning is a promising direction for MMKGC, bridging the gap between graph-structured data and vision-language reasoning models.

title: The Bitter Lesson of Tool Calling
summary: Tool use transforms LLMs into agents that act beyond their training data, and for code-capable models, programmatic tool calling extends this further by replacing rigid JSON calls with scripts that chain and parallelize naturally. However, a systematic evaluation of tools as code on an established benchmark across current and prior model generations under real-world task conditions has not been conducted. In this work, we empirically compare programmatic tool calling (PTC) to native JSON tool calling across 14 language models on BFCL v4. In the programmatic tool calling paradigm, tools are exposed as typed Python stubs that the model invokes through code, with execution and results handled in a single agent turn. Programmatic tool calling matches or exceeds native JSON tool calling in 11 of 14 models on BFCL v4, with the GPT-5.6 family achieving a 10.6% improvement over the JSON tool calling baseline. Further, it matches or outperforms baseline in 13 of 14 models under parallel fan-out, and holds stable under context rot conditions where baseline degrades 2.3% on average. Our results demonstrate that programmatic tool calling is a viable and robust alternative to JSON tool calling, with performance tracking model capability across release generations.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates programmatic tool calling (PTC)—where LLMs call tools via Python code—against traditional JSON tool calling across many models on BFCL v4, finding PTC generally matches or outperforms JSON in accuracy and robustness.
AI.motivation: While LLMs can call tools via JSON, this interface is rigid and doesn’t naturally support chaining, parallelization, or more complex tool use; code-capable models could instead invoke tools via scripts, but there has been no systematic, benchmarked comparison of this programmatic approach versus JSON across model generations and realistic conditions.
AI.method: The authors expose tools as typed Python function stubs and let models generate code that calls these tools, executes them, and consumes their outputs in a single agent turn. They then compare this programmatic tool calling paradigm to standard native JSON tool calling on the BFCL v4 benchmark using 14 different language models, including the GPT‑5.6 family, and stress-test both approaches under scenarios like parallel fan-out and context rotation (context rot).
AI.result: Across the 14 evaluated models, programmatic tool calling matches or exceeds JSON tool calling performance for 11 models on BFCL v4; GPT‑5.6 models gain about 10.6% accuracy over their JSON baseline. Under parallel fan-out conditions, PTC matches or outperforms JSON in 13 of 14 models and remains stable under context-rotated inputs, whereas JSON tool calling degrades by an average of 2.3%.
AI.conclusion: Programmatic tool calling via code is a strong, robust alternative to JSON-based tool calling. It scales with model capability, often improves performance, handles parallel and complex tool use better, and maintains robustness under noisy or reordered context, indicating it is a promising default interface for tool-augmented, code-capable LLM agents.

title: Runtime Observability for Heterogeneous Attention Memory
comment: 29 pages, 5 figures. Code, artifacts, and Lean 4 development: https://github.com/metask-ai/witprobe-attention-memory
summary: Modern models no longer keep a plain KV cache: latent caches, learned sparse selectors and recurrent states each carry the model's memory in a different form, and each fails differently under compression. We give a runtime observability contract that covers all four memory classes with three operators, instantiate it on six model configurations across five architecture families, and compose the per-stage bounds into an executable request-level risk ledger. Contracts carry their error metric as a type -- composition is only defined when metrics match, and this check rejected our own first composed chain; the repaired chain crosses metrics through two proved bridges, and whatever no formal system can certify is measured instead, dropping the composed tier to empirical automatically: every claim is certified, partially certified, or empirical, composition inherits the weakest tier, and the tier is decided by the machine. Replayed over $12.4$M entry reads and run under eight-way concurrency with per-request budgets and fail-closed identity attribution, the ledger quantifies the honest trade-off on today's witness and holds its risk budget with zero violations. A fused always-on probe observes a declared one-layer subset under CUDA graphs inside the serving noise floor. Applied to a served DeepSeek-V4 stack with a packed compressed-KV prototype, the same machinery localizes a silent corruption to a precise structural boundary -- exact in the eviction-free, identity-isolated regime, with every observed failure in an eviction or slot-reuse regime -- through a machine-adjudicated discrimination campaign whose calculus rejected two of our own confounded inferences along the way. All artifacts, guards, and the Lean development are released at https://github.com/metask-ai/witprobe-attention-memory; every number in this paper regenerates from the shipped artifacts by one command.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a unified, formally-checked way to observe and bound errors from various attention-memory compression schemes in modern LLMs, and demonstrates it on real serving stacks.
AI.motivation: Modern LLMs use diverse forms of attention memory (KV caches, latent caches, sparse selectors, recurrent states) that behave differently under compression, making it difficult to understand, bound, and operationalize the risk of accuracy loss or silent corruption in production. Existing tools focus on simple KV caches and lack a principled, formally-auditable method to compose guarantees across stages and models, especially under real serving conditions like concurrency and budgets.
AI.method: The authors define a "runtime observability contract" with three generic operators that can model four attention-memory classes. They instantiate these contracts on six model configurations across five architecture families, and compose stage-wise bounds into an executable, per-request "risk ledger" that tracks error budgets. Error metrics are encoded at the type level so that compositions are only allowed when metrics match; when not, they introduce formally proved metric-bridging transformations in Lean, and any step that cannot be formally certified is downgraded to empirical measurement. They run large-scale replay experiments (12.4M entry reads, 8-way concurrency, budgeted and fail-closed) with an always-on fused probe operating within the CUDA-graph serving noise floor, and apply the system to a DeepSeek-V4 stack using a compressed-KV prototype.
AI.result: The risk ledger executes under realistic load while keeping the configured risk budgets with zero observed violations, empirically validating the proposed contracts. The observability probe runs continuously without noticeable serving overhead. When applied to a DeepSeek-V4 deployment with compressed KV, the system pinpoints a previously silent corruption to a specific structural boundary, and further shows that all observed failures occur only under eviction or slot-reuse regimes. The formal type system and metric bridges catch compositional errors, rejecting some of the authors' own initial inferences and chains.
AI.conclusion: A unified, formally grounded observability and risk-accounting framework can cover heterogeneous attention-memory mechanisms and their compressions in modern LLMs, supporting executable risk ledgers that run in production-like environments. The approach provides machine-checked guarantees where possible, falls back to empirical characterization where necessary, and is effective at both enforcing risk budgets and diagnosing subtle memory-corruption issues. The released artifacts and Lean proofs make the results reproducible and auditable.

title: Learning When to Trust via Selective Context Preference Optimization
comment: Project Page at https://worldbench.github.io/scope GitHub Repo at https://github.com/worldbench/SCOPE HF Dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/worldbench/MIST-Bench
summary: Language models increasingly condition their answers on external signals, and a single misleading one can turn a correct answer wrong. The obvious remedy, training models to resist such signals, hides a failure mode: a model that ignores all context looks robust yet is useless when the context is worth trusting. We recast the problem as selective trust and introduce MIST, a human-annotated benchmark that renders each reasoning item under four matched conditions (clean, misleading, correct-context, and irrelevant-context), together with SC2W, a paired metric counting how often a misleading signal flips a clean-correct answer to wrong. Across a comprehensive benchmark study, we observe that such a susceptibility is universal. We then propose SCOPE, which mines clean-correct/misleading-wrong failures and optimizes a standard Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) objective over matched preference pairs balanced equally across all four conditions, rather than over misleading items alone. Our approach substantially reduces SC2W on popular open-sourced models while preserving accuracy when the added context is clean, correct, or irrelevant. With this work, we argue that models should be judged on selective trust, not on resistance alone.

AI.tldr: Paper studies how language models can selectively trust external context instead of blindly following or ignoring it, introduces a benchmark and metric to measure this, and proposes a training method that reduces harmful influence from misleading context while keeping benefits from helpful context.
AI.motivation: Existing language models often condition on external signals (like retrieved documents, tools, or system prompts). A single misleading signal can flip an otherwise correct answer to an incorrect one. Simply training models to resist external context is not sufficient, because a model that ignores all context appears robust but fails when the context is actually useful. There is a need to measure and improve models’ ability to *selectively* trust context—using reliable signals while discounting misleading ones.
AI.method: The authors reformulate robustness to external signals as a selective-trust problem and build MIST, a human-annotated benchmark where each reasoning question is presented in four controlled variants: (1) clean (no extra context), (2) misleading, (3) correct-context, and (4) irrelevant-context. They define SC2W, a metric that counts how often a misleading signal changes a clean-correct answer into a wrong one. They run a benchmark study across many models to assess susceptibility. Then they introduce SCOPE, a training approach that identifies examples where clean answers are correct but become wrong under misleading context, and uses these instances to construct balanced preference pairs across all four conditions. They optimize a Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) objective on these matched pairs, instead of only on misleading-context items.
AI.result: The benchmark study shows that susceptibility to misleading external context (as measured by SC2W) is widespread across popular language models. Applying SCOPE to open-source models significantly lowers SC2W, indicating less harmful influence from misleading cues, while keeping performance high when provided with clean, correct, or irrelevant context. Thus, the trained models better distinguish between trustworthy and untrustworthy external information.
AI.conclusion: Models should be evaluated and trained not only for resistance to misleading context but for selective trust: leveraging good signals and discounting bad ones. The MIST benchmark and SC2W metric expose how often misleading context flips correct answers, and the SCOPE training method effectively reduces this vulnerability without sacrificing the benefits of conditioning on accurate or neutral context. The work argues that future robustness research should adopt selective trust as a primary objective and evaluation lens.

title: Seeing Is Not Deciding: Can Multimodal LLMs Act as Effective CEOs?
summary: Large language models are increasingly applied as autonomous decision-making agents. However, in executive business decisions, existing benchmarks are limited to textonly settings. This makes it unclear whether models can perceive visual business evidence and effectively integrate it to improve decision quality. We introduce C-SUITEBENCH, a controlled multimodal benchmark that includes five decision tasks under paired text-only and multimodal conditions across 50 scenarios. We place nine frontier models in the role of a chief executive officer and evaluate their decision-making ability. Multimodal inputs consistently improve evidence-centric reasoning, with the largest and most reliable gains appearing in risk forecasting and board-facing justification. However, we uncover a multimodal integration paradox: adding visual business information degrades constrained resource allocation for all nine models, even as visual grounding itself improves. Ablation experiments reveal that this failure emerges from signal crowding, although each visual channel helps individually, their combination disrupts constraint satisfaction during decoding. These findings demonstrate that visual perception and constrained action are separable bottlenecks in multimodal agents, and that indiscriminate visual augmentation can harm high-stakes decision making, motivating selective grounding strategies for future executive AI systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces C-SUITEBENCH, a multimodal benchmark to test large language models acting as CEOs, showing that visual inputs help evidence-based reasoning but can harm constrained resource allocation due to signal crowding.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM benchmarks for business decision-making are mostly text-only, so it is unknown whether models can properly use visual business data (e.g., charts, dashboards) and whether this improves or harms decision quality in realistic executive settings. The authors want to systematically test multimodal capabilities in high-stakes, structured business decisions.
AI.method: They design C-SUITEBENCH, a controlled benchmark with five executive decision tasks (including risk forecasting, justifying decisions to a board, and resource allocation) across 50 scenarios. Each scenario has paired conditions: text-only vs multimodal (text plus visual business evidence). Nine frontier multimodal models are prompted to act as CEOs and evaluated on decision quality, evidence-centric reasoning, constraint satisfaction, and integration of visual inputs. Ablation studies remove or vary visual channels to diagnose the source of performance changes.
AI.result: Across models, providing visual inputs generally improves evidence-centric reasoning, especially for risk forecasting and generating board-facing justifications. However, when visual information is added in resource allocation tasks with hard constraints, performance consistently worsens for all nine models. Visual grounding (understanding the visuals) improves, but constraint satisfaction deteriorates. Ablation experiments show that each visual channel alone is beneficial, yet combining them leads to signal crowding that disrupts proper decoding under constraints.
AI.conclusion: Visual perception and constrained decision-making are distinct challenges for multimodal LLM agents. Simply adding more visual business data can harm performance on tightly constrained tasks, even when it improves general reasoning. Future executive AI systems should use selective and structured visual grounding instead of indiscriminate multimodal augmentation, and benchmarks like C-SUITEBENCH are necessary to reveal such counterintuitive failures.

title: Improving Interoperability among Defence and National Security Ontologies: Analysis and Evaluation Tasks
comment: Paper accepted at the Resource Track, the 25th International Semantic Web Conference (ISWC 2026), 25 - 29 October 2026, Bari, Italy
summary: The use of ontologies and knowledge graphs is becoming increasingly widespread in the defence and national security domain. Numerous ontologies have been developed through initiatives led by academia, industry, and government. Achieving interoperability across diverse defence and national security ontologies remains a major challenge due to the domain's breadth and specialisation. In this work, we analyse and document over 60 publicly available ontologies and introduce a new track for the Ontology Alignment Evaluation Initiative (OAEI). This track comprises eight matching tasks, consensus alignments and manually-curated (silver-standard) mappings. The consensus alignments are derived by aggregating the outputs of several state-of-the-art ontology alignment systems. The silver-standard is obtained from the manual validation of the consensus alignment together with a subset of the unique mappings (i.e., mappings suggested by only one system).

AI.tldr: The paper surveys over 60 defence and national security ontologies and creates a new Ontology Alignment Evaluation Initiative (OAEI) track with curated benchmark mappings to evaluate ontology matching systems.
AI.motivation: In defence and national security, many ontologies and knowledge graphs have been independently developed by academia, industry, and government. This has led to severe interoperability problems because these ontologies cover a broad, highly specialised domain and are not easily aligned with each other. There is a need for systematic benchmarks and evaluation tracks to compare and improve ontology alignment systems specifically in this domain.
AI.method: The authors first collect and analyse more than 60 publicly available ontologies related to defence and national security. They then design a new evaluation track for OAEI that includes eight ontology matching tasks. For each task, they produce consensus alignments by aggregating the outputs of several state-of-the-art ontology alignment tools. They further manually validate the consensus alignments and a selection of unique mappings (those suggested by only one system) to construct a higher-quality, manually curated ‘silver-standard’ reference alignment set.
AI.result: The main product is a publicly available OAEI track tailored to defence and national security ontologies, containing eight matching tasks, consensus alignments for each, and a silver-standard set of manually checked mappings. This provides a concrete, reusable benchmark for testing and comparing ontology matching systems in this complex domain.
AI.conclusion: By systematically analysing existing defence and national security ontologies and building a dedicated OAEI track with consensus and silver-standard alignments, the paper enables more reliable evaluation and improvement of ontology alignment methods in this domain. This is a step toward better semantic interoperability across heterogeneous defence and national security knowledge systems.

title: Personalized Deep Research Query Refinement with Graph-Scaffolded Evidence Grounding
summary: User requests serve as research specifications for deep research agents, shaping what evidence to seek and how to synthesize it. In personalized deep research, these specifications must additionally reflect user goals, constraints, preferences, and evaluation criteria. User context can be incorporated either within the deep research pipeline or into the research specification provided as its input. We focus on the latter, refining the user request into a personalized research specification before passing it to an unchanged deep research agent. This requires resolving three coupled decisions: which framing factors are relevant, whether the available user context sufficiently supports them, and whether to retrieve user memory, ask the user, or stop and refine the query. For training, G-STEER organizes framing factors as elicitation targets in an Intent Elicitation Graph that captures their dependencies. It learns a clarification policy from graph-scaffolded trajectories spanning diverse factor dependencies and evidence conditions. The policy produces a refined query while balancing target coverage against the costs of evidence acquisition. Experiments show that G-STEER achieves the strongest overall weighted target coverage and the highest downstream report personalization across both evaluated DRAs, while asking roughly one third as many user questions as a strong clarification baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes G-STEER, a method for turning an initial user request into a personalized research specification for deep research agents, using a learned clarification policy that decides what to ask the user, what to retrieve from memory, and when to stop, improving personalization while reducing user questions.
AI.motivation: Deep research agents typically treat user requests as generic specifications and do not fully leverage user-specific goals, constraints, and preferences. Personalizing these agents requires systematically incorporating user context into the research specification without redesigning the research pipeline itself. There is a need for a principled way to determine which aspects of user context matter for a given request, how to elicit or retrieve them efficiently, and how to balance personalization benefits against the cost of asking users clarification questions.
AI.method: The paper introduces G-STEER, which treats personalization-relevant aspects of a user request as \\"framing factors\\" organized into an Intent Elicitation Graph. This graph encodes dependencies among elicitation targets (e.g., goals, constraints, preferences) and the evidence sources that may support them (user-provided information, user memory, or existing context). Using graph-scaffolded trajectories that simulate different dependency structures and evidence availability, the authors train a clarification policy. At inference time, this policy decides: (1) which framing factors are relevant to the request, (2) whether current user context sufficiently instantiates them, and (3) whether to retrieve memory, query the user, or stop and produce a refined, personalized research specification to feed into an unchanged deep research agent.
AI.result: In experiments across multiple deep research agents (DRAs), G-STEER achieves superior performance on a weighted target coverage metric, indicating that it more successfully fills in relevant framing factors. It also yields the highest measured degree of downstream report personalization, meaning the resulting research outputs better align with user-specific goals and preferences. Additionally, G-STEER accomplishes these gains while asking only about one third as many clarification questions as a strong clarification baseline, demonstrating improved efficiency and reduced user burden.
AI.conclusion: G-STEER provides an effective and efficient approach to personalizing deep research agents by front-loading user intent elicitation into a refined research specification, without modifying the underlying research pipeline. By leveraging an Intent Elicitation Graph and a learned clarification policy, it can selectively elicit or retrieve user context, achieving better personalization and coverage of relevant factors while significantly reducing the number of user interactions needed. This demonstrates that structured, policy-driven clarification is a promising direction for scalable, user-friendly personalization in deep research systems.

title: AppDeltaWorld: Transition-Grounded Delta Code World Model for Mobile GUI Agents
summary: Mobile GUI agents can operate apps through pixel perception and touch actions, making them a promising interface for collecting and improving long-horizon mobile interaction policies. However, real trajectories are difficult to obtain for sensitive apps and privacy-critical operations. At the same time, existing simulated environments are costly to scale up, and GUI world models still suffer from unstable generation, limited modality coverage, and inconsistent action-transition logic. To address these limitations, we propose AppDeltaWorld, a transition-grounded delta code world model that predicts the next GUI as a reachable code update rather than as an unconstrained image or text description. AppDeltaWorld retrieves app-specific Level-1 HTML references under an action-transition constraint, generates Level-2 executable HTML conditioned on the current screen, action, predicted next-screen text, and retrieved structure, and inserts generated visual assets into image slots before browser rendering. As a world model, AppDeltaWorld achieves the highest fidelity on CMGUIBench-500 under Code2World evaluation, with clear gains in structural layout and UI element reconstruction over image-only and code-only baselines. As a training environment, AppDeltaWorld supports filtered closed-loop SFT data construction that, when combined with public supervision, enables AppDeltaAgent to achieve state-of-the-art performance on AndroidLens and consistent gains on MobileGym and MobileWorld. Moreover, world-model-based test-time reinforcement learning enables policy adaptation and shows further improvements without additional interaction with real apps.

AI.tldr: AppDeltaWorld is a transition-grounded GUI world model that predicts next mobile screens as structured HTML/code deltas instead of raw images or text, enabling high-fidelity simulation and better training for mobile GUI agents.
AI.motivation: Collecting long-horizon interaction data from real mobile apps is difficult due to privacy, sensitivity of some apps, and limited access. Existing simulators are hard to scale, and current GUI world models generate unstable, low-fidelity screens with poor action-transition consistency, limiting their use as training and evaluation environments for GUI agents. A more faithful, structured and controllable world model is needed.
AI.method: The authors introduce AppDeltaWorld, a world model that predicts the next GUI screen as a reachable update (delta) to executable HTML rather than generating unconstrained pixels or text. Given the current screen, an action, and predicted next-screen text, the model: (1) retrieves app-specific Level-1 HTML templates under an action-transition constraint; (2) generates Level-2 executable HTML by conditioning on current screen, action, text prediction and retrieved structure; (3) inserts appropriate visual assets into image slots and renders via a browser. They also use this world model as a simulator to build filtered, closed-loop supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data for training an agent, AppDeltaAgent, and combine it with test-time reinforcement learning within the model-based environment.
AI.result: On the CMGUIBench-500 benchmark under a Code2World evaluation protocol, AppDeltaWorld attains the highest fidelity among baselines, showing better structural layout and UI element reconstruction than image-only or code-only models. As a training environment, it enables construction of SFT datasets that, when merged with public supervision data, allow AppDeltaAgent to reach state-of-the-art performance on AndroidLens and achieve consistent improvements on MobileGym and MobileWorld. Additionally, applying world-model-based test-time RL further boosts policy performance without requiring extra interaction with real applications.
AI.conclusion: Representing next GUIs as structured, transition-grounded HTML/code deltas produces a more faithful and controllable mobile world model than unconstrained image or text generation. AppDeltaWorld serves both as a high-fidelity simulator and as a data engine that, together with public supervision, yields an agent (AppDeltaAgent) that outperforms prior methods on multiple mobile interaction benchmarks. Model-based test-time reinforcement learning within this world further enhances policies while avoiding additional data collection from real apps, indicating that delta-code world models are a practical path toward scalable training and adaptation of mobile GUI agents.

title: ECG-LENS: Lead-Aware Clinical Context Enriched ECG Report Generation and Evaluation
summary: Electrocardiography (ECG) is one of the most widely used non-invasive tools for diagnosing cardiovascular disease, but transforming multi-lead ECG recordings into reliable clinical reports remains challenging.
