Automating ECG report generation could reduce clinicians' interpretive workload, improve diagnostic efficiency, and expand access to cardiac assessment in underserved communities. Unlike image-based report-generation tasks, ECG interpretation requires the analysis of subtle temporal morphologies, followed by coherent diagnostic reasoning expressed in dense clinical terminology. Existing systems predominantly focus on classification, while current report-generation methods often produce outputs that remain inadequate for practical clinical use. To address these challenges, we propose ECG-LENS, an end-to-end ECG report-generation framework that jointly integrates multi-lead signal modeling, diagnosis-aware representations, and clinically grounded text generation. ECG-LENS combines lead-wise encoders that preserve localized waveform morphology with a global encoder that captures inter-lead dependencies. To guide report generation, we fuse signal representations with clinically enriched textual prompts that condition a GPT-2 decoder. We further introduce an ECG-specific report-preprocessing strategy that helps the model focus on clinically meaningful findings. Finally, because lexical metrics may under- or overestimate report quality, we propose F1-ECGBERT, a BERT-based, ECG-specific metric that measures agreement between diagnostic labels extracted from generated and reference reports. In-domain experiments on PTB-XL and cross-domain evaluation on MIMIC-IV-ECG show that ECG-LENS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with absolute gains of 4.0%, 6.3%, and 11.5% in METEOR, ROUGE-L, and F1-ECGBERT, respectively, over the strongest baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ECG-LENS, an end-to-end framework for generating clinically useful textual reports from multi-lead ECG signals, along with a new ECG-specific evaluation metric (F1-ECGBERT), and shows it outperforms existing methods on multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: ECG is widely used for diagnosing cardiovascular diseases, but converting multi-lead ECG signals into detailed, reliable clinical reports is difficult and time-consuming. Existing automated approaches mostly treat ECG understanding as a classification task and current report-generation systems produce text that is not yet accurate or rich enough for real clinical use. There is also a lack of good, ECG-specific metrics to evaluate the clinical quality of generated reports, since general lexical similarity scores can misrepresent diagnostic correctness.
AI.method: The authors propose ECG-LENS, an end-to-end ECG report-generation framework. It uses lead-wise encoders to model local waveform morphology for each ECG lead and a global encoder to capture inter-lead relationships. These signal representations are fused with clinically enriched textual prompts that condition a GPT-2 decoder to generate reports. They also introduce an ECG-specific report preprocessing pipeline to emphasize clinically important findings in the training text. For evaluation, they design F1-ECGBERT, a BERT-based metric that compares diagnostic labels extracted from generated and reference reports, aiming to better reflect clinical agreement than generic lexical metrics.
AI.result: On the in-domain PTB-XL dataset and cross-domain MIMIC-IV-ECG dataset, ECG-LENS achieves consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. It yields absolute gains of 4.0% on METEOR, 6.3% on ROUGE-L, and 11.5% on the proposed F1-ECGBERT metric compared with the strongest existing methods, showing better textual overlap and better diagnostic label agreement with ground-truth reports.
AI.conclusion: ECG-LENS effectively bridges multi-lead ECG signal modeling with clinically grounded natural language generation, producing higher-quality ECG reports than prior methods. The architecture’s combination of local and global encoders, diagnosis-aware prompting, and tailored text preprocessing improves both linguistic and clinical fidelity. The new F1-ECGBERT evaluation metric offers a more clinically meaningful way to assess ECG report generation, and together with ECG-LENS moves automated ECG reporting closer to practical deployment in real-world clinical settings.

title: GSBF: Gaussian Splatting for Environment-Aware Beamforming
summary: Beamforming plays a key role in multiple-input-multiple-output (MIMO) communication systems. However, conventional beamforming design normally requires accurate instantaneous channel state information (CSI) and iterative optimization, which incur substantial pilot overhead and computational complexity. Recognizing that radio propagation is intrinsically governed by the physical geometry, we develop a 3D Gaussian splatting for environment-aware beamforming (GSBF) pipeline based on multi-modal data, which characterizes the environment through a persistent 3D Gaussian representation. Specifically, GSBF models the environmental scattering response with reciprocity-preserving bidirectional spherical Gaussian (Bi-SG) kernels and performs two-sided electromagnetic rasterization to render an angular propagator map. The rendered map is then aggregated through an over-complete array-manifold dictionary and projected to the constant-modulus beamformers, thereby synthesizing beams directly from the access point (AP) pose and user position without online instantaneous CSI. Simulations demonstrate that GSBF consistently outperforms baselines such as exhaustive beam alignment (EBA) with lower latency.

AI.tldr: Proposes GSBF, a 3D Gaussian-splatting-based, environment-aware beamforming pipeline that designs beams from geometry instead of instantaneous CSI, achieving better performance and lower latency than conventional schemes like exhaustive beam alignment.
AI.motivation: Conventional MIMO beamforming requires accurate, instantaneous CSI and iterative optimization, which leads to high pilot overhead and computational complexity. Since radio propagation is fundamentally determined by the surrounding physical geometry, there is a need for a method that exploits environment structure to design beams without relying on frequent CSI acquisition.
AI.method: The paper develops a 3D Gaussian splatting for environment-aware beamforming (GSBF) pipeline using multi-modal data to build a persistent 3D Gaussian representation of the environment. It models environmental scattering responses using reciprocity-preserving bidirectional spherical Gaussian (Bi-SG) kernels. A two-sided electromagnetic rasterization process then renders an angular propagator map. This map is aggregated via an over-complete array-manifold dictionary and projected onto constant-modulus beamformers to synthesize beams directly from the AP pose and user position, avoiding online instantaneous CSI and iterative optimization.
AI.result: Simulation results show that GSBF consistently achieves better beamforming performance than baseline methods, including exhaustive beam alignment (EBA), while also offering lower latency, indicating both accuracy and efficiency gains.
AI.conclusion: Environment-aware beamforming can be effectively realized via a 3D Gaussian splatting representation of the radio environment. By leveraging geometric information and Bi-SG-based rasterization, GSBF can synthesize practical constant-modulus beamformers from AP and user locations without requiring instantaneous CSI, outperforming conventional alignment methods in both performance and latency.

title: CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities
summary: Student mobility programs such as Erasmus+ enable students to take courses at other universities, broadening their academic and cultural horizons. However, this flexibility also leads to a practical challenge: ensuring that students do not take courses elsewhere that substantially overlap with courses in their home curriculum. In this work, we propose CourseGraph, a methodology that automates the evaluation of external courses based on insights obtained from the process followed by curriculum administrators when assessing courses for inclusion in a degree program. Course- Graph extracts information such as course titles, descriptions, and learning outcomes from the course webpage. Then, this information is represented semantically using a BERT-based language model, after which the pair-wise similarity between courses can be computed. This information is then used by a Random Forest classifier to determine whether a candidate course abroad overlaps with a course already contained in the student's curriculum. We evaluate CourseGraph using (1) the Computer Science program at Eindhoven University of Technology, which contains information about courses with substantial overlap, and (2) six approved international programs from students enrolled in the Computer Science program at Lund University, including the corresponding decisions made by a curriculum administrator. The experimental results indicate that CourseGraph provides an effective approach for identifying overlapping courses and supporting curriculum alignment across universities.

AI.tldr: Proposes CourseGraph, an automated method to detect overlapping courses between home and host universities using semantic representations and machine learning, to support curriculum alignment in mobility programs.
AI.motivation: Student mobility programs like Erasmus+ allow students to follow courses at other universities, but this creates the risk that students take external courses that substantially overlap with courses already in their home curriculum. Currently, curriculum administrators manually assess overlap, which is time-consuming, subjective, and difficult to scale across many institutions and course catalogs. There is a need for an automated, systematic way to identify overlapping courses to maintain curriculum coherence and avoid redundancy for students studying abroad.
AI.method: The authors design CourseGraph, a pipeline that: (1) scrapes or extracts information from course webpages, including titles, descriptions, and learning outcomes; (2) represents this textual information semantically using a BERT-based language model to embed courses into a vector space; (3) computes pair-wise similarity scores between courses based on their embeddings; and (4) feeds these similarity features into a Random Forest classifier that predicts whether a candidate external course substantially overlaps with a course in the home curriculum. They then apply this methodology to real program data from two universities to evaluate its effectiveness.
AI.result: Using data from the Computer Science program at Eindhoven University of Technology, which has labeled instances of overlapping courses, and from six real international study plans from Lund University (including the administrator’s decisions), the authors show that CourseGraph can effectively detect when external courses overlap with existing curriculum courses. The experimental evaluation indicates good predictive performance of the classifier and demonstrates that the approach meaningfully supports course-matching and overlap detection processes used by administrators.
AI.conclusion: CourseGraph is a promising automated solution for identifying overlapping courses in the context of student mobility programs. By leveraging semantic representations from BERT and a Random Forest classifier, it can approximate the decisions of human curriculum administrators and thereby support curriculum alignment and study-plan approval processes across universities. This can reduce manual workload, improve consistency in decisions, and help ensure that students’ external studies are complementary rather than redundant.

title: GAUGE: A Measurement-Grounded Benchmark for Physical Fidelity in Simulation Engines and Video World Models
summary: Physics engines facilitate large-scale training and evaluation for embodied intelligence, while generative video world models are emerging as implicit simulators of future states and interactions. However, existing evaluations of physical fidelity are often conducted in isolation and rely heavily on perceptual similarity or human judgments, providing limited insight into which physical principles or parameters are violated. We introduce GAUGE, a real-world-grounded diagnostic benchmark for jointly evaluating how numerical simulators and generative video world models reproduce or deviate from real-world physics. It comprises 22 controlled task families covering rigid bodies, flexible cables, textiles, and volumetric deformable objects. Grounded in real-world trajectories and paired with calibrated physical metadata, uncertainty annotations, and task-specific observables, these tasks cover fundamental physical processes including collision, friction, momentum transfer, oscillation, self-contact, and deformation across diverse materials and conditions. We benchmark Isaac Sim, Genesis, and Newton on 14 task families using generalized trajectory errors, and evaluate 6 image-to-video models on 5 rigid-body tasks by testing physical-law consistency and the temporal stability of inferred parameters. Our results reveal no uniformly faithful physics engine, with the largest discrepancies arising in impulsive contact, rapid textile motion, and volumetric deformation. We further find that video world models can produce trajectories with the expected equation form while recovering incorrect accelerations, momentum transfer, and oscillation timing. GAUGE lays the groundwork for developing more physically faithful simulators and world models for embodied intelligence.

AI.tldr: GAUGE is a benchmark to systematically compare how well physics engines and generative video world models match real-world physics across many controlled tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of physics engines and video-based world models focus mainly on perceptual similarity or human judgment, which makes it unclear which concrete physical laws or parameters are being violated. There is a need for a real-world-grounded, diagnostic benchmark that can consistently test and compare the physical fidelity of both numerical simulators and generative video models, and highlight where and how they fail.
AI.method: The authors build GAUGE, a benchmark consisting of 22 task families using real-world recorded trajectories of different physical scenarios involving rigid bodies, flexible cables, textiles, and volumetric deformable objects. Each task includes calibrated physical metadata, uncertainty annotations, and task-specific observables related to key physical processes such as collision, friction, momentum transfer, oscillation, self-contact, and deformation. They evaluate several physics engines (Isaac Sim, Genesis, Newton) on 14 task families using generalized trajectory error metrics, and evaluate six image-to-video generative models on five rigid-body tasks by checking whether their generated trajectories respect physical-law forms and by analyzing the temporal stability of inferred physical parameters.
AI.result: No evaluated physics engine accurately reproduces real-world physics across all tasks. The largest mismatches occur in impulsive contacts, fast textile motion, and volumetric deformation. Generative video world models often generate motions that fit the qualitative form of physical equations but encode incorrect quantitative aspects, such as accelerations, momentum transfer, and oscillation timing.
AI.conclusion: GAUGE provides a structured, real-world-grounded diagnostic benchmark to evaluate both numerical physics simulators and generative video world models, revealing key failure modes in current systems. This resource can guide the development and comparison of more physically accurate simulators and world models for embodied intelligence applications.

title: VLMs for Videogame Data Annotation
summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents have revolutionized how engineers approach complex problems in real-world applications. Their adoption in video games is on the other hand limited by the extreme variability of the synthetic scenarios and their poor compliance with real-world physics. Here we investigate the use of VLMs for annotating video game frame sequences with reward signals, a task with several potential applications including, among others, conditioned training and offline reinforcement learning. We show that VLMs often struggle to answer basic questions on racing video games (although we observed a similar behavior on other game genres) and discuss countermeasures such as VLM output mixing and prompt optimization. We also show how input sequence length, resolution, and question batching affect the annotation quality and its token consumption.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how well vision-language models can label video game frames with reward signals, finding current models struggle, and explores techniques to improve their reliability and efficiency.
AI.motivation: While VLMs and AI agents are very powerful in real-world tasks, their use in video games is limited because games differ greatly from reality and often break real-world physics. Automatically annotating game video with reward signals would enable conditioned training and offline reinforcement learning, but it is unclear how well current VLMs can handle synthetic game environments.
AI.method: The authors apply VLMs to sequences of frames from racing (and some other) video games, asking them to generate reward-related annotations. They then probe the models with basic questions about the game states and systematically vary factors such as input sequence length, image resolution, and batching of questions. They also test countermeasures like combining outputs from multiple VLMs and optimizing prompts to improve performance.
AI.result: They find that VLMs frequently fail at answering even simple queries about racing games, suggesting that synthetic, physics-inconsistent environments pose challenges. The experiments show measurable effects of sequence length, resolution, and question batching on annotation quality and token usage, and that techniques like output mixing and prompt optimization can partially mitigate the problems.
AI.conclusion: Current VLMs are not yet robust annotators for synthetic gaming environments, even for straightforward racing scenarios. However, careful engineering—such as mixing model outputs, tuning prompts, and choosing appropriate input resolutions and batch configurations—can improve annotation quality and efficiency, informing how to better use VLMs for reward labeling in game-based RL settings.

title: Training a Conditioned Video Game Agent on a VLM Annotated Dataset
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a powerful but far from easy-to-use technique for policy learning. In the specific case of video games, access to the game engine is required to get rewards for training (e.g. to collect rewards from the environment). Furthermore, the proper identification and weighting of the rewards generally requires a difficult trial-and-error approach. Lastly, rewards are often sparse and understanding how they eventually affect the learned policy is a non-trivial exercise. To ease these issues we propose annotating a video game dataset with Vision Language Models (VLMs) instructed to extract human defined rewards. We show that offline RL can then be used to train a conditioned agent that responds accordingly to the desired returns and we discuss the difficulties and limitations that emerged in our early experiments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using vision-language models to automatically annotate gameplay data with human-defined rewards, enabling offline reinforcement learning for controllable game agents without needing direct game engine access.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning for video games typically requires direct access to the game engine to compute rewards, careful trial-and-error reward design, and coping with sparse rewards, all of which make RL hard to use in practice. The authors want a way to leverage existing gameplay datasets and human-understandable objectives without intricate reward engineering or engine integration.
AI.method: They instruct vision-language models to process video game data (e.g., frames, trajectories) and output human-defined reward signals as annotations. Using these annotated datasets, they then apply offline reinforcement learning to train a policy conditioned on desired return levels, so that agents can be guided by specifying target rewards. They also empirically investigate the process, identifying practical obstacles and limitations in this pipeline.
AI.result: The experiments demonstrate that it is feasible to extract reward annotations from game data using VLMs and to train an offline RL agent conditioned on desired returns. The conditioned agent can adjust its behavior in line with different specified reward levels, though the performance and stability are constrained by the quality and consistency of the VLM-generated rewards and by other offline RL challenges.
AI.conclusion: Annotating game datasets with VLM-derived, human-defined rewards is a promising approach to making RL more accessible for video games and to decouple policy learning from direct engine access and hand-crafted reward functions. However, current VLM and offline RL limitations introduce noise, bias, and control difficulties, so further work is needed to improve annotation reliability, agent robustness, and the interpretability of the resulting policies.

title: Stability of Ranking-dependent Pair-wise Comparison Patterns in the Analytic Hierarchy Process
summary: The paper addresses several ranking-dependent decision support methods. Ordinal information on compared objects can be used to improve the quality of expert data during estimation and help reduce the number of comparisons that the experts need to perform. In the paper we compare three incomplete ranking-dependent pair-wise comparison patterns which can be used in the Analytic Hierarchy Process - Best-worst method, Best-Second Best (Top 2) method, and the original maximum difference method. The first two comparison patterns (and respective methods) are incomplete, while the third can be a complete one. We determine conditions under which these three methods can be compared in terms of stability to expert errors. We also present the results of a simulation-type experiment, in which the three methods are compared. The research allows us to define the most stable incomplete ranking-dependent pair-wise comparison pattern and reduce the number of comparisons without loss of credibility of expert session results. The research contributes to algorithmic, cognitive, and applied aspects of decision support in uncertain environments.

AI.tldr: The paper compares three ranking-dependent pairwise comparison patterns for AHP (Best-Worst, Top-2, and maximum difference) to find which is most stable to expert errors while requiring fewer comparisons.
AI.motivation: Expert-based multi-criteria decision-making often relies on pairwise comparisons that are cognitively demanding and time-consuming. Using ordinal rankings of alternatives could reduce the number of required comparisons, but different ranking-dependent schemes may vary in robustness to expert mistakes. There is a need to understand which incomplete comparison patterns provide the best trade-off between efficiency (fewer comparisons) and reliability (stability to errors) in the Analytic Hierarchy Process under uncertainty.
AI.method: The authors study three specific comparison patterns: (1) Best-Worst method, (2) Best-Second Best (Top 2) method, and (3) the original maximum difference method. They analyze, theoretically, the conditions under which these patterns can be compared in terms of stability to expert error. They then conduct a simulation-type experiment, generating expert judgments under uncertainty and injecting errors, to empirically compare the stability and performance of the three methods while varying the level of incompleteness in pairwise comparisons.
AI.result: They identify formal conditions that allow a meaningful comparison of the three methods with respect to their sensitivity to expert errors. The simulation results show how each method behaves in terms of stability and credibility of derived priorities when judgments are noisy. Among the considered approaches, one incomplete ranking-dependent pattern emerges as the most stable while still requiring fewer comparisons than a complete pattern.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that it is possible to substantially reduce the number of pairwise comparisons in AHP by using a carefully chosen incomplete ranking-dependent pattern, without degrading—and potentially even improving—the robustness of results to expert errors. The identified most-stable incomplete method enhances algorithmic efficiency, aligns better with human cognitive limitations, and improves practical decision support in uncertain environments.

title: Temporal Bridges for Spatial Resolution: Enhancing Climate Data Super-Resolution with Bidirectional Alignment
summary: High-resolution climate data is crucial for meteorological predictions and for informing decision support across diverse domains. However, the acquisition of such high-resolution climate information is often prohibitively costly, necessitating the development of data-driven meteorological prediction models. These models aim to generate fine-grained climate data from low-resolution inputs, a process termed climate data super-resolution (SR). Nevertheless, recent advancements in deep learning for climate data SR have primarily focused on leveraging single-frame spatial information, largely neglecting the temporal correlations between different time frames that could enhance SR outcomes. Furthermore, climate data are inherently stochastic and noisy, rendering widely used temporal alignment methods, such as optical flow models, ineffective in this context. Consequently, the development of a framework tailored for climate data SR that effectively captures implicit temporal correlations remains an unresolved challenge. To this end, we propose a novel Temporal-Enhanced framework with bidirectional temporal alignment. In essence, our framework establishes a temporal bridge to enhance spatial resolution in climate data SR through bidirectional alignment, leading to improved SR performance. Within this framework, Paired Latent Mapping achieves spatial alignment and noise reduction by unifying latent spaces. Then a Bidirectional Temporal Alignment captures temporal correlations by training forward and backward networks on consecutive latent frames. Temporal Enhanced Super-resolution then optimizes the entire framework for climate data SR. Experiments on large-scale real-world datasets demonstrated the superior performance of our framework.

AI.tldr: They propose a deep-learning framework that uses bidirectional temporal information and latent-space alignment to improve super-resolution of noisy, stochastic climate data, outperforming existing single-frame methods.
AI.motivation: High-resolution climate data are important but expensive to obtain. Existing data-driven climate super-resolution models mainly use spatial information from single frames and ignore temporal correlations across time, and conventional temporal alignment like optical flow fails due to the noisy, stochastic nature of climate fields. There is a need for a temporal-aware SR framework specifically tailored to the characteristics of climate data.
AI.method: They design a Temporal-Enhanced framework with three main components: (1) Paired Latent Mapping, which maps inputs into unified latent spaces to achieve spatial alignment and denoising; (2) Bidirectional Temporal Alignment, which trains forward and backward networks on consecutive latent frames to implicitly capture temporal correlations without relying on explicit optical flow; and (3) a Temporal Enhanced Super-resolution module that jointly optimizes the whole pipeline for climate data SR.
AI.result: On large-scale real-world climate datasets, their method achieves better super-resolution performance than existing approaches, indicating that incorporating bidirectional temporal alignment and latent-space mapping effectively exploits temporal information and handles noise.
AI.conclusion: A climate-specific, temporally enhanced SR framework that uses bidirectional temporal alignment and latent-space unification can more effectively reconstruct high-resolution climate fields from low-resolution inputs, demonstrating clear performance gains over prior single-frame or purely spatial methods and highlighting the value of implicit temporal modeling for noisy, stochastic climate data.

title: AgentOPSD: Recursive Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards constructs trajectory-level advantage estimates, yet it often fails to credit the few pivotal decisions that determine outcomes in long-horizon, multi-turn agentic tasks. Recent work introduces privileged self-distillation for credit assignment, providing denser supervision, but it remains unclear how such local signals should represent sequential credit. We propose AgentOPSD, a critic-free, recursive method for turn-level credit assignment in agentic reinforcement learning. AgentOPSD aggregates token-level teacher-student log-probability gaps into turn-level evidence and recursively updates a Bayesian belief state in log-odds space. This yields a principled reweighting scheme that converts sparse outcome supervision into turn-level credit signals and identifies pivotal turns through the marginal belief revision between consecutive states. The method is fully compatible with standard policy optimization and requires neither an additional critic nor extra rollouts. We evaluate AgentOPSD on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA using Qwen2.5 models at two scales (3B and 7B). AgentOPSD outperforms GRPO and strong self-distillation baselines, achieving 89.1% success on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B. Ablation studies attribute the gains to turn-level aggregation and history-dependent recursive belief updates.

AI.tldr: AgentOPSD is a critic-free, Bayesian, turn-level credit assignment method for agentic RL using privileged self-distillation, converting sparse outcome rewards into per-turn signals and outperforming GRPO and self-distillation baselines on several benchmarks.
AI.motivation: In long-horizon, multi-turn agentic RL tasks, outcomes often hinge on a few pivotal decisions. Standard RL with trajectory-level advantage estimates struggles to assign credit to these key turns. Privileged self-distillation offers denser local supervision but lacks a principled way to represent sequential credit over time. The authors aim to develop a method that can (1) exploit privileged self-distillation signals, (2) assign interpretable, turn-level credit in long sequences, and (3) integrate smoothly into existing policy optimization without requiring extra critics or rollouts.
AI.method: The authors propose AgentOPSD, a critic-free, recursive turn-level credit assignment framework built on privileged self-distillation. First, they compute token-level teacher–student log-probability gaps, treating these as dense local supervision signals. These token-level signals are aggregated into turn-level evidence. Next, AgentOPSD maintains a Bayesian belief state in log-odds space about task success; this belief is recursively updated across turns using the aggregated evidence. The change in belief (marginal belief revision) between consecutive turns defines the turn-level credit, identifying pivotal turns that significantly affect the expected outcome. This generates per-turn weights that reweight trajectories in standard policy optimization, without an external critic or additional rollouts. The approach is model-agnostic and plugs into standard RL fine-tuning pipelines.
AI.result: AgentOPSD is evaluated on three agentic RL benchmarks—ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA—using Qwen2.5 models of sizes 3B and 7B. Across these tasks, AgentOPSD consistently outperforms GRPO and strong self-distillation baselines. On ALFWorld, using Qwen2.5-7B, AgentOPSD achieves 89.1% success, a new state-of-the-art for the tested setting. Ablation studies indicate that both the aggregation from token-level to turn-level evidence and the history-dependent recursive Bayesian belief updates are key contributors to performance gains; removing either significantly degrades results.
AI.conclusion: AgentOPSD provides a principled, critic-free way to convert sparse trajectory-level supervision into dense, turn-level credit signals for agentic RL. By aggregating token-level teacher–student gaps and performing recursive Bayesian updates in log-odds space, it can highlight pivotal decisions and improve learning efficiency. The method integrates seamlessly with standard policy optimization, requires no additional critic or extra rollouts, and yields superior performance on multiple benchmarks. The ablations suggest that explicitly modeling sequential credit via recursive belief updates and turn-level aggregation is crucial in long-horizon, multi-turn RL with language models.

title: ECHO: A Locally-Deployable Agentic Health Assistant with Temporal Memory, Safety Guardrails, and Speech Assessment
summary: This paper presents ECHO (Enhanced Care \& Health Observer), a locally-deployable conversational health assistant for long-term chronic care management. ECHO integrates three complementary software modules developed under shared supervision as a unified system. The core module is an agentic chatbot built on a ReAct loop orchestrated via LangGraph, equipped with 17 clinical tools and a temporal knowledge graph for persistent cross-session memory; it achieves a 94.9\% tool-execution pass rate across a 59-scenario benchmark with GPT-5 Mini. A two-stage hybrid safety layer intercepts all incoming queries: a rule-based layer handles explicit crisis signals and jailbreak attempts in under 1ms, while a signed graph neural network (GNN) with APPNP-style propagation classifies boundary cases by clinical intent, achieving 88.8\% accuracy and 90.6\% unsafe recall on a 2,537-query annotated Turkish health dataset while outperforming zero-shot LLM baselines including Llama 3.3 70B. A multimodal speech assessment module combining Whisper acoustic encoding and BERT text encoding with cross-attention fusion estimates emotion, depression, and pain, reaching a mean macro F1 of 0.652. The full system is implemented as a web application that can run entirely on consumer hardware, with no patient data transmitted to external services, supporting compliance with GDPR and KVKK.

AI.tldr: ECHO is a locally-deployable conversational health assistant for chronic care, combining an agentic clinical chatbot, a hybrid safety filter, and a multimodal speech assessment module into a privacy-preserving web app that runs on consumer hardware.
AI.motivation: Chronic care management needs safe, reliable, and privacy-preserving conversational assistants that can operate without sending sensitive health data to external servers, while handling complex clinical reasoning, safety-critical triage, and affective state monitoring over long-term interactions.
AI.method: The authors build ECHO, integrating three modules: (1) an agentic chatbot based on a ReAct loop orchestrated with LangGraph, using 17 clinical tools and a temporal knowledge graph for persistent memory; (2) a two-stage safety layer with a fast rule-based filter and a signed GNN with APPNP-style propagation to classify risky or boundary queries by clinical intent; and (3) a multimodal speech assessment system that fuses Whisper-based acoustic encodings and BERT-based text encodings via cross-attention. They evaluate on a 59-scenario tool-use benchmark, a 2,537-query Turkish safety dataset, and emotion/depression/pain estimation tasks.
AI.result: The agentic chatbot achieves a 94.9% tool-execution pass rate on a 59-scenario benchmark using GPT-5 Mini. The safety GNN obtains 88.8% accuracy and 90.6% unsafe recall on the Turkish health dataset, outperforming zero-shot large LLM baselines such as Llama 3.3 70B. The multimodal speech module reaches a mean macro F1 of 0.652 for estimating emotion, depression, and pain. The system is deployed as a web app that runs fully on consumer hardware without transmitting patient data externally.
AI.conclusion: ECHO demonstrates that it is feasible to build a locally-deployable, privacy-preserving conversational health assistant for chronic care that combines agentic clinical reasoning, robust safety filtering, and multimodal affective assessment, achieving strong performance on tool use, safety classification, and speech-based health indicators while remaining compliant with regulations like GDPR and KVKK.

title: OPERA: Operator-residual feedback for reliable autonomous optical experiments with language-model agents
summary: Autonomous agents choose actions using scores that may not reflect experimental success. We developed OPERA, an operator-residual framework for optical experiments. It represents experimental actions as optical operators and evaluates their outcomes using physically interpretable residuals. Operators specify executable changes to measurement, control or reconstruction, while residuals report departures from specified physical conditions. The agent uses both to select, combine or generate operators, and physical performance is evaluated independently against a withheld reference. Across three optical tasks, score-only feedback produced score increases without physical improvement in 23.6--39.0\% of decisions, compared with 0.9--1.9\% for operator-residual feedback. Operator-residual feedback increased the probability of reaching and maintaining task targets and reduced experimental budgets. Protocols selected in digital twins were transferred to three optical instruments, and repeated experiments showed a lower projection budget in structured-light reconstruction. Together, operators and residuals guide autonomous decisions using measurable physical evidence.

AI.tldr: Introduces OPERA, an operator-residual framework that guides autonomous optical experiments using physically interpretable feedback instead of opaque scores.
AI.motivation: Autonomous agents in experimental physics often optimize abstract scores that do not reliably correspond to true physical improvement, leading to score inflation without actual experimental success. There is a need for a framework that grounds decision-making in physically meaningful quantities so that autonomous systems can more reliably and efficiently achieve experimental targets and transfer learned protocols between simulation and hardware.
AI.method: The authors design OPERA, in which experimental actions are encoded as optical operators (concrete, executable modifications to measurement, control, or reconstruction) and their consequences are evaluated via residuals that quantify deviations from desired physical conditions. An agent uses these operators and residuals to select, combine, or synthesize new actions. Physical performance is assessed against an independent withheld reference. They test this on three optical tasks, compare operator-residual feedback to conventional score-only feedback, and verify transfer of protocols from digital twins to three real optical instruments, including structured-light reconstruction experiments.
AI.result: Across three optical tasks, agents trained with score-only feedback frequently increased their internal scores without real physical improvements in 23.6–39.0% of decisions, whereas OPERA’s operator-residual feedback reduced such failure cases to only 0.9–1.9%. OPERA-based feedback raised the likelihood of reaching and stably maintaining target performance and lowered experimental resource usage (budgets). Learned protocols from simulations successfully transferred to three distinct optical instruments, and repeated structured-light reconstruction experiments demonstrated reduced projection budgets when using OPERA-derived protocols.
AI.conclusion: By explicitly representing experimental actions as operators and evaluating them with physically interpretable residuals, OPERA enables autonomous agents to make decisions grounded in measurable physical evidence rather than opaque scores. This substantially reduces misleading optimization, improves reliability in reaching and maintaining target performance, cuts experimental costs, and facilitates robust transfer from simulations to real-world optical setups, suggesting a generalizable approach for autonomous experimental control in optics and beyond.

title: From Siloed Algorithms to Compliance-First Agentic Platforms: A Multi-Layered Architecture for Hospital AI Systems
summary: Hospitals are rapidly adopting artificial intelligence for triage, imaging, scheduling etc., yet most deployments remain isolated point solutions locked inside departmental silos, resulting in duplicated effort, hidden risks, and unrealized enterprise value. Despite explosive growth of AI in healthcare market and accelerating investment, an estimated 70-80% of healthcare AI pilots fail to scale, largely due to governance gaps, fragmented data, and missing integration blueprints. This research proposes a hospital-specific, compliance-first, Agentic AI architecture with multiple interoperable layers, extending existing hospital AI platform models with: (i) an Agent Orchestration Layer for multi-agent workflows across clinical, operational, and financial domains, (ii) a Compliance and Policy Layer that centralizes policy-as-code for HIPAA, GDPR, the EU AI Act, DISHA Act, India's DPDP Act, and ISO/IEC security and safety standards, and (iii) a Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric that plugs federated learning, differential privacy, and secure enclaves into real-world Hospital Information Management System (HIMS) flows. Using a synthetic but structurally realistic hospital dataset and an open, ready-to-deploy prototype implementation, this study demonstrates the end-to-end orchestration of triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging, achieving substantial simulated reductions in task turnaround times and manual documentation effort while maintaining policy-guarded data access. The resulting architecture offers hospital leaders a pragmatic blueprint to move from ad hoc tools to a governed, globally compliant, ROI-focused AI platform that can be tailored to on-premise, hybrid and cloud-native deployments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hospital-wide, compliance-first Agentic AI architecture that moves healthcare AI from isolated point solutions to an integrated, governed platform, demonstrating efficiency gains and robust policy-controlled data use via a prototype on synthetic hospital data.
AI.motivation: Most hospital AI deployments are isolated point solutions within departmental silos, leading to duplicated effort, unrecognized risks, and limited enterprise value. Despite heavy investment and rapid market growth, 70–80% of healthcare AI pilots fail to scale due to governance gaps, fragmented data, and lack of integration blueprints. The authors seek to address these systemic barriers so hospitals can reliably scale AI across clinical, operational, and financial workflows while meeting stringent regulatory and privacy requirements.
AI.method: The authors design a hospital-specific, multi-layer Agentic AI architecture that is compliance-first and interoperable. It extends existing hospital AI platform models with: (i) an Agent Orchestration Layer enabling multi-agent workflows across clinical, operational and financial domains; (ii) a centralized Compliance and Policy Layer that encodes regulations (HIPAA, GDPR, EU AI Act, DISHA, India’s DPDP Act) and relevant ISO/IEC standards as policy-as-code; and (iii) a Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric integrating federated learning, differential privacy, and secure enclaves into Hospital Information Management System (HIMS) data flows. They implement an open, ready-to-deploy prototype and evaluate it using a synthetic but structurally realistic hospital dataset, simulating end-to-end orchestration for triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging.
AI.result: In simulation on synthetic hospital data, the architecture supports end-to-end orchestration of triage risk prediction, operational workflow optimization, and automated compliance logging. The prototype shows substantial reductions in simulated task turnaround times and manual documentation burden, while preserving policy-guarded access to data through the compliance and privacy layers. The system demonstrates that complex multi-agent workflows can be coordinated across domains without violating encoded regulatory and security constraints.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Agentic AI architecture provides a practical blueprint for hospitals to transition from fragmented, ad hoc AI tools to an integrated, governed, and globally compliant AI platform. By combining multi-agent orchestration, policy-as-code compliance, and privacy-preserving data management, it enables scalable, ROI-focused AI deployments that can be tailored to on-premise, hybrid, or cloud-native environments. This framework aims to help hospital leaders systematically unlock value from AI while managing risk and regulatory obligations.

title: Hybrid Machine Learning Framework for Herd-Level Cattle Growth Pattern and Weight Gain Forecasting in Grazing-Based Production Systems
summary: Commercial grazing systems yield irregular livestock observations, which challenge cattle growth forecasting. This study developed a hybrid machine learning framework for herd level cattle weight forecasting using automated sensing observations collected between 2022 and 2024 in southeastern Australia. Weekly live weight observations, demographic variables, and lagged environmental predictors were integrated into structured forecasting datasets. Herd level forecasting trajectories were generated through temporal aggregation of animal level predictions. Four hybrid architecture families were evaluated, including residual, stacked, cascade, and ensemble assisted frameworks. ARIMA, LSTM, and GRU models were used as comparative baselines. Independent testing demonstrated strong predictive agreement across multiple forecasting horizons. The cascade GB to RF to NN architecture achieved the best performance, with a test R^2 of 0.889, RMSE of 21.319 kg, and MAE of 15.462 kg. Hybrid architectures maintained greater robustness than recurrent sequential models under sparse observation conditions. Forecasting error increased progressively across extended prediction horizons. Feature importance analysis identified animal age, rainfall, and temperature as dominant predictors influencing herd level growth forecasting. The proposed framework may support feed allocation, grazing management, and livestock marketing decisions under heterogeneous sensing environments.

AI.tldr: Hybrid machine learning architectures were developed to forecast herd-level cattle weight from irregular commercial grazing data, outperforming traditional ARIMA and recurrent models and aiding management decisions.
AI.motivation: In commercial grazing systems, livestock are observed irregularly, making it difficult to accurately forecast cattle growth, which is crucial for feed planning, grazing management, and marketing. Existing methods such as ARIMA and recurrent neural networks struggle with sparse, heterogeneous sensing data, so there is a need for more robust forecasting frameworks that can effectively leverage available environmental and demographic information.
AI.method: The authors collected automated sensing data from 2022–2024 in southeastern Australia, including weekly live weight, demographic variables, and lagged environmental predictors. They formed structured forecasting datasets and produced herd-level trajectories via temporal aggregation of animal-level predictions. Four hybrid ML architecture families—residual, stacked, cascade, and ensemble-assisted—were designed and evaluated. Within these, gradient boosting (GB), random forest (RF), and neural networks (NN) were arranged in different combinations, and their performance was compared to ARIMA, LSTM, and GRU baselines across multiple forecasting horizons. They also performed feature importance analysis to interpret key drivers.
AI.result: Independent test sets showed strong agreement between predicted and observed herd-level cattle weight across several forecasting horizons. The best-performing model was a cascade architecture chaining gradient boosting to random forest to neural network, achieving test R^2 = 0.889, RMSE = 21.319 kg, and MAE = 15.462 kg. Across conditions with sparse observations, hybrid architectures were more robust than recurrent models like LSTM and GRU. Forecast errors increased as prediction horizons extended, and feature importance analysis highlighted animal age, rainfall, and temperature as the dominant predictors.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid machine learning frameworks, particularly a cascade GB→RF→NN architecture, can provide accurate and robust herd-level cattle weight forecasts in commercial grazing systems with irregular observations. These models outperform traditional ARIMA and recurrent neural networks under sparse sensing conditions. The resulting forecasts can inform practical decisions in feed allocation, grazing management, and livestock marketing, demonstrating the value of integrating demographic and environmental data into cattle growth prediction models.

title: Poli-Bias: Understanding and Measuring Large Language Model Biases in International Political Conflicts
summary: Measuring political bias in large language models (LLMs) remains challenging as it can manifest through subtle differences in framing, argumentation, and legal reasoning that are difficult to capture with a single metric. In this work, we introduce Poli-Bias, a counterfactual framework for measuring whether LLMs treat legally equivalent conflict scenarios differently depending on the countries involved. Poli-Bias compares responses to paired prompts in which country identities are systematically swapped across diverse geopolitical relationships, legal violations, and reasoning tasks. Rather than reducing bias to a single judgment, our framework decomposes response disparities into five interpretable dimensions, revealing how and where unequal treatment manifests. Across 13 contemporary LLMs spanning diverse model families and sizes, we find that country identities and user affiliations can systematically affect how equivalent actions are described, evaluated, and defended under international law. Our results thus establish Poli-Bias as a fine-grained framework for auditing political even-handedness and sycophancy in LLMs.

AI.tldr: Introduces Poli-Bias, a counterfactual framework to measure how LLMs treat legally equivalent international conflict scenarios differently depending on the countries involved.
AI.motivation: Existing measures of political bias in LLMs are inadequate because bias can appear in subtle ways—through framing, argumentation, and legal reasoning—especially in international-law and geopolitical contexts. There is a need for a systematic way to detect whether LLMs treat equivalent scenarios differently based solely on country identities or user affiliations.
AI.method: Design paired prompts that describe legally equivalent conflict scenarios, then systematically swap country identities across diverse geopolitical relationships, legal violations, and legal reasoning tasks. Collect responses from 13 contemporary LLMs, and decompose differences between responses into five interpretable dimensions that characterize where and how unequal treatment manifests, instead of collapsing results into a single bias score.
AI.result: Across 13 diverse LLMs, the study finds that both country identities and user affiliations systematically influence how equivalent actions are described, morally/legally evaluated, and defended under international law. The framework uncovers fine-grained, multidimensional disparities rather than a single bias metric.
AI.conclusion: Poli-Bias is validated as a fine-grained auditing framework that exposes unequal treatment of countries and users by LLMs in international-law scenarios, enabling more detailed analysis of political even-handedness and sycophancy than prior single-metric approaches.

title: HERALD: Counterfactual Audits and Minimal Repairs for Proof-of-Retrieval Rewards
summary: Search-agent rewards mix answer quality, citation grounding, tool cost, and anti-hacking terms; a high score therefore need not imply that cited evidence was retrieved, and added penalties can cancel. We introduce HERALD, an offline audit that applies exact same-question interventions, separates candidate-visible from oracle information, and enumerates detector contracts before policy optimization. On four Qwen3-8B pools from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue, $R_0$ rejects search deletion and fake IDs, but a label-free citation-laundering attack succeeds. A complete $2^3$ ablation identifies targeted strengthening of $L$---citing a corpus passage absent from the retrieved evidence---as the observed inclusion-minimal repair: $R[L]$ has zero empirical ASR with a 0.50% one-sided cluster upper bound. The gap persists across pool rules, a visible BM25 attacker, and four models; broader hardening remains vulnerable when the attack removes an oracle support-ID penalty. Under strict 5M-token matched training evaluated on 256 paired questions per benchmark, $R[L]$ meets the EM non-inferiority gate on HotpotQA and 2Wiki but not MuSiQue. Equal-suite citation precision and support recall improve by 2.02 and 1.46 points, unsupported citations fall by 1.69, and laundering attackability falls on 2Wiki and MuSiQue. Natural $L$ is not reduced, and the detector appears in only 18 of 58,368 training trajectories. HERALD thus separates robust scoring, sparse learning signal, and policy transfer.

AI.tldr: Introduces HERALD, an offline audit framework to robustly evaluate and harden search-agent reward models against citation laundering and related attacks, identifying a minimal repair that strengthens penalties for citing non-retrieved evidence without hurting natural citation behavior or answer quality on most benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing search-agent reward models combine multiple objectives (answer quality, citation grounding, tool cost, anti-hacking constraints) into a single score. Because different terms can cancel, high rewards may not actually guarantee correct use of retrieved evidence, and some adversarial behaviors (like citation laundering or tampering with retrieval signals) can slip through. There is a need for a principled way to audit and repair these reward functions so that they robustly enforce citation grounding while preserving performance.
AI.method: The paper proposes HERALD, an offline audit framework that: (1) re-evaluates the same questions under controlled interventions; (2) separates what information is visible to the candidate policy from oracle-only information; and (3) systematically enumerates and evaluates different detection/reward contracts before running any policy optimization. They test HERALD on four Qwen3-8B policy pools trained on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue, study several adversarial attacks (e.g., deleting search operations, using fake IDs, and citation laundering), and run a full 2^3 ablation over reward components to identify the smallest effective repair. The key modification is a targeted strengthening of a term L that penalizes citing corpus passages that are not in the retrieved evidence set. They then retrain under a strict matched-token budget and evaluate exact match, citation precision, support recall, unsupported citations, and attack success rates.
AI.result: Baseline reward R0 successfully rejects search deletion and fake ID attacks but is vulnerable to a label-free citation-laundering attack. The ablation study shows that enhancing the L term (penalizing citations to non-retrieved passages) is the minimal change that closes this vulnerability: the repaired reward R[L] achieves zero empirical attack success rate with a tight one-sided upper confidence bound of 0.50%. This robustness improvement generalizes across different data pool rules, a visible BM25-based attacker, and four Qwen3-8B agent pools. Even broader hardening strategies remain vulnerable when certain oracle-based penalties are removed, underscoring the importance of L. Under a 5M-token matched training budget on 256 question pairs per benchmark, R[L] maintains non-inferior exact-match performance on HotpotQA and 2Wiki but slightly underperforms on MuSiQue. Citation metrics improve: citation precision and support recall increase by about 2.02 and 1.46 points, respectively, unsupported citations drop by 1.69 points, and laundering attackability is reduced on 2Wiki and MuSiQue.
AI.conclusion: HERALD provides a systematic offline procedure to diagnose and repair weaknesses in search-agent reward functions, especially around citation grounding. By isolating candidate-visible vs. oracle information and enumerating detector contracts before training, the framework identifies a minimal, targeted modification—strengthening penalties for citing non-retrieved evidence—that significantly improves robustness to citation-laundering attacks without degrading natural citation behavior or most answer-quality metrics. The detector plays only a sparse role in training trajectories yet yields strong downstream policy transfer, suggesting that carefully designed, localized reward terms can meaningfully harden search agents against adversarial misuse of citations.

title: Schema-Guided Hierarchical Information Extraction and Semantic Evaluation Using Generative AI
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables. To be published in Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE 22nd International Conference on e-Science (e-Science), Naples, Italy
summary:
We present a schema-based framework for extracting complex, structured information from unstructured text documents using generative AI, followed by automated semantic evaluation of the extracted information against a gold standard. The schema, serving as an information model encoding domain knowledge, provides a unified, systematic, and consistent framework for extraction of hierarchical, nested information, with attributes of variable cardinality, and subsequent evaluation of the results. Information extraction from a document is performed in a single call to the model, in zero-shot mode.
  In the evaluation step, we introduce a path-based semantic matching algorithm to align the nested, variable-cardinality attributes in the extracted results with those in the gold standard. We use generative AI for semantic comparison of the extracted and gold standard values of an attribute, and introduce a rubric to classify the result of the comparison, according to domain-specific considerations, as an exact, semantic, useful, or non-match.
  We were able to extract 12 out of 14 attributes with an F1 score of $>$90\% from documents published by the health technology assessment organisation NICE, using the generative AI model Claude Opus 3. The time needed to extract the attributes from a document was $\sim$30 times lower than the time taken by a human domain expert. We further demonstrate generalisability of this framework across different generative AI models and transferability across different HTA organisations and languages.

AI.tldr: A schema-based, generative-AI framework extracts complex, nested information from unstructured HTA documents and evaluates it semantically against a gold standard, achieving high accuracy and large time savings over human experts.
AI.motivation: Unstructured documents, such as health technology assessment (HTA) reports, contain rich but complex, hierarchical data that must be converted into structured form for analysis and reuse. Traditional information extraction methods struggle with nested, variable-cardinality attributes and often require task-specific training and multiple processing steps. There is a need for a unified, schema-driven approach that can both extract such complex structures using generative AI, and rigorously evaluate extraction quality in a domain-aware, semantic way across different organizations and languages.
AI.method: The authors define an explicit schema that encodes domain knowledge and specifies a hierarchical, nested information model with attributes of variable cardinality. Using this schema, they prompt a generative AI model (primarily Claude 3 Opus) to perform zero-shot extraction of all schema attributes from each document in a single model call. For evaluation, they propose a path-based semantic matching algorithm that aligns extracted attributes with a gold standard across nested structures and variable-length lists. They then use generative AI to semantically compare the values of aligned attribute pairs and apply a rubric that categorizes each comparison as exact match, semantic match, useful match, or non-match, based on domain-specific criteria. Performance is measured via F1 scores and timing comparisons versus human experts, and they test different models, organizations, and languages to assess generalisability and transferability.
AI.result: On NICE HTA documents, the framework successfully extracted 12 out of 14 target attributes with F1 scores above 90%. The automated extraction was approximately 30 times faster than manual extraction by human domain experts. Experiments across different generative AI models and across HTA organizations and languages show that the schema-based framework and evaluation approach generalise beyond the initial setting, indicating robustness and transferability.
AI.conclusion: A schema-based, generative-AI-driven framework can reliably and efficiently extract complex, nested, variable-cardinality information from unstructured HTA documents in a zero-shot, single-call setting. The proposed path-based semantic matching and rubric-based evaluation enable nuanced, domain-aware assessment of extraction quality. The high F1 scores, substantial time savings, and evidence of cross-model and cross-organization transferability suggest that this approach is practical and scalable for real-world information extraction tasks involving rich document structures.

title: From Economic Agents to Agentic Economies: A Systems Blueprint for Economic World Models
summary: Economic World Models (EWMs) are generative economic models that simulate how economies evolve from within by modeling heterogeneous agents, their beliefs and actions, and the market and institutional mechanisms through which their interactions produce aggregate outcomes. This paper develops an implementation roadmap for building economic world models as generative engines in which heterogeneous agents act, interact, adapt, and co-evolve with markets and institutions, thereby producing economic dynamics from the inside. We organize EWM systems into a six-level capability ladder, from fixed rule-based agent worlds to adaptive and LLM-based agent worlds, self-evolving agents, evolving institutional worlds, and sim-to-real economic twins aligned with real observations. A systematic literature survey across these levels reveals that existing work remains concentrated in lower-level agent and simulation environments, while systems with self-evolving agents, endogenous institutions, persistent empirical alignment, and validated economic mechanisms remain rare. By translating the EWM agenda into an implementation blueprint, this paper aims to accelerate the development of the next generation of economic simulation environments that can serve as high-fidelity sandboxes for human decision-makers and as training, planning, evaluation, and safety substrates for AI agents. We release a curated paper list and related resources to support future research.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and structures a research agenda for Economic World Models (EWMs), generative simulations of economies with heterogeneous agents and evolving institutions, and provides an implementation roadmap and survey to guide future work.
AI.motivation: Traditional economic models often rely on simplified representative agents and static or exogenous institutions, limiting their ability to capture complex, adaptive, and emergent economic dynamics relevant for both policy and AI alignment. With the rise of powerful AI agents and multi-agent simulations, there is a need for a coherent framework and roadmap to build rich, generative economic environments where heterogeneous agents and institutions co-evolve and where simulations can be empirically aligned with real-world data.
AI.method: The authors conceptualize Economic World Models as multi-agent, generative economic simulations and organize existing and prospective systems into a six-level capability ladder, from simple rule-based agents to fully evolving institutional worlds and sim-to-real economic twins. They perform a systematic literature survey across these levels to map where current research is concentrated and where gaps exist, and from this analysis derive an implementation roadmap and design blueprint for future EWM development. They also compile and release a curated list of papers and resources.
AI.result: The survey shows that current work is heavily concentrated at the lower capability levels, focusing on fixed or modestly adaptive agents and relatively static environments, while advanced capabilities—such as self-evolving agents, endogenously evolving institutions, persistent empirical alignment with real data, and validated economic mechanisms—are rare. The authors synthesize these findings into a structured capability ladder and an implementation blueprint for building more advanced EWMs, paired with a curated resource list.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that realizing the full potential of Economic World Models requires moving beyond current low-level simulations toward systems with adaptive, self-evolving agents, dynamic institutions, and tight empirical grounding. By articulating a six-level capability ladder, identifying gaps in the literature, and providing a concrete implementation roadmap and resources, the work aims to accelerate the development of high-fidelity economic simulation environments that can support both human decision-making and the training, evaluation, and safety of AI agents operating in economic contexts.

title: HarnessOpt-Bench: Evaluating LLMs at Harness Optimization
summary: As LLMs are increasingly deployed within agentic systems, their capabilities depend not only on the model weights but also on the harness: the prompts, tools, control flow, memory, and orchestration code surrounding them. This makes automated harness optimization -- the iterative and evaluation-guided improvement of a harness by an AI system -- both an important route to improving AI systems and a demanding capability for AI systems themselves. Yet the community lacks a common protocol for measuring how well frontier LLMs perform at this task. We introduce HarnessOpt-Bench, a benchmark for end-to-end harness optimization under expensive and stochastic evaluation. An optimizer, an LLM paired with a coding harness, receives a target agent's seed harness, graded evaluation feedback, and a fixed target-evaluation budget. It edits the harness and nominates a final candidate, which is scored by its normalized gain over the seed on a held-out test partition that remains inaccessible throughout search. A trusted execution environment enforces the evaluation boundary, meters target-agent resource use, and preserves candidate versions for audit. We evaluate 5 frontier LLMs as optimizers both under a shared coding harness and under their native harnesses across 4 downstream tasks, over 111 scored runs. Experiment results show that optimizer models separate more than the coding harnesses they act through, native harnesses are not consistently superior, and gains vary substantially across tasks and seed regimes. These results establish harness optimization as a measurable and discriminative capability with large space for improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces HarnessOpt-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating how well large language models can automatically optimize the “harness” (prompts, tools, control flow, etc.) surrounding target agents under realistic constraints like expensive, noisy evaluations.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly embedded in complex agentic systems, their real-world performance is heavily influenced not just by model weights but by the surrounding harness (prompts, tools, control logic, memory, orchestration). Improving this harness automatically is both a promising way to boost system performance and a challenging task that tests an LLM’s ability to reason, code, and optimize under constraints. However, there is currently no standardized protocol to measure or compare how well different frontier LLMs can perform this kind of harness optimization, especially in settings with costly and stochastic evaluations.
AI.method: The authors design HarnessOpt-Bench, an end-to-end benchmark where an optimizer (an LLM plus a coding harness) is given: (1) a seed harness for a target agent, (2) graded evaluation feedback, and (3) a fixed budget of evaluations. The optimizer iteratively edits the harness—changing prompts, tools use, or control flow—while receiving feedback from evaluations that are expensive and noisy. A trusted execution environment controls and meters access to the target agent, enforces an evaluation boundary so optimizers cannot circumvent the protocol, and records candidate harness versions for audit. Performance is measured by the normalized gain of the final nominated harness over the initial seed on a held-out test partition that remains hidden during search. The authors run 5 frontier LLMs as optimizers, under both a shared coding harness and each model’s native harness, across 4 downstream tasks, yielding 111 scored runs.
AI.result: Across the 111 runs, the study finds that differences between optimizer LLMs are more pronounced than differences between the coding harnesses they use, suggesting that the model’s intrinsic optimization capability matters more than the specific coding wrapper. Native harnesses (the ones normally used with each LLM) do not consistently outperform the shared harness, indicating that current native setups are not universally optimal for this optimization task. Performance gains from optimization vary widely across tasks and starting seed harness quality, showing that some tasks and initial conditions are more amenable to effective automatic harness optimization than others.
AI.conclusion: Harness optimization can be framed and measured as a concrete, discriminative capability of LLMs. HarnessOpt-Bench provides a standardized way to evaluate this capability under realistic constraints like expensive and stochastic evaluations, enforced by a trusted execution environment. The empirical results show substantial room for improvement in current systems, highlight that optimizer model choice is more critical than the surrounding coding harness, and demonstrate that native harnesses are not yet reliably superior. This establishes harness optimization as an important future benchmark and research direction for improving agentic LLM systems.

title: Integrating Implicit and Explicit Relational Biases through Graph-Based Multiple Instance Learning: A Case Study in Skin Lesion Diagnosis
comment: Accepted as a short paper for presentation at the 21st International Conference on Computational Intelligence Methods for Bioinformatics and Biostatistics (CIBB 2026)
summary: Relational inductive biases are essential for capturing structural dependencies among data. This study investigates a dual-level relational framework for image classification, bridging the gap between implicit representation learning and explicit structural modelling. We begin by establishing a baseline using an EfficientNetB3 architecture. To move beyond standard convolutional biases, we adopt a patch-based strategy, employing a convolutional masked autoencoder to learn implicit inter-patch relationships through self-supervised reconstruction. We then extend this approach by incorporating explicit relational modelling, organizing the learned embeddings into various graph topologies, including grid-based, random, and k-nearest neighbour structures. Experimental results on the ISIC-2018 and ISIC-2019 skin lesion diagnosis benchmarks show that combining implicit inter-patch modelling with explicit graph-based message passing yields the best performance. On the ISIC-2018 test set, the baseline model achieves a balanced accuracy of 76.17%, which improves to 77.12% with implicit patch-based relational modelling. The fully integrated grid-structured Graph Attention Network further increases performance to 79.27%. Similarly, on ISIC-2019, the implicit approach reaches 59.84% balanced accuracy, while the combination of implicit and explicit modelling yields 60.67%.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dual-level relational framework for image classification that combines implicit patch-based modelling with explicit graph-based message passing to better capture structural dependencies, achieving improved balanced accuracy on skin lesion benchmarks compared to an EfficientNetB3 baseline.
AI.motivation: Convolutional neural networks like EfficientNet implicitly model local spatial structure but struggle to explicitly capture richer relational dependencies among image regions, which can limit performance on complex tasks such as skin lesion diagnosis where structural patterns and relationships between regions are important. The authors aim to bridge the gap between implicit representation learning and explicit structural modelling to more fully exploit relational information in images.
AI.method: The authors first establish a CNN baseline using EfficientNetB3. They then adopt a patch-based strategy with a convolutional masked autoencoder to perform self-supervised reconstruction of masked patches, thereby learning implicit inter-patch relationships. Next, they explicitly model relations by arranging the learned patch embeddings into different graph topologies (grid, random, k-nearest neighbours) and apply a Graph Attention Network (GAT) for message passing over these graphs. They compare the baseline, implicit-only, and combined implicit+explicit relational models on skin lesion classification benchmarks (ISIC-2018 and ISIC-2019).
AI.result: On ISIC-2018, the baseline EfficientNetB3 achieves 76.17% balanced accuracy. Adding implicit patch-based relational modelling increases this to 77.12%. Incorporating explicit grid-structured GAT on top of the implicit model further improves performance to 79.27%. On ISIC-2019, implicit modelling reaches 59.84% balanced accuracy, while combining implicit and explicit relational modelling yields 60.67%, demonstrating consistent though moderate gains from the relational framework.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that dual-level relational inductive biases—implicit inter-patch modelling via masked autoencoding and explicit graph-based message passing—complement each other and lead to better image classification performance than standard CNNs alone. Organizing patch embeddings into structured graphs, especially grid-based ones processed by GATs, effectively captures structural dependencies critical for tasks like skin lesion diagnosis, suggesting that integrating both implicit and explicit relational components is a promising direction for visual recognition systems.

title: Beyond Top-K: Replacing Black-Box Retrieval with Interpretable Agentic Operations
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation over long documents is dominated by one design: chunk the text, embed the chunks, and surface the top-k nearest neighbours of the query. We argue that for an important class of documents -- financial statements, audit reports, regulatory returns -- this design is structurally unsound, and we make the argument measurable. On a 780-page government financial report, 86.8% of content lines are table rows, thousands of near-identical figures compete in one embedding space, and a figure inherits its unit from a header a median of 13 lines above it -- so a chunk boundary routinely separates a number from whether it is in lakh or crore, an error of two orders of magnitude. A table-aware chunker built as a steelman fixes the unit problem but leaves 27-30% of numeric chunks with no fiscal-year header at every chunk size we tried. We propose READ (Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search), in which an agent reads the raw document through three deterministic operations -- normalized lexical search, structural navigation, and bounded span reads -- exposed over the Model Context Protocol, so a trajectory is a replayable audit trail, not an opaque similarity score. On 51 verified questions READ answers 58.8% against dense retrieval's 15.7% (p_Holm = 2 x 10^-5) -- or 35.3% tuned, which READ still leads by 23.5 points (p_Holm = 0.017). An agent given the same loop but a top-k tool reaches only 27.5%, locating the gain in the interface rather than in iteration. We also report what the evidence does not support: BM25 is statistically indistinguishable from READ, so our result separates embedding-based from embedding-free retrieval, not agentic from lexical search.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that standard chunk-and-embed RAG is structurally unreliable for long, numeric, table-heavy financial documents and proposes an embedding-free, agentic search method (READ) that substantially improves QA accuracy while remaining auditable.
AI.motivation: Current RAG systems dominate long-document QA by chunking and embedding text, then retrieving top-k chunks by similarity. For financial and regulatory documents, which are highly tabular and numeric, this design often breaks crucial associations (e.g., numbers from their units or fiscal years) and creates noisy embedding spaces with many near-identical figures. The authors want to quantify how severe these structural issues are and to design a method that avoids them while remaining transparent and auditable, which is particularly important in finance and regulation.
AI.method: They empirically analyze a 780-page government financial report to measure document structure: proportion of table rows, distribution of numeric entries, distances from numbers to unit and year headers, and how chunking affects these relationships. They then build a strong table-aware chunker as a baseline, showing that even careful chunking leaves many numeric chunks without necessary context. The proposed method, READ (Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search), replaces dense retrieval with an agent that interacts with the raw document via three deterministic tools exposed over the Model Context Protocol: normalized lexical search, structural navigation, and bounded span reads. They compare READ against dense retrieval RAG, a tuned dense retrieval baseline, and an agent that uses the same agentic loop but with a top-k retrieval tool. They also compare against BM25 to isolate embedding-based vs embedding-free differences.
