AI.result: For the studied 780-page financial report, they find that 86.8% of content lines are table rows, that numeric entries are highly repetitive, and that units (e.g., lakh vs crore) are typically specified many lines above numbers (median distance 13 lines), leading to frequent separation of numbers from their units under standard chunking. Even with a table-aware chunker, 27–30% of numeric chunks lack a fiscal-year header across chunk sizes. On a set of 51 independently verified questions, READ answers 58.8% correctly versus 15.7% for standard dense retrieval RAG (statistically significant with Holm-corrected p = 2×10^-5). A tuned dense retrieval system improves to 35.3%, but READ still leads by 23.5 percentage points (p_Holm = 0.017). An agent using the same iterative loop but relying on a top-k retrieval tool instead of READ achieves only 27.5% accuracy, indicating that the main improvements come from the READ interface (lexical/structural operations) rather than agentic iteration alone. BM25 performance is statistically indistinguishable from READ.
AI.conclusion: Standard chunk-and-embed RAG is structurally unreliable for table-heavy, numeric financial documents because chunk boundaries and embedding competition routinely destroy essential contextual relationships such as units and fiscal years. Even carefully engineered table-aware chunkers cannot fully fix these issues. The proposed READ framework, which is embedding-free and uses deterministic lexical and structural operations under an agentic control loop, significantly outperforms dense retrieval-based RAG on financial QA tasks while providing replayable, auditable search trajectories. However, the gains are specifically over embedding-based retrieval: lexical methods like BM25 perform comparably to READ, suggesting that for this document class, the key distinction is embedding-free vs embedding-based retrieval, not agentic vs non-agentic search.

title: When History Lies: Evaluating and Improving Tool Use under Misleading Multi-Turn Histories
summary: Tool-calling agents infer task state from accumulated dialogue and tool traces. In persistent interactions, however, historical traces may remain structurally valid and semantically plausible after they cease to be authoritative for the current request. We show that such history can hijack a policy the model already possesses: on Qwen3-1.7B, pollution flips 32.1% of decisions that are correct under the original trajectory and frequently induces reuse of corrupted entities or interface conventions. We introduce bench, a paired benchmark with synchronized Original, Polluted, and Oracle State views that preserve the system policy, current tools, latest request, and gold next action. Eleven gold-preserving interventions isolate failures in decision state, entity binding, and interface execution across complete calls and non-call decisions. We further propose ours, which transfers an Oracle-conditioned teacher policy to a student observing only polluted history through soft supervision on student-generated prefixes. On Qwen3-1.7B, ours achieves 87.0% Balanced Tool-Use Accuracy, outperforming Gold-SFT (66.3%), Oracle sequence distillation (82.3%), and off-policy token distillation (85.0%). The method scales consistently: an 8B teacher raises the same compact 1.7B student to 91.9%, while an 8B student reaches 93.0%. The resulting policies further transfer to clean histories, unseen functions, independently regenerated evaluation contexts, external tool-use benchmarks, and noisy multi-hop question answering. These results establish history reliability as a distinct tool-use bottleneck and demonstrate reliable-state policy transfer as an effective and scalable solution.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how past tool-use history can corrupt tool-calling agents’ decisions and proposes a benchmark and training method to make them robust to such polluted histories.
AI.motivation: In long, persistent interactions, tool-using language models rely on historical dialogue and tool traces as state. Old traces can stay syntactically and semantically plausible even after they’re no longer correct for the current task. This “history pollution” can mislead the model into wrong tool calls, reused stale entities, or outdated interfaces. The authors aim to quantify this problem and develop methods to make tool-use policies robust to unreliable histories.
AI.method: 1) Construct a benchmark with paired views: Original (clean history), Polluted (with stale but plausible traces), and Oracle State (ideal current state). All views share the same underlying policy, tools, request, and gold next action. 2) Design 11 controlled interventions that preserve the gold action while isolating different failure sources: decision state, entity binding, and interface execution, spanning both calls and non-call decisions. 3) Propose a training method that distills a robust policy: an Oracle-conditioned teacher sees correct state, while a student only sees polluted histories. The teacher’s policy is transferred to the student by soft supervision on prefixes generated by the student itself, enabling reliable-state policy transfer. 4) Evaluate on Qwen3-1.7B and larger variants, and test generalization to various out-of-distribution settings (clean histories, new tools, new contexts, external benchmarks, and noisy QA).
AI.result: 1) On Qwen3-1.7B, polluted histories flip 32.1% of decisions that were correct under clean trajectories and often cause reuse of corrupted entities or outdated interface conventions. 2) The proposed benchmark (“bench”) and interventions show distinct failure modes tied to decision state, entity binding, and interface execution. 3) The proposed reliable-state policy transfer method attains 87.0% Balanced Tool-Use Accuracy, beating Gold-SFT (66.3%), Oracle sequence distillation (82.3%), and off-policy token distillation (85.0%). 4) Scaling the teacher and student models further improves performance: an 8B teacher boosts the 1.7B student to 91.9%, and an 8B student reaches 93.0%. 5) The learned policies transfer well to settings with clean history, unseen tools, regenerated evaluation contexts, external tool-use benchmarks, and noisy multi-hop QA.
AI.conclusion: History reliability is a key, previously underexplored bottleneck in tool-use agents: historical traces that remain structurally and semantically plausible can still be wrong and significantly derail decision-making. The authors’ benchmark formally exposes this vulnerability, while their reliable-state policy transfer approach effectively teaches models to act correctly even when their observed history is polluted. This method scales to larger models and generalizes across tasks and settings, suggesting that decoupling policy learning from noisy historical state is a practical path toward more robust tool-using agents.

title: Signal or Spurious Cue? A Randomized Audit of Survey-Country Metadata in LLM Social Inference
summary: Survey-country metadata can improve an LLM's forecast of an individual response when informative, yet the same cue may redirect the forecast when assigned at random. A within-record audit tests whether disclosing a random label's uniform, record-independent origin reduces its country-directed uptake, and whether verified survey country lowers held-out Brier loss. Independent population anchors and recorded human answers measure direction and consequence across five fixed API models, six countries, and seven development-selected targets. In the primary post-review 72-record panel, opaque and disclosed-random labels each produced country-direction shifts of 0.214. Paired attenuation was 0.0003 (95% CI [-0.0157, 0.0166]). Verified country reduced Brier loss by 0.040 (95% CI [0.024, 0.056]), while random-label regret included zero. A non-overlapping mixed-coverage consistency panel retained positive disclosed-random movement and verified utility, while attenuation remained uncertain. On the selected targets, verified metadata was useful in both panels, but disclosure did not reliably attenuate random-label uptake. PROV-FORECAST contains 14,400 paired item-level probability distributions from the corrected panel.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how survey-country metadata affects LLM forecasts of individual responses, and whether telling the model that country labels are random reduces its misleading influence, finding that real country metadata helps but disclosure does not reliably reduce the impact of random labels.
AI.motivation: LLMs increasingly forecast human survey responses using metadata like country, but such cues can be beneficial when accurate and harmful when spurious. The authors want to quantify both (1) the predictive value of true country metadata for probabilistic forecasts, and (2) the extent to which LLMs are misled by random country labels, and whether explicitly disclosing their randomness mitigates that problem. This addresses concerns about robustness, bias, and provenance-aware prompting when using LLMs in social science and forecasting contexts.
AI.method: They run a within-record audit using fixed API LLMs across six countries and seven survey targets. For each survey record, they generate probabilistic forecasts under different metadata conditions: verified survey country, random country labels, and random labels with explicit disclosure that they are uniform and record-independent. They measure (a) country-direction shifts in predicted distributions relative to population anchors and actual human responses, and (b) predictive accuracy using held-out Brier loss and regret. They conduct a primary 72-record post-review panel and a separate mixed-coverage consistency panel, and compile all item-level probability distributions into the PROV-FORECAST dataset (14,400 paired distributions).
AI.result: Opaque random country labels and random labels disclosed as random each induced similarly sized country-direction shifts (~0.214) in the primary panel, showing that LLMs still meaningfully respond to labels even when told they are random. The estimated attenuation from disclosure was essentially zero (0.0003, 95% CI including zero). In contrast, supplying verified country metadata significantly improved predictive accuracy, lowering Brier loss by 0.040 with a tight positive confidence interval, whereas random-label regret included zero, indicating no clear benefit. In the separate consistency panel, they again found positive movement from disclosed-random labels and utility from verified metadata, but the degree of attenuation remained statistically uncertain.
AI.conclusion: True survey-country metadata improves LLM forecasts of individual survey responses, but LLMs also pick up and follow random country labels, and simply disclosing that those labels are random does not reliably reduce their influence. Provenance-aware disclosure alone is insufficient to prevent misleading uptake of spurious metadata. The PROV-FORECAST dataset provides a resource for further study of how LLMs use provenance cues and how to design more robust prompting and training strategies that distinguish informative from non-informative metadata.

title: Evaluating Investment Logic in Large Language Models: A Real-World Benchmark Towards Personalzied Financial Agents
summary:
Investment competence is inherently personalized: the same market evidence can justify different actions for investors with different goals, horizons, portfolios, and risk boundaries. Yet financial LLMs are evaluated either by static question answering or by terminal profit and loss. The former omits agency; the latter cannot reveal whether a profitable action was grounded, profile-consistent, or merely lucky. We ask whether the community is using the wrong ruler for consequential agents.
  We introduce \textsc{InvestLogicBench}, a process-native benchmark containing 201,247 documented decisions from 151 real-world investors. Each episode instantiates a \textbf{P$\rightarrow$E$\rightarrow$R$\rightarrow$D$\rightarrow$O} trace: investor \textit{Profile}, observable market \textit{Events}, investment \textit{Reasoning}, executable \textit{Decision}, and delayed \textit{Outcome}. The release includes profile construction, point-in-time event binding, structured logic, horizons, outcomes, and post-mortems, and supports comprehension, profile-conditioned generation, and end-to-end replay. Across four leading LLMs, logical plausibility remains near 4/5 while event grounding is only 0.8--2.8/5; return and process quality also disagree. These results expose polished but weakly grounded reasoning that outcome-only evaluation hides. We further argue that P$\rightarrow$E$\rightarrow$R$\rightarrow$D$\rightarrow$O should be a data-system interface, requiring versioned profiles, temporal provenance, inspectable retrieval, decision ledgers, and replayable outcomes. Finance is our stress test for a broader class of personalized, consequential agents.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces InvestLogicBench, a large benchmark of real-world investment decisions that captures not just outcomes but full decision processes, showing that current financial LLMs often produce plausible yet weakly grounded reasoning, and arguing for richer, process-aware evaluation and data infrastructure for personalized, high-stakes agents.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of financial LLMs focus either on static Q&A or on final profit and loss. Static Q&A ignores that investment actions must be tailored to an investor’s unique profile (goals, horizon, risk, portfolio), while outcome-based metrics cannot distinguish justified, profile-consistent decisions from lucky gains or well-reasoned but temporarily unprofitable ones. This mismatch risks overestimating the competence and safety of consequential agents that advise on investments. The authors therefore question whether the community is using the wrong evaluation paradigm ("wrong ruler") and seek to design a benchmark that reflects the full, personalized decision process.
AI.method: The authors construct InvestLogicBench, a process-native benchmark built from 201,247 decisions made by 151 real-world investors. Each decision episode is represented as a P→E→R→D→O trace: (P) investor Profile; (E) observable market Events at the time; (R) the investor’s Reasoning; (D) the executed Decision; and (O) the delayed Outcome. The dataset includes structured profiles, point-in-time event binding, explicit reasoning logic, investment horizons, realized outcomes, and post-mortem analyses. They design tasks for comprehension, profile-conditioned text generation, and end-to-end replay of decisions. Four leading LLMs are evaluated along dimensions such as logical plausibility, event grounding, return quality, and process quality, disentangling surface coherence from factual grounding and decision soundness.
AI.result: Across four state-of-the-art LLMs, the models achieve relatively high logical plausibility scores (around 4/5), indicating that their explanations sound coherent and well-structured. However, their grounding in actual market events is poor, with scores between 0.8 and 2.8/5, revealing that the reasoning often does not faithfully track the underlying data. Moreover, measures of realized returns and process quality (how well the reasoning aligns with the investor profile, horizon, and events) do not correlate well, showing that seemingly successful outcomes can be driven by luck or misaligned logic. This contrast exposes a pattern of polished but weakly grounded reasoning that would be invisible under outcome-only evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that current evaluation approaches for financial LLMs are inadequate for assessing personalized, high-stakes investment agents. InvestLogicBench demonstrates the need to evaluate both process and outcome, emphasizing personalized profiles, temporal context, and reasoning quality. The authors advocate for treating the P→E→R→D→O structure as a general data-system interface: systems should maintain versioned investor profiles, track temporal provenance of information, provide inspectable retrieval mechanisms, log decisions in ledgers, and support replayable outcomes. Finance serves as a demanding test case, but the proposed framework is intended for a broader class of personalized, consequential AI agents beyond investing.

title: Mind the Gaps: Mixture-of-Minds for Human Simulation
summary: Predicting how a population will answer a new question is a long-standing goal. Statistical methods succeed at the level of the mass but falter at the level of the individual. Large language model simulators inherit this gap. They recover a population's central tendencies while flattening its heterogeneity, and they carry social biases and prompt brittleness that distort individual predictions. This paper introduces Anacreon, an audience simulation model that targets the individual level within a narrow, well-specified domain. Anacreon learns an authorship embedding that separates individuals, clusters a real qualitative corpus around seed people, and trains a dedicated adapter for each cluster, a mixture of minds, on a Gemma~4 12B base. It harvests demographics, psychological traits, and survey responses from public text, and augments each record with a chain-of-emotion. It reduces prompt brittleness by shuffling response options and reduces positive bias by balancing the training distribution. On a large, externally sourced survey, Anacreon reaches a state-of-the-art ordinal alignment of 0.775, the individual-level accuracy measure on which the field has converged, with a small residual bias. The work is a step toward drawing aggregate insight from faithfully simulated individuals.

AI.tldr: Anacreon is a specialized audience simulation model that predicts individual-level responses within a well-defined domain, improving accuracy and reducing bias compared to standard large language model simulators.
AI.motivation: Existing statistical and LLM-based audience simulation methods can capture population-level trends but fail to accurately model individual-level heterogeneity. They also suffer from social biases and prompt brittleness, which distort predictions for specific people. The authors aim to create a system that can more faithfully simulate how distinct individuals would respond, within a constrained domain, to enable better aggregate insights built from realistic individual models.
AI.method: The authors propose Anacreon, an audience simulation model built on a Gemma 4 12B base model with several key components: (1) learning an authorship embedding that differentiates individuals; (2) clustering a qualitative corpus around seed individuals to form groups of similar people, each representing a "mixture of minds"; (3) training a dedicated adapter for each cluster on top of the base model; (4) automatically extracting demographics, psychological traits, and survey responses from public text for each person; (5) augmenting each record with a chain-of-emotion representation; (6) mitigating prompt brittleness by shuffling response options; and (7) reducing positive bias by balancing the training distribution.
AI.result: On a large, externally sourced survey dataset, Anacreon achieves an ordinal alignment score of 0.775, which is the current state-of-the-art metric for individual-level prediction accuracy in this field. The model still exhibits a small residual bias but significantly improves fidelity of individual-level simulations compared with previous approaches.
AI.conclusion: Anacreon demonstrates that tailoring language model simulations to clusters of individuals, enriched with demographic, psychological, and emotional information, can substantially improve individual-level response prediction while mitigating some common LLM biases and prompt sensitivities. This represents progress toward building aggregate insights from more faithful simulations of individuals rather than relying solely on population-level averages.

title: Contextual Information Policy Optimization for Search Agents
summary: Search agents extend large language models beyond static parametric memory by enabling them to acquire and use ex ternal evidence during multi-step reasoning. For knowledge intensive tasks involving complex or evolving information, their reliability depends not only on retrieving relevant ev idence but also on using it to guide subsequent reasoning. However, existing methods primarily reward final-answer cor rectness or intermediate progress, without directly assessing whether post-retrieval actions are grounded in the retrieved evidence. This misalignment encourages prior-driven reason ing: agents form conclusions based on internal knowledge and use retrieval mainly to confirm them, resulting in confirma tion bias and inefficient evidenceuse.Toaddressthisissue, we propose Contextual Information Policy Optimization (CIPO), an evidence-oriented reinforcement learning framework that explicitly aligns policy optimization with external evidence use. CIPO assigns dense, turn-level credit to reasoning ac tions influenced by retrieved information, while combining this evidence-use signal with a global outcome reward to pre serveanswercorrectness.Withthismanner,CIPOdiscourages evidence-detached guesses and promotes reasoning trajecto ries in which retrieved facts can guide or revise subsequent reasoning. Importantly, CIPO requires neither human process annotations nor an additional reward model. Extensive exper iments on seven in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks show that CIPO reduces the prevalence of prior-driven rea soning and achieves excellent performance on most tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CIPO, a reinforcement learning framework that trains search-augmented LLM agents to actually use retrieved evidence in their reasoning, not just to reach the right final answer.
AI.motivation: Search-augmented LLM agents can access external information for multi-step reasoning, which is crucial for knowledge-intensive or evolving domains. However, existing training methods mostly reward final answer accuracy or coarse intermediate progress, ignoring whether each reasoning step is genuinely grounded in the retrieved evidence. This leads to prior-driven reasoning where agents rely on their parametric knowledge and use retrieval mainly for confirmation, causing confirmation bias, weak evidence utilization, and unreliable behavior in domains where external evidence should dominate.
AI.method: The authors propose Contextual Information Policy Optimization (CIPO), an evidence-oriented RL framework for training search agents. CIPO defines a dense, turn-level reward that measures how much each reasoning action is influenced by the retrieved context, and combines this with a global outcome reward for final correctness. The RL objective is thus aligned with evidence use: actions that are better supported or shaped by the retrieved evidence receive higher credit, while actions detached from that evidence receive lower credit. CIPO does this without requiring human step-by-step annotations or an extra learned reward model, operating directly over the agent’s multi-step trajectories and retrieval results.
AI.result: Across seven benchmarks, including both in-domain and out-of-domain knowledge-intensive tasks, agents trained with CIPO show reduced prior-driven reasoning compared with baselines. They more frequently revise or guide their reasoning based on retrieved facts instead of sticking to prior beliefs, and they achieve strong or state-of-the-art performance on most evaluated tasks, indicating that better grounding in evidence does not sacrifice accuracy and can in fact improve it.
AI.conclusion: Grounding reinforcement learning for search-augmented LLM agents in explicit evidence use, rather than only in final answer correctness, mitigates confirmation bias and improves reliability on knowledge-intensive tasks. CIPO provides a practical way to assign turn-level credit for evidence-informed actions without extra supervision, encouraging reasoning trajectories where retrieval results genuinely shape or correct the model’s thinking and yielding strong empirical gains across multiple benchmarks.

title: FinEvo-Bench: A Longitudinal Benchmark for Self-Evolving Agents in Professional Financial Workflows
summary: Most agent benchmarks evaluate tasks independently and cannot measure whether experience from one task helps with later tasks. Existing self-evolution benchmarks do not jointly cover professional workflows, open-ended deliverables, and multi-aspect evaluation. We introduce FinEvo-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark with 120 real-case-grounded tasks, 20 business scenes across six financial domains. Institution-provided professional procedures define the required operations and constraints. Eligible institution-provided and publicly documented cases supply the task facts. Each scene contains six related but substantively distinct cases that share a professional procedure and a manually reviewed rubric for task quality and financial compliance. We compare four self-evolving agent scaffolds using the same Qwen3.7-Max backbone and three independently shuffled, globally interleaved task streams. Paired non-evolving controls estimate each scaffold's self-evolution gain from retained experience, while an independent Claude Code scoring agent backed by Claude Opus 4.6 evaluates all outputs. Letta achieves the highest evolved score (91.65) and fewest compliance issues (0.09 per task); Codex achieves the largest self-evolution gain (+19.37). Across scaffolds, the evolving condition raises scores by 9.33-19.37 points and reduces compliance issues by 0.12-0.44 per task. Paired score gains at within-scene ranks 4-6 exceed those at ranks 1-3 by 6.10-8.70 points. In Claude Code, skill-only evolution produces higher task quality and fewer compliance issues than memory-only and combined memory-skill evolution. Across all four scaffolds, rubric feedback also yields higher scores and fewer compliance issues than reference-answer feedback. FinEvo-Bench measures both professional performance and self-evolution ability: how effectively an agent turns prior experience into later improvement.

AI.tldr: FinEvo-Bench is a longitudinal benchmark to test how well AI agents in finance improve over sequences of related real-world tasks, showing that evolving agents outperform non-evolving ones in both quality and compliance.
AI.motivation: Existing agent benchmarks mostly test tasks in isolation and thus cannot quantify whether experience on earlier tasks improves performance on later ones. Current self-evolution benchmarks also lack realistic professional workflows, open-ended deliverables, and rich multi-aspect evaluation, especially in high-stakes domains like finance. There is a need for a rigorous, longitudinal, domain-grounded benchmark that can evaluate both task performance and the ability of agent scaffolds to self-evolve over time while respecting professional procedures and compliance constraints.
AI.method: The authors construct FinEvo-Bench, a benchmark of 120 tasks organized into 20 business scenes across six financial domains. Each scene has six distinct but related cases sharing an institution-provided professional procedure and a manually reviewed evaluation rubric focused on task quality and financial compliance. Real and publicly documented institutional cases provide factual grounding. They test four different self-evolving agent scaffolds built on the same Qwen3.7-Max model, running them on three independently shuffled, globally interleaved task streams. For each scaffold, a paired non-evolving control (no experience retention) is used to estimate self-evolution gains. An independent Claude Code scoring agent, backed by Claude Opus 4.6, evaluates outputs on quality and compliance. They also ablate different evolution mechanisms (skill-only, memory-only, combined) and different feedback types (rubric vs reference-answer feedback).
AI.result: Letta achieves the best overall evolved performance (score 91.65) and the fewest compliance issues (0.09 per task), while Codex shows the largest self-evolution gain (+19.37 points). Across all scaffolds, enabling evolution increases scores by 9.33–19.37 points and reduces compliance issues by 0.12–0.44 per task relative to non-evolving controls. Later tasks in a scene (ranks 4–6) benefit more from evolution than early tasks (ranks 1–3), with paired score gains larger by 6.10–8.70 points. Among evolution strategies within Claude Code, skill-only evolution yields higher quality and fewer compliance issues than memory-only or combined memory-skill approaches. Rubric-based feedback consistently outperforms reference-answer feedback in both score and compliance across the four scaffolds.
AI.conclusion: FinEvo-Bench offers a realistic, longitudinal benchmark for financial-domain agents that captures both professional task performance and the capacity for self-evolution from prior experience. The results show that self-evolving scaffolds meaningfully improve quality and reduce compliance violations over time, with larger benefits on later, related tasks. Skill-focused evolution and rubric-based feedback are more effective than memory-focused or reference-answer-based approaches. The benchmark can serve as a standard for comparing agent scaffolds and designing mechanisms that turn accumulated experience into safer, higher-quality performance in professional workflows.

title: PaDoc: Layout-Grounded Parallel Decoding for Document Parsing
summary: End-to-end document parsers provide a unified interface, but serialize page layouts and regional contents into one autoregressive sequence. This formulation forces independent regions onto a decoding path whose length grows with the total content, whereas crop-based two-stage parsers expose region-level parallelism at the cost of repeated visual prefills and fragmented page context. To retain full-page context while removing dependencies, we propose PaDoc, a layout-grounded parser that treats the predicted layout as a branching structure over a shared page representation. Under a region-sufficiency assumption, we derive a prefix-conditioned factorization in which the layout stream and regional content branches advance concurrently, reducing the decoding depth to the longest layout-content path. We realize this factorization within a single MLLM: packed variable-length ancestor attention preserves the visibility under standard next-token training, while masked parallel decoding creates branches that the evaluated vLLM backend serves as concurrent requests with cache-resident shared-prefix reuse. On OmniDocBench Full, PaDoc attains an Overall layout F1 of 91.1 and, among end-to-end parsers, a top-tier Overall score of 94.24 together with the best Text Edit (0.038) and Formula CDM (95.59). On a 384-page subset and one A800 GPU, it is the fastest end-to-end parser at five concurrency levels, improving valid-page throughput by 67.4-118% and reducing P95 latency by 39.2-54.9% relative to a same-backbone Sequential SFT baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/Longin-Yu/Padoc

AI.tldr: PaDoc is an end-to-end document parser that uses a branching, layout-grounded decoding structure over a shared page representation to enable parallel parsing of page regions, achieving higher accuracy and significantly better throughput and latency than sequential parsers.
AI.motivation: Existing end-to-end document parsers serialize entire page layouts and content into a single autoregressive sequence, making decoding depth scale with total content and unnecessarily coupling independent regions. Two-stage crop-based systems enable regional parallelism but require repeated visual processing and lose holistic page context. There is a need for a parser that keeps full-page context while enabling parallel, efficient decoding of independent regions.
AI.method: The authors propose PaDoc, a layout-grounded document parser that interprets the predicted layout as a branching structure defined over a shared page representation. Assuming that each region is self-sufficient given its context, they derive a prefix-conditioned factorization where a layout token stream and multiple regional content streams advance in parallel, reducing decoding depth to that of the longest layout-content path. PaDoc is implemented in a single multimodal LLM using packed variable-length ancestor attention to preserve correct visibility patterns under standard next-token training, and a masked parallel decoding scheme that turns branches into concurrent decoding requests. These requests are served by a vLLM backend that reuses cache for shared prefixes across branches.
AI.result: On OmniDocBench Full, PaDoc achieves an Overall layout F1 of 91.1 and, among end-to-end parsers, a top-tier Overall score of 94.24 with best-in-class Text Edit distance (0.038) and Formula CDM (95.59). On a 384-page subset using a single A800 GPU, PaDoc is the fastest end-to-end parser across five concurrency levels, improving valid-page throughput by 67.4–118% and reducing 95th-percentile latency by 39.2–54.9% compared to a sequential SFT baseline with the same backbone.
AI.conclusion: PaDoc demonstrates that reinterpreting document parsing as layout-grounded branching over a shared representation enables parallel decoding that preserves full-page context while significantly improving both accuracy and efficiency. The approach scales better with page complexity than fully sequential end-to-end parsers and avoids the redundancy and context fragmentation of crop-based two-stage systems, establishing a new state of the art on OmniDocBench and strong practical advantages in high-throughput settings.

title: CogVis: Must Open-Vocabulary Change Detection Perceive the Scene Anew for Every Query?
comment: 19 pages, 11 figures, including 3 supplementary figures. Code: https://github.com/KotlinWang/CogVis
summary: Earth-surface monitoring requires change detection models capable of recognizing arbitrary semantic categories. Open-Vocabulary Change Detection (OVCD) addresses this need. However, existing methods often entangle temporal perception, semantic discrimination, and region verification, causing unstable results and redundant computation. Inspired by human visual change perception, we propose CogVis, a cognitive memory-guided framework that reformulates OVCD as a perception-memory-verification paradigm. CogVis first employs a Scene Change Perceptron (SCP) to extract a reusable, category-agnostic change prior from frozen bi-temporal features, thereby decoupling temporal evidence from semantic category decisions. A Semantic Memory Calibrator (SMC) then compensates for category-dependent score shifts by dynamically estimating an image-query-specific decision threshold. Finally, an Adaptive Region Filter (ARF) filters connected candidates using learned semantic, temporal, and structural reliability. Experiments on seven benchmarks spanning semantic change detection, binary change localization, and building-damage assessment show that CogVis achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated datasets. By sharing scene-level change perception, CogVis further avoids repeating category-agnostic temporal perception across queries and improves inference throughput by 28.50%.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CogVis, a cognitive memory-guided framework for open-vocabulary change detection that decouples temporal change perception from semantic decisions and adds memory-based calibration and region verification, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy and faster inference on multiple remote-sensing benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Earth-surface monitoring applications (e.g., land use, damage assessment) require detecting changes for arbitrary semantic categories, which is the focus of Open-Vocabulary Change Detection (OVCD). Existing OVCD methods mix three aspects—temporal change perception, semantic category discrimination, and spatial region verification—into a single process, leading to unstable performance, poor generalization to new categories, and repeated computation for each query. The authors aim to build a more human-like, modular change detection system that can generalize across categories and queries while being computationally efficient.
AI.method: They introduce CogVis, framed as a perception–memory–verification pipeline. (1) Scene Change Perceptron (SCP): from frozen bi-temporal image features, it extracts a reusable, category-agnostic “change prior”, effectively isolating temporal change evidence from semantic classification; this prior can be shared across different text or category queries. (2) Semantic Memory Calibrator (SMC): given an image and query, it dynamically estimates a decision threshold that compensates for query- and image-dependent score shifts, acting like a learned semantic memory to normalize scores across categories. (3) Adaptive Region Filter (ARF): after initial change predictions, it filters connected candidate regions using learned measures of semantic, temporal, and structural reliability, improving spatial precision and reducing false positives. The overall design mimics human visual change perception, combining early generic change sensing, semantic calibration, and final region-level verification.
AI.result: Across seven benchmarks covering semantic change detection, binary change localization, and building-damage assessment, CogVis attains state-of-the-art performance on all evaluated datasets. In addition to accuracy gains, by sharing the scene-level, category-agnostic change prior among different queries, it avoids re-running temporal perception for each query and improves inference throughput by 28.50%, demonstrating both effectiveness and efficiency benefits.
AI.conclusion: CogVis successfully reformulates OVCD into a modular perception–memory–verification framework, with a category-agnostic change prior, semantic memory-based calibration, and adaptive region filtering. This design stabilizes change detection, improves generalization to arbitrary categories, and reduces redundant computation. The framework sets new state-of-the-art results on several remote-sensing change detection tasks while significantly speeding up inference, indicating that cognitively inspired decoupling of temporal and semantic processing is a promising direction for open-vocabulary Earth-surface monitoring.

title: iARCS: Iterative Agentic RL for Controllable 3D Scene Generation
summary: Synthetic 3D scene generation is increasingly used as a data source for computer vision and embodied AI, but existing generators often optimize perceptual realism without reliably satisfying task-critical functional constraints. This mismatch limits the usefulness of synthetic data for downstream training, where accessibility, traversability, and spatial rule compliance are often essential. We present iARCS, an iterative agentic reinforcement learning framework that adapts a pretrained scene generator to natural-language task requirements. iARCS uses a two-stage strategy: universal-reward pretraining to improve physical plausibility and layout quality, followed by task-specific fine-tuning with LLM-generated reward programs that are iteratively refined from training feedback. Experiments show improved constraint fidelity on walkability, reachability, and clearance-focused tasks, effective task-specific constraint optimization, and competitive scene diversity. We further show that data generated by iARCS improves a base generator, supporting its value as a practical synthetic data generation tool rather than only a controllable scene editing method.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces iARCS, an RL-based framework that adapts 3D scene generators to satisfy functional, task-specific constraints from natural-language instructions while preserving diversity.
AI.motivation: Existing synthetic 3D scene generators focus on visual realism but often violate functional constraints critical for downstream tasks (e.g., robotics and embodied AI), such as walkability, reachability, and spatial rules. There is a need for a way to systematically adapt pretrained generators so that they respect such constraints defined in natural language.
AI.method: The authors propose iARCS, an iterative agentic reinforcement learning framework. It works in two stages: (1) universal-reward pretraining, where a pretrained scene generator is optimized with general rewards for physical plausibility and layout quality; and (2) task-specific fine-tuning, where large language models generate reward programs from natural-language requirements. These reward programs are iteratively refined using feedback from training outcomes to better enforce specific constraints. The framework modifies the generator’s behavior while maintaining diversity of scenes.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that iARCS produces 3D scenes with higher fidelity to constraints related to walkability, reachability, and clearance, and can effectively optimize scene layouts for various task-specific constraints. It also maintains competitive scene diversity compared to baselines. Additionally, training a base generator on data produced by iARCS further improves the base generator’s quality, showing that iARCS-generated data is useful beyond just on-the-fly scene editing.
AI.conclusion: iARCS successfully bridges the gap between visually realistic but functionally unreliable synthetic scenes and the needs of downstream embodied AI tasks. By leveraging RL and LLM-generated reward programs, it enables controllable, task-aligned 3D scene generation and also serves as a practical tool for producing better training data for future generators.

title: MicroEvo: Knowledge-Guided LLM Sampling for Efficient Microarchitecture Design Space Exploration
summary: Microarchitecture design space exploration suffers from expansive search spaces and expensive PPA evaluation, leaving only a small simulation budget for design decision-making. Existing methods perform blind search without considering microarchitectural dependencies and fail to learn from the iterative search effectively, leading to wasted evaluations and weak Pareto convergence. In this paper, we propose MicroEvo, a knowledge-guided framework that couples off-the-shelf LLMs with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for multi-objective microarchitecture optimization. MicroEvo combines LLM-driven evolutionary operators, a Pareto-aware tree policy that balances Pareto contribution and diversity, an active knowledge accumulation mechanism that extracts and reuses optimization insights, and state-aware directives that adapt the search behavior online. Experiments show that MicroEvo improves Pareto-front quality by up to 36.2% over NSGA-II and achieves 10.6x higher search efficiency, and also demonstrates strong scalability to a complex industrial-scale core. The code repository is available at: https://github.com/GEAR-SEU/MicroEvo-ICCAD-26.

AI.tldr: MicroEvo is a knowledge-guided LLM+MCTS framework that efficiently explores microarchitecture design spaces for better PPA Pareto fronts.
AI.motivation: Microarchitecture design space exploration has huge, complex search spaces and costly PPA evaluations, so only a small number of simulations can be run. Existing optimization methods largely perform blind, unguided search that ignores dependencies between microarchitectural parameters and does not effectively reuse knowledge from prior evaluations, leading to inefficient use of the simulation budget and poor Pareto-front convergence.
AI.method: MicroEvo couples large language models with Monte Carlo Tree Search for multi-objective microarchitecture optimization. It uses LLM-driven evolutionary operators to generate and mutate candidate designs; a Pareto-aware tree policy in MCTS that explicitly balances a candidate’s contribution to the current Pareto front and the diversity of explored designs; an active knowledge accumulation mechanism that extracts optimization insights from the search history and reuses them later; and state-aware directives that adapt the search strategy online based on the current search status.
AI.result: On benchmark microarchitecture design problems, MicroEvo improves Pareto-front quality by up to 36.2% over NSGA-II and yields 10.6x higher search efficiency, and it scales effectively to an industrial-scale core design. Code is publicly released at the provided GitHub repository.
AI.conclusion: Coupling LLM-guided evolutionary operators, Pareto-aware MCTS, and active knowledge reuse enables much more sample-efficient and higher-quality microarchitecture design space exploration than traditional evolutionary baselines like NSGA-II, and the approach scales to real industrial designs.

title: Comparative Approaches to Agent Retrieval over Large Skill Libraries
summary: Agents backed by large skill libraries must decide which skills to load and in what order. Loading the entire library into context is expensive and provides no structure for autonomous sequencing. We study two systems for this problem over a corpus of 690 skills: a hybrid ranker combining lexical and dense-embedding retrieval for sparse, on-demand loading, and a typed knowledge graph encoding workflow relations such as prerequisites, data flow, and ordering. On a set of 117 realistic, non-echoing queries, the hybrid ranker retrieves the correct skill within the top five in 73.5% +/- 8.0 of cases, leaving roughly a quarter of queries unserved. When used as the design intended (substituting graph neighbours for additional ranked results at matched token budget), the graph is significantly worse (-11.2 points, p = 0.0007). Its LLM-generated edge layer adds nothing over neighbours obtained free from a local embedding pass, and 73% of the queries the ranker misses are not reachable through the graph at all. We attribute this to a pre-filter topology bound. Because the graph's candidate edges are drawn from the same embedding neighbourhood the ranker already searches, 98.6% of typed edges connect skills the ranker had already surfaced together. The graph can enrich relation semantics but cannot extend retrieval reach. We further show that evaluating on author-written queries overstates hit@5 by up to 44 points, which would have hidden these results entirely. Our contribution is a mechanistic account of why added structure does not improve retrieval over a strong ranker, and identify the conditions under which adding structural interdependence into the retrieval is optimal.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates why adding structured knowledge (a typed workflow graph) on top of a strong hybrid ranker does not improve skill retrieval for large tool libraries, and explains when such structure could actually help.
AI.motivation: Large agents rely on many skills/tools, but loading all skills into context is expensive and sequencing them is hard. Designers hope that structured representations like knowledge graphs can guide retrieval and composition better than pure embedding-based search, yet it is unclear whether such added structure truly improves which skills are found and used.
AI.method: The authors construct a corpus of 690 skills and two retrieval systems: (1) a hybrid ranker that combines lexical features and dense embeddings to retrieve skills on demand; (2) a typed knowledge graph encoding workflow relations among skills (prerequisites, data flow, ordering), whose edges are largely generated by an LLM based on local embedding neighborhoods. They evaluate both systems on 117 realistic user queries that do not simply echo skill names, comparing hit@5 and analyzing how graph topology and edge construction interact with the ranker’s candidate space.
AI.result: The hybrid ranker alone retrieves the correct skill in the top 5 results for about 73.5% of realistic queries, leaving roughly a quarter unsatisfied. When the knowledge graph is used as intended—substituting graph neighbors for extra ranked items under the same token budget—performance drops by about 11.2 hit@5 points, a statistically significant degradation. The LLM-generated typed edges do not outperform cheaper local embedding neighbors, 73% of missed queries are not reachable via the graph, and 98.6% of graph edges connect skills that the ranker already co-retrieves, indicating that the graph mostly densifies already-known neighborhoods instead of expanding coverage.
AI.conclusion: Because graph edges are drawn from the same embedding neighborhoods already exploited by the hybrid ranker, the graph cannot extend retrieval reach, only enrich semantics; thus adding this structural layer does not improve and can even harm retrieval under a fixed budget. The paper offers a mechanistic explanation—pre-filter topology bound—for why the added structure fails, shows that author-written queries can drastically overestimate performance, and outlines conditions under which incorporating structural interdependence into retrieval would be beneficial, namely when graph construction is decoupled from the ranker’s candidate space so that structure can actually expand the set of reachable skills.

title: EnvACE: Internalizing Environment Dynamics via World Rehearsal for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Training large language model agents for long-horizon tool use typically relies on interactions with real or synthesized executable environments, whose construction and verification are costly, or on external simulators that are difficult to ground. We introduce EnvACE, an agentic reinforcement learning method that replaces external environment interaction during training with world rehearsal. The policy alternates between acting and rehearsal: it first generates a tool call, then plays the role of the environment to produce the response induced by that action, and conditions subsequent decisions on the rehearsed response. Both roles are jointly optimized end-to-end using task-success rewards. Through world rehearsal, the policy internalizes the relationship between actions and their environment responses in its parameters, yielding an agent world model that directly supports decision making. Across BFCL-v4, tau^2-Bench, VitaBench, and FinMCP-Bench, EnvACE achieves strong and transferable performance, outperforming environment-scaling baselines in the overall evaluation. Controlled studies further show that world rehearsal consistently improves policy learning across model scales. At test time, the internalized world model enables private rehearsal before committed execution, yielding further gains under a moderate rehearsal budget without additional external interaction. Our findings establish world rehearsal as a new path toward scaling LLM agent training beyond the constraints of external environments. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Within-yao/EnvACE.

AI.tldr: EnvACE is a reinforcement learning framework where an LLM agent learns tool use by rehearsing both actions and environment responses internally, avoiding dependence on external executable environments and simulators.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for training LLM agents on long-horizon tool use require expensive, hard-to-verify executable environments or ungrounded simulators, which limit scalability and practicality. The authors aim to remove this bottleneck by letting the agent itself model and rehearse environment interactions during training, so that it can learn effective tool use without needing extensive external environment calls.
AI.method: EnvACE trains a single LLM policy that alternates between two roles: (1) acting as the agent to propose a tool call, and (2) acting as the environment to generate the response that would result from that tool call. This "world rehearsal" sequence is optimized end-to-end with reinforcement learning using task-success rewards. The model internalizes the mapping from actions to environment responses in its parameters, effectively learning a world model that is directly coupled to decision making. At test time, the same mechanism allows the agent to privately rehearse hypothetical tool calls before committing to real execution, within a bounded rehearsal budget.
AI.result: On four benchmarks targeting long-horizon tool use (BFCL-v4, tau^2-Bench, VitaBench, and FinMCP-Bench), EnvACE delivers strong and transferable performance, surpassing baselines that rely on scaling external environments. Ablation and controlled studies confirm that adding world rehearsal consistently improves policy learning over different model sizes, and test-time private rehearsal further boosts performance without increasing external environment interaction.
AI.conclusion: World rehearsal—having an LLM agent jointly learn both action selection and environment response generation—offers a scalable alternative to environment-dependent training for tool-using agents. By internalizing an agent-centric world model that supports both learning and inference-time rehearsal, EnvACE overcomes limitations imposed by external environments and sets a new direction for scaling LLM agent training for long-horizon tasks.

title: TS-RAG: Retrieval Augmented Generation for Time Series Forecasting
summary: While deep learning models, particularly transformer-based architectures, have shown impressive performance in time series forecasting, the application of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in this domain remains limited. Since RAG has proven effective in enhancing the capabilities of large language models by incorporating relevant external information, retrieving similar time series sequences as references might also improve accuracy in time series forecasting tasks. However, most time series models are constrained by limited training data, smaller parameter scales, and a lack of the extensive generative capabilities found in large language models. Simply concatenating reference sequences into the prompt, as done in language models, may not yield the expected results. To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach, TS-RAG, which leverages RAG to enhance forecasting performance. The framework introduces specially designed reference tokens to effectively fuse information from the input sequence with that from retrieved similar sequences, enabling a more robust capture of complex temporal dynamics. Experimental results demonstrate that TS-RAG achieves consistent state-of-the-art performance across several real-world forecasting benchmarks.

AI.tldr: They propose TS-RAG, a retrieval-augmented generation framework tailored for time series forecasting, which uses special reference tokens to fuse input and retrieved sequences and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based deep models work well for time series forecasting, but RAG—successful in LLMs—has been underused in this domain. Simply importing text-style RAG (concatenating retrieved sequences to the input) does not work well because time series models usually have less data, fewer parameters, and weaker generative capacity than LLMs. The authors want to exploit external similar sequences to improve forecasting while overcoming these structural limitations.
AI.method: They design TS-RAG, a RAG framework specific to time series. The system retrieves similar historical time series segments as external references and introduces specially designed reference tokens into the model. These tokens act as fusion interfaces that let the model effectively combine information from the original input sequence with that from retrieved sequences, allowing the transformer to better model complex temporal patterns.
AI.result: On several real-world time series forecasting benchmarks, TS-RAG delivers consistent and strong improvements, reaching state-of-the-art accuracy compared with existing forecasting methods that do not use this tailored RAG mechanism.
AI.conclusion: RAG can be successfully adapted from language tasks to time series forecasting when the architecture is redesigned rather than directly copied. By using reference tokens to integrate retrieved similar sequences with the current input, TS-RAG captures more complex temporal dynamics and achieves SOTA forecasting performance, indicating that retrieval-guided modeling is a promising direction for time series prediction.

title: DASH: Divergence-Adaptive Supervision Horizons for On-Policy Self-Distillation of Reasoning Models
comment: 17 pages, 4 figures, 9 tables. Code at https://github.com/DBtxy/DASH-OPSD
summary:
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models using automatically verifiable outcome signals, but these signals are typically sparse and at the sequence-level. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) mitigates this sparsity by querying a privileged teacher at student-visited prefixes and providing dense token-level distributional supervision. Although this dense supervision alleviates signal sparsity, we find that standard OPSD still underexploits the temporal structure of the rollout. It assigns every local divergence the same coefficient, regardless of its position or the divergence sequence in which it occurs. In on-policy autoregressive generation, the same divergence magnitude can follow different discrepancy histories, reflecting different evolutions of the mismatch between the teacher and student. Since the local scalar alone cannot distinguish these temporal contexts, standard OPSD cannot adapt its token-level weights to the realized discrepancy sequence. To address this limitation, we propose Divergence-Adaptive Supervision Horizons (DASH). DASH maps the gap between each local distillation signal and the sequence-level mean to an adaptive propagation gate and then uses these gates to control backward multi-step aggregation. By doing so, DASH adjusts token-level supervision weights according to how local divergences evolve during generation. Experiments on three mathematical reasoning benchmarks across three model scales show that DASH improves over our matched vanilla OPSD reruns on every benchmark at all three scales. DASH reuses the teacher and student distributions that OPSD already computes, so the gains require no additional teacher or student forward pass.
  Code: https://github.com/DBtxy/DASH-OPSD

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DASH, a method that improves on-policy self-distillation for RL with verifiable rewards by adapting token-level supervision weights based on how teacher–student divergences evolve over time, leading to better mathematical reasoning performance without extra compute.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves LLM reasoning but relies on sparse, sequence-level signals, making learning inefficient. On-policy self-distillation adds dense token-level supervision from a stronger teacher, but it treats all local divergences equally, ignoring their temporal context in the rollout. This underuses the temporal structure of autoregressive generation and limits how well the student can learn from the teacher’s distributional guidance.
AI.method: The authors analyze standard OPSD and identify that it cannot adapt token-level weights to the realized sequence of teacher–student divergences. They propose DASH (Divergence-Adaptive Supervision Horizons), which compares each local distillation signal to the sequence-level mean divergence, maps this gap to an adaptive propagation gate, and then uses these gates to control backward multi-step aggregation of supervision. This mechanism effectively reweights token-level distillation according to how divergences evolve over the generated sequence, using only distributions already computed by OPSD.
AI.result: On three mathematical reasoning benchmarks and across three different model scales, DASH consistently outperforms carefully matched vanilla OPSD baselines on every benchmark at all scales. The method achieves these gains without any additional teacher or student forward passes beyond what OPSD already requires, indicating improved sample and compute efficiency.
AI.conclusion: DASH shows that exploiting the temporal structure of teacher–student divergences in on-policy self-distillation leads to better use of distillation signals and improved reasoning performance. By adaptively weighting token-level supervision with divergence-aware propagation horizons, DASH enhances RL with verifiable rewards at essentially no extra inference cost, suggesting a practical path for more effective training of reasoning-focused LLMs.

title: Improving the Realism of Synthetic Clinical Benchmarks Under Utility Constraints
summary:
Synthetic clinical benchmarks for enterprise AI agents can pass existing utility checks and still remain structurally unrealistic, especially in privacy-sensitive healthcare settings where operational data are hard to access. We study how to improve such benchmarks without breaking the downstream utility checks already used in practice.
  We formulate benchmark revision as utility-constrained realism improvement: dataset changes should increase realism while staying above an operational utility floor. We instantiate this idea on a care-gap benchmark derived from Synthea-generated patients exercised through demonstration electronic health record workflows and then processed by the same downstream pipeline as operational data. Realism is measured through missingness structure, simplicity, structural plausibility, and population alignment.
  The baseline benchmark is extremely thin: sampled-pair missingness is 79.44%, only 12.75% of rows are actionable, 38.94% of patients have zero actionable measures, and top-three token concentration reaches 100.0%. Two deterministic revisions improve these panels while remaining above the current utility floor, whereas a naive densification control preserves unrealistic templating. We further show that internal benchmark realism and source fidelity to an aggregate operational reference are related but distinct objectives. These results suggest that synthetic benchmark quality should be optimized explicitly, with utility treated as one constraint rather than as sufficient evidence of realism.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a way to systematically make synthetic clinical benchmarks more realistic without reducing their practical utility for evaluating AI systems.
AI.motivation: Existing synthetic clinical benchmarks used to test enterprise AI agents can pass current utility checks (i.e., they are usable for existing evaluation pipelines) but still be structurally unrealistic compared with real operational healthcare data. In privacy-sensitive settings, access to real data is limited, so high-quality synthetic benchmarks are crucial. The authors are motivated to find a principled way to improve the realism of these synthetic datasets while ensuring they still work with existing downstream evaluation tools and do not fall below a minimum acceptable utility level used in practice.
AI.method: The authors formalize benchmark revision as a utility-constrained realism improvement problem: modify the dataset to increase realism subject to staying above an operational utility floor (a minimum threshold of performance on existing utility checks). They instantiate this on a care-gap detection benchmark built from Synthea-generated synthetic patients, which are passed through demonstration EHR workflows and then processed by the same downstream pipeline as real operational data. They define and measure realism along several dimensions: missingness structure, simplicity, structural plausibility, and population alignment. They compare a baseline benchmark to several revised versions: two deterministic revision strategies designed to improve realism, and a naive densification control that adds data but preserves templated, unrealistic structure.
AI.result: The baseline synthetic benchmark is shown to be very unrealistic: very high missingness (79.44% sampled-pair missingness), few actionable rows (12.75%), many patients with no actionable measures (38.94%), and extreme token concentration (top-three token concentration at 100%). The two deterministic revision approaches substantially improve these realism metrics while maintaining performance above the current operational utility floor. In contrast, the naive densification approach fails to improve structural realism and maintains unrealistic templating. The authors also empirically demonstrate that internal benchmark realism and fidelity of the synthetic data to an aggregate operational reference dataset are correlated but ultimately distinct optimization objectives.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic benchmark realism cannot be assumed merely because a benchmark passes existing utility checks; utility alone is not sufficient evidence of realism. Benchmark construction should explicitly optimize for data realism under a utility constraint, rather than treating current utility metrics as proxies for quality. This reframing highlights the need for principled, multi-dimensional realism criteria and suggests that healthcare organizations should invest in systematic optimization of synthetic benchmarks if they wish to use them reliably to evaluate enterprise AI agents.

title: The Illusion of Visual Tool-Use: A Causal Audit of Thinking with Images
summary: The "thinking-with-images" paradigm equips multimodal LLMs with active visual operations such as crop-and-zoom. However, models using these operations often achieve only marginal or negative gains over direct inference at substantially higher token cost. They may also repeatedly crop irrelevant regions and fail on questions that direct inference answers correctly. We ask whether the returned visual evidence causally affects the answer. To answer this question, we formulate visual tool-use as a causal graph that separates observation-mediated paths from action-induced shortcuts. We then audit it through interventions at the three levels: policy (comparing tool-use with direct inference), trajectory (corrupting all observations during rollout), and step (counterfactually replacing one individual observation under a fixed prefix). Our step-level estimand, Visual Evidence Gain, isolates the contribution of each returned observation. Across six representative models and five fine-grained perception benchmarks, we uncover policy miscalibration with two failure modes. In Calling Without Looking, returned observations have no causal effect on the answer. In Looking Without Planning, observations are informative but the call schedule is incoherent. A trajectory-level diagnostic decomposes the policy-level accuracy gain and shows that the gain is concentrated in a Calibrated minority. We term this discrepancy the illusion of visual tool-use: despite aggregate accuracy gains, visual tool-use is not causally effective across a broad range of rollouts. The code is available at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/CauAudit.

AI.tldr: The paper audits whether visual tool-use (like crop-and-zoom) in multimodal LLMs truly causes better answers, finding that observed accuracy gains often do not come from the visual evidence itself.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs can actively manipulate images using tools such as cropping and zooming, but these capabilities bring high token cost and often yield only marginal or even negative performance gains. Moreover, models sometimes worsen answers they would have gotten right with direct inference, suggesting that tool calls may not be effectively using visual evidence. The authors are motivated to rigorously test whether these tool-returned observations causally influence the final answer, rather than simply correlating with improved accuracy, and to understand where and how current tool-use policies fail.
AI.method: The authors formalize visual tool-use as a causal graph that separates observation-mediated causal paths (where visual evidence genuinely informs the answer) from action-induced shortcuts (where policy decisions or artifacts, not evidence, drive outcomes). They then perform a three-level causal audit: (1) policy level: compare tool-use runs against direct inference runs; (2) trajectory level: corrupt all observations during the rollout to see how much performance depends on real visual evidence; and (3) step level: define a counterfactual metric, Visual Evidence Gain, by replacing a single returned observation under a fixed prefix and measuring its causal contribution to the answer. They run these diagnostics across six multimodal models and five fine-grained perception benchmarks.
AI.result: The analysis reveals significant policy miscalibration across models. At the step level, many tool calls yield observations that have little or no causal impact on the final answer, even when aggregate accuracy with tools appears higher than without tools. Two main failure modes are identified: (1) Calling Without Looking, where the model invokes tools but the resulting observations do not causally influence the answer; and (2) Looking Without Planning, where the visual observations are informative but the timing and selection of tool calls is incoherent, so the information is poorly exploited. Trajectory-level diagnostics show that most of the policy-level accuracy gains from tool use are concentrated in a small subset of rollouts that are well calibrated, while many others see no effective use of visual evidence.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that current multimodal LLMs exhibit an “illusion of visual tool-use”: even when aggregate accuracy improves with visual tools, much of this gain does not stem from the causal influence of visual evidence across rollouts. Instead, tool-use policies are often miscalibrated, with frequent uninformative calls or poorly planned observation schedules. The proposed causal auditing framework, including the Visual Evidence Gain metric and trajectory-level diagnostics, provides a principled way to diagnose and quantify when and how visual tools genuinely contribute to model predictions. This work suggests that future efforts should focus less on adding tools and more on learning calibrated policies that use visual evidence causally and efficiently.

title: QuanTiMedAI: Quantum-Enhanced Time-Series Model guided by Agentic AI for Cardiac Arrest Mortality Prediction
summary: Cardiac arrest remains one of the most lethal conditions encountered in intensive care units. Despite the growing availability of electronic health record data, existing mortality prediction studies in this population largely depend on static summaries derived from early admission. Such approaches ignore the temporal progression of physiological deterioration and recovery that unfolds throughout a patient's ICU stay. To address this limitation, we introduce QuanTiMedAI, a quantum-agentic framework developed for cardiac arrest mortality prediction using agentic AI guided quantum enhancement time series model. The proposed system combines an agentic large language model (LLM) for clinically informed feature discovery with a compact quantum recurrent network for temporality aware mortality prediction. Our findings demonstrate that agentic LLM-guided feature selection consistently outperforms conventional feature selection approaches, and the proposed quantum architecture achieves competitive predictive performance through nonlinear feature enhancement while keeping the number of parameters very low. Through extensive experimentation on a MIMIC-IV cohort of cardiac arrest patients, QuanTiMedAI's quantum-enhanced architecture attains an AUROC of 0.852 using only 605 parameters, an improvement of approximately 2.9\% over a current state-of-the-art baseline for this task. A structured ablation study systematically validates the contribution of each architectural design choice. These results show that quantum-enhanced sequential modeling can exceed classical recurrent networks while using substantially fewer parameters.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes QuanTiMedAI, a quantum-enhanced, agentic-AI-driven time-series model for ICU cardiac arrest mortality prediction, achieving strong accuracy with very few parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing ICU mortality prediction models for cardiac arrest patients mainly use static, early-admission summaries and ignore the evolving temporal dynamics of patients’ physiological states. With rich EHR time-series now available, there is a need for models that (1) exploit temporal progression and (2) remain parameter-efficient, while also leveraging clinical insight for feature selection. The authors aim to build a system that better captures temporal patterns of deterioration and recovery, guided by clinically meaningful features and enhanced via quantum-inspired modeling.
AI.method: QuanTiMedAI integrates two key components: (1) an agentic large language model used as a clinical copilot for feature discovery and selection, where the LLM guides which EHR variables are most clinically relevant for mortality prediction; and (2) a compact quantum recurrent network that performs temporally aware mortality prediction, using quantum-inspired/nonlinear transformations to model time-series data with very few parameters. The model is trained and evaluated on a MIMIC-IV cohort of cardiac arrest ICU patients and compared against state-of-the-art classical baselines. A structured ablation study is conducted to isolate the impact of each architectural choice, including LLM-guided feature selection and the quantum recurrent design.
AI.result: On the MIMIC-IV cardiac arrest cohort, QuanTiMedAI achieves an AUROC of 0.852 using only 605 trainable parameters. This performance is about 2.9% better than a strong state-of-the-art baseline for the same task. The LLM-guided feature selection consistently surpasses standard feature selection techniques, and the quantum recurrent architecture delivers competitive or superior predictive performance with drastically reduced parameter count. Ablation experiments confirm that both the agentic LLM feature selection and the quantum-enhanced sequential modeling materially contribute to the performance gains.
AI.conclusion: QuanTiMedAI demonstrates that quantum-enhanced sequential modeling, coupled with agentic LLM-guided feature discovery, can improve mortality prediction for cardiac arrest ICU patients while using a very small number of parameters. The work suggests that quantum-inspired recurrent networks can outperform classical recurrent models in this setting, particularly in terms of parameter efficiency, and that integrating clinically informed, LLM-driven feature selection is a powerful way to exploit EHR time-series data. This framework could be extended to other ICU prediction tasks where temporal dynamics and model compactness are important.

title: Bias Analysis of L2 Speaking Assessment Systems Using Concept Activation Vectors
summary: Automatic speaking assessment systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings to mark second language (L2) learners' speaking tests, making it critical to show that their scores depend on speaking proficiency rather than irrelevant speaker attributes such as first language (L1) or age. Transformer-based foundation models have improved the accuracy of these L2 speaking graders, but their black-box representations make fairness and interpretability analysis more difficult. Building on prior work that used Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to detect bias towards unwanted attributes (`concepts') in feature-based graders, we extend CAV-based analysis to two neural speaking assessment systems: a text-based BERT grader and a speech-and-text multimodal grader based on Whisper. CAVs represent human-interpretable concepts as directions in a model's activation space, allowing us to distinguish between whether a concept is encoded in a model's internal representations and whether it influences the predicted score, the latter quantified using a gradient-based sensitivity metric. Since CAVs rely on linear separability, which is less likely in complex neural embedding spaces, we also investigate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide cleaner concept directions by learning CAVs in a sparse latent space and mapping them back to activation space. Our analysis shows that concept recoverability depends strongly on the representation and architecture being probed, rather than on the concept alone. Sensitivity to concepts is also architecture-dependent. SAEs make concepts more linearly recoverable, but attenuate the original activation-space sensitivity, especially in low-dimensional layers. These findings highlight the need to distinguish concept recoverability from concept influence when auditing bias in speaking assessment systems.

AI.tldr: The paper audits fairness in neural L2 speaking assessment systems by using concept activation methods to see whether non-proficiency attributes (like L1, age) are encoded and actually influence scores, comparing raw activations vs. sparse-autoencoder-transformed spaces.
AI.motivation: Automatic L2 speaking graders are now used in high-stakes exams, so it is crucial to ensure their scores reflect true speaking proficiency rather than irrelevant attributes (e.g., first language, age). Transformer-based models boost accuracy but are harder to interpret, making it challenging to diagnose and mitigate bias. Existing CAV-based bias analyses focus on feature-based models, leaving a gap for modern neural, especially multimodal, systems.
AI.method: The authors apply Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to two neural graders: a text-only BERT grader and a multimodal Whisper-based grader. They construct CAVs for human-interpretable attributes (concepts) and probe model layers to assess (1) whether concepts are linearly recoverable from internal representations and (2) whether these concept directions influence predicted scores, via a gradient-based sensitivity metric. They further train sparse autoencoders on model activations, learn CAVs in the sparse latent space, and map them back to the original activation space to test if sparsity yields cleaner, more interpretable concept directions.
AI.result: Concept recoverability varies strongly by model architecture and layer, indicating that whether a concept is detectable depends more on representation space than on the concept itself. Sensitivity of the predicted scores to concepts is also architecture-dependent. Introducing sparse autoencoders makes concepts more linearly separable (improving recoverability) but weakens the measured sensitivity of scores to these concepts, particularly in low-dimensional layers, suggesting a trade-off between linear interpretability and preserving the original influence structure.
AI.conclusion: Bias auditing in neural speaking assessment systems must carefully distinguish between (a) whether a concept can be recovered from internal representations and (b) whether it actually affects scoring decisions. Architecture and representation choices critically shape both aspects. Sparse autoencoders can aid interpretability by enhancing linear concept recoverability but may distort or attenuate the original influence of concepts on outputs, so they should be used with caution when drawing fairness conclusions.

title: TRAJDEBUG: Tracing Error Lifecycle to Identify Critical Failures in Long-Horizon Agent Trajectories
summary: LLM-based agentic systems have shown remarkable capabilities in complex domains, while suffering from cascading errors and difficulty in debugging.
